mastodyny.c: Mastodyny Mastodynia ‖Mas`to*dyn"i*a (?), Mas*tod"y*ny (?), n. [NL. mastodynia, fr. Gr. masto`s the breast +? pain.] (Med.) Pain occuring in the mamma or female breast, -- a form of neuralgia.

mastoid.c: Mastoid Mas"toid (?), a. [Gr.?; masto`s the breast + e'i^dos form: cf. F. mastoïde.] (Anat.) (a) Resembling the nipple or the breast; -- applied specifically to a process of the temporal bone behind the ear. (b) Pertaining to, or in the region of, the mastoid process; mastoidal.

mastoiditis.c: Mastoiditis Mas`toid*i*tis (?), n. [NL. See Mastoid, and -itis.] (Med.) Inflammation in the mastoid process of the temporal bone.

mastology.c: Mastology Mas*tol"o*gy (?), n. [Gr. masto`s the breast + -logy: cf. F. mastologie.] The natural history of Mammalia.

masturbation.c: masturbation mas`tur*ba"tion (?), n. [L. masturbatus, p. p. of masturbari to practice onanism: cf. F. masturbation.] The act of masturbating; sexual self-gratification; onanism.

masty.c: Masty Mast"y (?), a. [See 1st Mast.] Full of mast; abounding in acorns, etc.

masula.c: Masula boat Ma*su"la boat` (?). Same as Masoola boat.

mat.c: Mat Mat (măt), n. [Cf. Matte.] A name given by coppersmiths to an alloy of copper, tin, iron, etc., usually called white metal. [Written also matt.]
Mat Mat, a. [OF. See 4th Mate.] Cast down; dejected; overthrown; slain. [Obs.]

Mat Mat, n. [AS. matt, meatt, fr. L. matta a mat made of rushes.] 1. A thick flat fabric of sedge, rushes, flags, husks, straw, hemp, or similar material, placed on the floor and used for wiping and cleaning shoes at the door, for covering the floor of a hall or room to protect its surface, and for other purposes.
Mat Mat, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Matted (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Matting.] 1. To cover or lay with mats. Evelyn.
Mat Mat, v. i. To grow thick together; to become interwoven or felted together like a mat, as hair when wetted with a sticky substance; as, a long-haired cat whose fur is matted.

matabeles.c: Matabeles Matabele { Mat`a*be"le (?), or Mat`a*be"les (?) }, prop. n. pl., sing. Matabele. [Written also Matabili.] (Ethnol.) A warlike South African Kaffir tribe.

matachin.c: Matachin ‖Ma`ta*chin" (?), n. [Sp.] An old dance with swords and bucklers; a sword dance.

mataco.c: Mataco Mat"a*co (?), n. (Zool.) The three-banded armadillo (Tolypeutis tricinctus). See Illust. under Loricata.

matadore.c: Matadore Matador { Mat"a*dor, Mat"a*dore} (?), n. [Sp. matador, prop., a killer, fr. matar to kill, L. mactare to sacrifice, kill.] 1. The killer; the man appointed to kill the bull in bullfights; a bullfighter; a toreador.

matagasse.c: Matagasse Mat`a*gasse" (?), n. (Zool.) A shrike or butcher bird; -- called also mattages. [Prov. Eng.]

matajuelo.c: Matajuelo Ma`ta*jue"lo (mä`tȧ*hwā"lō; 239), n. [Cf. Sp. matajudío a kind of fish.] A large squirrel fish (Holocentrus ascensionis) of Florida and the West Indies.
Matajuelo blanco Ma`ta*jue"lo blan"co (mä`tȧ*hwā"lō bläṉ"kō). [Sp. blanco white.] A West Indian food fish (Malacanthus plumieri) related to the tilefish.

matamata.c: Matamata ‖Ma`ta*ma"ta (?), n. [Pg.] (Zool.) The bearded tortoise (Chelys fimbriata) of South American rivers.

matanza.c: Matanza Ma*tan"za (?), n. [Sp., slaughter, fr. matar to kill.] A place where animals are slaughtered for their hides and tallow. [Western U. S.]

match.c: Match Match (măch), n. [OE. macche, F. mèche, F. mèche, fr. L. myxa a lamp nozzle, Gr. my`xa mucus, nostril, a lamp nozzle. Cf. Mucus.] Anything used for catching and retaining or communicating fire, made of some substance which takes fire readily, or remains burning some time; esp., a small strip or splint of wood or cardboard dipped at one end in a substance which can be easily ignited by friction, as a preparation of phosphorus or chlorate of potassium.

Match Match, n. [OE. macche, AS. gemaecca; akin to gemaca, and to OS. gimako, OHG. gimah fitting, suitable, convenient, Icel. mark suitable, maki mate, Sw. make, Dan. mage; all from the root of E. make, v. See Make mate, and Make, v., and cf. Mate an associate.]
Match Match, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Matched (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Matching.] 1. To be a mate or match for; to be able to complete with; to rival successfully; to equal.
Match Match, v. i. 1. To be united in marriage; to mate.
Match game Match game. A game arranged as a test of superiority; also, one of a series of such games.
Match play Match play. (Golf) Play in which the score is reckoned by counting the holes won or lost by each side; -- distinguished from medal play.

matchable.c: Matchable Match"a*ble (?), a. Capable of being matched; comparable on equal conditions; adapted to being joined together; correspondent. -- Match"a*ble*ness, n.

matchcoat.c: Match-coat Match"-coat` (?), n. A coat made of match-cloth.

matcher.c: Matcher Match"er (?), n. One who, or that which, matches; a matching machine. See under 3d Match.

matchlock.c: Matchlock Match"lock` (?), n. An old form of gunlock containing a match for firing the priming; hence, a musket fired by means of a match.

matchmaker.c: Matchmaker Match"mak`er (?), n. 1. One who makes matches for burning or kinding.

matchmaking.c: Matchmaking Match"mak`ing, n. 1. The act or process of making matches for kindling or burning.
Matchmaking Match"mak`ing, a. Busy in making or contriving marriages; as, a matchmaking woman.

mate.c: Mate ‖Ma"te (mä"ta), n. [Sp.] The Paraguay tea, being the dried leaf of the Brazilian holly (Ilex Paraguensis). The infusion has a pleasant odor, with an agreeable bitter taste, and is much used for tea in South America.
Mate Mate (māt), n. [F. mat, abbrev. fr. échec et mat. See Checkmate.] (Chess) Same as Checkmate.
Mate Mate, v. t. [F. mater to fatigue, enfeeble, humiliate, checkmate. See Mate checkmate.]

Mate Mate, n. [Perhaps for older make a companion; cf. also OD. maet companion, mate, D. maat. Cf. Make a companion, Match a mate.] 1. One who customarily associates with another; a companion; an associate; any object which is associated or combined with a similar object.
Mate Mate, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Mated; p. pr. & vb. n. Mating.] 1. To match; to marry.
Mate Mate, v. i. To be or become a mate or mates, especially in sexual companionship; as, some birds mate for life; this bird will not mate with that one.

matelasse.c: Matelasse ‖Mate`las`sé" (mȧ`lȧ`sa"), a. [F., p.p. of matelasser to cushion, to cover as with a mattress, fr. matelas mattress. See Mattress.] Ornamented by means of an imitation or suggestion of quilting, the surface being marked by depressed lines which form squares or lozenges in relief; as, matelassé silks.
Matelasse ‖Mate`las`sé", n. A quilted ornamented dress fabric of silk or silk and wool.

mateless.c: Mateless Mate"less, a. [Cf. Matchless.] Having no mate.

matelotte.c: Matelotte Matelote { Mat"e*lote (măt"e*lōt), Mat"e*lotte (măt"e*lŏt) }, n. [F. matelote, fr. matelot a sailor; properly, a dish such as a sailors prepare.] 1. A stew, commonly of fish, flavored with wine, and served with a wine sauce containing onions, mushrooms, etc.

mateology.c: Mateology Ma`te*ol"o*gy (mā`te*ŏl"o*jy̆), n. [Gr. mataiologi`a; ma`taios useless, vain + lo`gos discourse: cf. F. matéologie.] A vain, unprofitable discourse or inquiry. [R.]

mateotechny.c: Mateotechny Ma`te*o*tech"ny (mā`te*o*tĕk"ny̆), n. [Gr. mataiotechni`a; ma`taios vain + te`chnh art, science.] Any unprofitable science. [Obs.]

mater.c: Mater ‖Ma"ter (?), n. [L., mother. See Mother.] See Alma mater, Dura mater, and Pia mater.

material.c: Material Ma*te"ri*al (?), a. [L. materialis, fr. materia stuff, matter: cf. F. matériel. See Matter, and cf. Matériel.]
Material Ma*te"ri*al, n. The substance or matter of which anything is made or may be made.
Material Ma*te"ri*al, v. t. To form from matter; to materialize. [Obs.] Sir T. Browne.

materialism.c: Materialism Ma*te"ri*al*ism (?), n. [Cf. F. matérialisme.] 1. The doctrine of materialists; materialistic views and tenets; called also philosophical materialism.

materialist.c: Materialist Ma*te"ri*al*ist (mȧ*tē"rĭ*ail*ĭst), n. [Cf. F. matérialiste.] 1. One who denies the existence of spiritual substances or agents, and maintains that spiritual phenomena, so called, are the result of some peculiar organization of matter. A believer in philosophical materialism.

materialistical.c: Materialistical Materialistic { Ma*te`ri*al*is"tic (?), Ma*te`ri*al*is"tic*al (?), } a. Of or pertaining to materialism or materialists; of the nature of materialism.

materialization.c: Materialization Ma*te`ri*al*i*za"tion (?), n. The act of materializing, or the state of being materialized.

materialize.c: Materialize Ma*te"ri*al*ize (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Materialized (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Materializing (?).] [Cf. F. matérialiser.] 1. To invest with material characteristics; to make perceptible to the senses; hence, to present to the mind through the medium of material objects.
Materialize Ma*te"ri*al*ize, v. i. 1. To appear as a material form; to take substantial shape. [Colloq.]

materially.c: Materially Ma*te"ri*al*ly, adv. 1. In the state of matter.

materialness.c: Materialness Ma*te"ri*al*ness, n. The state of being material.

materia.c: Materia medica ‖Ma*te"ri*a med"i*ca (?). [L. See Matter, and Medical.] 1. Material or substance used in the composition of remedies; -- a general term for all substances used as curative agents in medicine.

materiated.c: Materiated Materiate { Ma*te"ri*ate (?), Ma*te"ri*a`ted (?), } a. [L. materiatus, p. p. of materiare to build of wood.] Consisting of matter. [Obs.] Bacon.

materiation.c: Materiation Ma*te`ri*a"tion (?), n. [L. materiatio woodwork.] Act of forming matter. [Obs.] Sir T. Browne.

materiel.c: Materiel ‖Ma`té`ri`el" (?), n. [F. See Material.] Those objects in a complex system which constitute the materials, or instruments employed, in distinction from the personnel, or men; for example, the buildings, libraries, and apparatus of a college, in distinction from its officers; -- used in a collective sense.

maternal.c: Maternal Ma*ter"nal (?), a. [F. maternel, L. maternus, fr. mater mother. See Mother.] Of or pertaining to a mother; becoming to a mother; motherly; as, maternal love; maternal tenderness.

maternally.c: Maternally Ma*ter"nal*ly, adv. In a motherly manner.

maternity.c: Maternity Ma*ter"ni*ty (?), n. [F. maternité, LL. maternitas.] 1. The state of being a mother; motherhood.

matfelon.c: Matfelon Mat"fel*on (?), n. [W. madfelen.] (Bot.) The knapweed (Centaurea nigra).

math.c: Math Math (măth), n. [AS. mǣð; akin to māwan to mow, G. mahd math. See Mow to cut (grass).] A mowing, or that which is gathered by mowing; -- chiefly used in composition; as, an aftermath. [Obs.]

mathematic.c: Mathematic Math`e*mat"ic (?), a. [F. mathématique, L. mathematicus, Gr.? disposed to learn, belonging to learning or the sciences, especially to mathematics, fr.? that which is learned, learning, pl.? things learned, learning, science, especially mathematical science, fr.?,?, to learn; akin to E. mind. See Mind.] See Mathematical.

mathematical.c: Mathematical Math`e*mat"ic*al (?), a. [See Mathematic.] Of or pertaining to mathematics; according to mathematics; hence, theoretically precise; accurate; as, mathematical geography; mathematical instruments; mathematical exactness. -- Math`e*mat"ic*al*ly, adv.

mathematician.c: Mathematician Math`e*ma*ti"cian (?), n. [Cf. F. mathématicien.] One versed in mathematics.

mathematics.c: Mathematics Math`e*mat"ics (?), n. [F. mathématiques, pl., L. mathematica, sing., Gr.? (sc.?) science. See Mathematic, and -ics.] That science, or class of sciences, which treats of the exact relations existing between quantities or magnitudes, and of the methods by which, in accordance with these relations, quantities sought are deducible from other quantities known or supposed; the science of spatial and quantitative relations.

mathes.c: Mathes Math"es (?), n. [Perh. corrupted fr. L. anthemis camomile, Gr.?.] (Bot.) The mayweed. Cf. Maghet.

mathesis.c: Mathesis ‖Ma*the"sis (?), n. [L., fr. Gr.?, from?,?, to learn.] Learning; especially, mathematics. [R.] Pope.

mathurin.c: Mathurin Math"u*rin (?), n. (R. C. Ch.) See Trinitarian.

matico.c: Matico Ma*ti"co (?), n. (Bot.) A Peruvian plant (Piperelongatum or Artanthe elongatum), allied to the pepper, the leaves of which are used as a styptic and astringent.

matie.c: Matie Mat"ie (?), n. (Zool.) A fat herring with undeveloped roe. [Written also matty.] [Eng. & Scot.]

matin.c: Matin Mat"in (?), n. [F. fr. L. matutinum the morning, matutinus of the morning, Matuta the goddess of the morning. See Matutinal.] 1. Morning. [Obs.] Shak.
matin mat"in, a. Of or pertaining to the morning, or to matins; used in the morning; matutinal.

matinal.c: matinal mat"in*al (?), a. Relating to the morning, or to matins; matutinal.

matinee.c: matinee mat`i*née" (?), n. [F., from matin. See Matin.] A reception, or a musical or dramatic entertainment, held in the daytime. See Soirée.

matrass.c: matrass ma*trass" (?), n. [F. matras; perh. so called from its long narrow neck; cf. OF. matras large arrow, L. materis, mataris, matara, a Celtic javelin, pike; of Celtic origin.] (Chem.) A round-bottomed glass flask having a long neck; a bolthead.

matriarch.c: matriarch ma"tri*arch (?), n. [L. mater mother + -arch.] 1. The mother and ruler of a family or of her descendants; a ruler by maternal right.

matriarchal.c: matriarchal ma`tri*ar"chal (?), a. Of or pertaining to a matriarch; governed by a matriarch or matriarchs; as, a matriarchal society.

matriarchate.c: Matriarchate Ma"tri*ar"chate (?), n. The office or jurisdiction of a matriarch; a matriarchal form of government.

matrice.c: Matrice Ma"trice (?), n. [Cf. F. matrice. See Matrix.] See Matrix.

matricidal.c: Matricidal Mat"ri*ci`dal (?), a. Of or pertaining to matricide.

matricide.c: Matricide Mat"ri*cide (?), n. [L. matricidium; mater mother + coedere to kill, slay: cf. F. matricide. See Mother, and cf. Homicide.] 1. The murder of a mother by her son or daughter.

matriculate.c: Matriculate Ma*tric"u*late (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Matriculated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Matriculating.] [L. matricula a public roll or register, dim. of matrix a mother, in respect to propagation, also, a public register. See Matrix.] To enroll; to enter in a register; specifically, to enter or admit to membership in a body or society, particularly in a college or university, by enrolling the name in a register.
Matriculate Ma*tric"u*late, v. i. To go though the process of admission to membership, as by examination and enrollment, in a society or college.
Matriculate Ma*tric"u*late (?), a. Matriculated. Skelton. -- n. One who is matriculated. Arbuthnot.

matriculation.c: Matriculation Ma*tric`u*la"tion (?), n. The act or process of matriculating; the state of being matriculated.

matrimonial.c: Matrimonial Mat`ri*mo"ni*al (?), a. [L. matrimonialis: cf. F. matrimonial. See Matrimony.] Of or pertaining to marriage; derived from marriage; connubial; nuptial; hymeneal; as, matrimonial rights or duties.

matrimonially.c: Matrimonially Mat`ri*mo"ni*al*ly, adv. In a matrimonial manner.

matrimony.c: Matrimony Mat"ri*mo*ny (?), n. [OE. matrimoine, through Old French, fr. L. matrimonium, fr. mater mother. See Mother.] 1. The union of man and woman as husband and wife; the nuptial state; marriage; wedlock.

matrix.c: matrix ma"trix (mā"trĭks), n.; pl. Matrices (măt"rĭ*sēz). [L., fr. mater mother. See Mother, and cf. Matrice.]

matron.c: Matron Ma"tron (?), n. [F. matrone, L. matrona, fr. mater mother. See Mother.] 1. A wife or a widow, especially, one who has borne children; a woman of staid or motherly manners.

matronage.c: Matronage Mat"ron*age (?), n. 1. The state of a matron.

matronal.c: Matronal Mat"ron*al (?), a. [L. matronalis.] Of or pertaining to a matron; suitable to an elderly lady or to a married woman; grave; motherly.

matronhood.c: Matronhood Ma"tron*hood (?), n. The state of being a matron.

matronize.c: Matronize Mat"ron*ize (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Matronized (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Matronizing (?).] 1. To make a matron of; to make matronlike.

matronlike.c: Matronlike Ma"tron*like` (?), a. Like a matron; sedate; grave; matronly.

matronly.c: Matronly Ma"tron*ly, a. 1. Advanced in years; elderly.

matronymic.c: Matronymic Mat`ro*nym"ic (?), n. [L. mater mother + -nymic, as in patronimic.] See Metronymic.

matross.c: Matross Ma*tross" (?), n. [D. matroos, fr. F. matelot.] (Mil.) Formerly, in the British service, a gunner or a gunner's mate; one of the soldiers in a train of artillery, who assisted the gunners in loading, firing, and sponging the guns. [Obs.]

mattages.c: Mattages Mat`ta*ges" (?), n. (Zool.) A shrike or butcher bird; -- written also matagasse. [Prov. Eng.]

mattamore.c: Mattamore Mat"ta*more` (?), n. [F. matamore, from Ar. maṭmōra.] A subterranean repository for wheat.

matte.c: Matte Matte (măt), n. [F. matte; cf. F. mat, masc., matte, fem., faint, dull, dim; -- said of metals. See Mate checkmate.] 1. (Metallurgy) A partly reduced copper sulphide, obtained by alternately roasting and melting copper ore in separating the metal from associated iron ores, and called coarse metal, fine metal, etc., according to the grade of fineness. On the exterior it is dark brown or black, but on a fresh surface is yellow or bronzy in color.

matted.c: Matted Mat"ted (?), a. [See Matte.] Having a dull surface; lusterless; unburnished; same as matte; as, matted gold leaf or gilding.
Matted Mat"ted, a. [See 3d Mat.] 1. Covered with a mat or mats; as, a matted floor.

matter.c: Matter Mat"ter (?), n. [OE. matere, F. matière, fr. L. materia; perh. akin to L. mater mother. Cf. Mother, Madeira, Material.] 1. That of which anything is composed; constituent substance; material; the material or substantial part of anything; the constituent elements of conception; that into which a notion may be analyzed; the essence; the pith; the embodiment.
Matter Mat"ter (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Mattered (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Mattering.] 1. To be of importance; to import; to signify.
Matter Mat"ter, v. t. To regard as important; to take account of; to care for. [Obs.]

matterless.c: Matterless Mat"ter*less, a. 1. Not being, or having, matter; as, matterless spirits. Davies (Wit's Pilgr.).

matteroffact.c: Matter-of-fact Mat"ter-of-fact" (?), a. Adhering to facts; not turning aside from absolute realities; not fanciful or imaginative; commonplace; dry.

mattery.c: Mattery Mat"ter*y (?), a. 1. Generating or containing pus; purulent.

matting.c: Matting Mat"ting (?), n. [From Mat, v. t. & i.] 1. The act of interweaving or tangling together so as to make a mat; the process of becoming matted.
Matting Mat"ting, n. [See Matte.] A dull, lusterless surface in certain of the arts, as gilding, metal work, glassmaking, etc.

mattock.c: Mattock Mat"tock (?), n. [AS. mattuc; cf. W. matog.] An implement for digging and grubbing. The head has two long steel blades, one like an adz and the other like a narrow ax or the point of a pickax.

mattoid.c: Mattoid Mat"toid (?), n. [It. matto mad (cf. L. mattus, matus, drunk) + -oid.] A person of congenitally abnormal mind bordering on insanity or degeneracy.

mattoir.c: Mattoir ‖Mat*toir" (?), n. [F. matoir.] (Engraving) A kind of coarse punch with a rasplike face, used for making a rough surface on etching ground, or on the naked copper, the effect after biting being very similar to stippled lines.

mattowacca.c: Mattowacca Mat`to*wac"ca (?), n. [Indian name.] (Zool.) An American clupeoid fish (Clupea mediocris), similar to the shad in habits and appearance, but smaller and less esteemed for food; -- called also hickory shad, tailor shad, fall herring, and shad herring.

mattress.c: Mattress Mat"tress (?), n. [OF. materas, F. matelas, LL. matratium; cf. Sp. & Pg. almadraque, Pr. almatrac; all from Ar. maṭrah a place where anything is thrown, what is thrown under something, fr. ṭaraha to throw.]

maturant.c: Maturant Mat"u*rant (?), n. [L. maturans, p. pr. See Maturate.] (Med.) A medicine, or application, which promotes suppuration.

maturate.c: Maturate Mat"u*rate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Maturated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Maturating (?).] [L. maturatus, p. p. of maturare to make ripe, fr. maturus ripe, mature. See Mature, v. & a.] 1. To bring to ripeness or maturity; to ripen.
Maturate Mat"u*rate, v. i. To ripen; to become mature; specifically, to suppurate.

maturation.c: Maturation Mat`u*ra"tion (?), n. [L. maturatio a hastening: cf. F. maturation.] The process of bringing, or of coming, to maturity; hence, specifically, the process of suppurating perfectly; the formation of pus or matter.

maturative.c: Maturative Mat"u*ra*tive (?), a. [Cf. F. maturatif.] Conducing to ripeness or maturity; hence, conducing to suppuration.
Maturative Mat"u*ra*tive, n. (Med.) A remedy promoting maturation; a maturant.

mature.c: Mature Ma*ture" (?), a. [Compar. Maturer (?); superl. Maturest.] [L. maturus; prob. akin to E. matin.]

Mature Ma*ture" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Matured (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Maturing.] [See Maturate, Mature.] To bring or hasten to maturity; to promote ripeness in; to ripen; to complete; as, to mature one's plans. Bacon.
Mature Ma*ture", v. i. 1. To advance toward maturity; to become ripe; as, wine matures by age; the judgment matures by age and experience.

maturely.c: Maturely Ma*ture"ly, adv. 1. In a mature manner; with ripeness; completely.

matureness.c: Matureness Ma*ture"ness, n. The state or quality of being mature; maturity.

maturer.c: Maturer Ma*tur"er (?), n. One who brings to maturity.

maturescent.c: Maturescent Mat`u*res"cent (?), a. [L. maturescens, p. pr. of maturescere to become ripe, v. incho. from maturus. See Mature, a.] Approaching maturity.

maturing.c: Maturing Ma*tur"ing (?), a. Approaching maturity; as, maturing fruits; maturing notes of hand.

maturity.c: Maturity Ma*tu"ri*ty (?), n. [L. maturitas: cf. F. maturité.]

matutinal.c: Matutinal Mat`u*ti"nal (?), a. [L. matutinalis, matutinus: cf. F. matutinal. See Matin.] Of or pertaining to the morning; early.

matweed.c: Matweed Mat"weed` (?), n. (Bot.) A name of several maritime grasses, as the sea sand-reed (Ammophila arundinacea) which is used in Holland to bind the sand of the seacoast dikes (see Beach grass, under Beach); also, the Lygeum Spartum, a Mediterranean grass of similar habit.

maty.c: Maty Mat"y (?), n. [Etymology uncertain.] A native house servant in India. Balfour (Cyc. of India).

matzoh.c: matzoh matzo matz"o, matz"oh (?), n.; pl. E. matzos or matzohs; Hebr. matzoth (#) [Heb. matstsōth, pl. of matstsāh unleavened.] A cake of unleavened bread eaten by the Jews at the feast of the Passover.

maucaco.c: Maucaco ‖Mau*ca"co (?), n. [From the native name.] (Zool.) A lemur; -- applied to several species, as the White-fronted, the ruffed, and the ring-tailed lemurs.

maud.c: Maud Maud (?), n. A gray plaid; -- used by shepherds in Scotland.

maudle.c: Maudle Mau"dle (?), v. t. To throw onto confusion or disorder; to render maudlin. [Obs.]

maudlin.c: Maudlin Maud"lin (?), a. [From Maudlin, a contr. of Magdalen, OE. Maudeleyne, who is drawn by painters with eyes swelled and red with weeping.] 1. Tearful; easily moved to tears; exciting to tears; excessively sentimental; weak and silly. “Maudlin eyes.” Dryden. “Maudlin eloquence.” Roscommon. “A maudlin poetess.” Pope. “Maudlin crowd.” Southey.

maudeline.c: Maudeline Maudlin { Maud"lin, Maude"line (?), } n. (Bot.) An aromatic composite herb, the costmary; also, the South European Achillea Ageratum, a kind of yarrow.

maudlinism.c: Maudlinism Maud"lin*ism (?), n. A maudlin state. Dickens.

maugre.c: Maugre Mauger { Mau"ger, Mau"gre } (mä"gẽr), prep. [OF. maugré, malgré, F. malgré. See Mal-, Malice, and Agree.] In spite of; in opposition to; notwithstanding. [Archaic]
Maugre Mau"gre, v. t. To defy. [Obs.] J. Webster.

maul.c: Maul Maul (?), n. [See Mall a hammer.] A heavy wooden hammer or beetle. [Written also mall.]
Maul Maul, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Mauled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Mauling.] 1. To beat and bruise with a heavy stick or cudgel; to wound in a coarse manner.

mauling.c: Mauling Maul"ing (?), n. A severe beating with a stick, cudgel, or the fist.

maulstick.c: maul-stick maulstick maul"stick`, maul"-stick` (?), n. [G. malerstock; maler a painter + stock stick.] A stick used by painters as a rest for the hand while working. [Written also mahl-stick and mahlstick.]

maund.c: Maund Maund (?), n. [AS. mand, mond.] A hand basket. [Obs.] Herrick.
Maund Maund, n. [Hind, & Per. man.] An East Indian weight, varying in different localities from 25 to about 82 pounds avoirdupois.

maunder.c: Maunder Maund { Maund (?), Maund"er (?), } v. i. [Cf. F. mendier to beg, E. mendicant.] 1. To beg. [Obs.] B. Jonson. Beau. & Fl.
Maunder Maund"er, v. t. To utter in a grumbling manner; to mutter.

maundril.c: Maundril Maun"dril (?), n. [Cf. Mandrel.] (Coal Mining) A pick with two prongs, to pry with.

maundy.c: Maundy Maun"dy (?), n. [See Maundy Thursday.] 1. The sacrament of the Lord's Supper. [Obs.]
Maundy money Maundy coins { Maundy coins or Maundy money }. Silver coins or money of the nominal value of 1d., 2d., 3d., and 4d., struck annually for the Maundy alms.

Maundy Thursday Maun"dy Thurs"day (?). [OE. maunde a command, OF. mandé, L. mandatum, from mandare to command. See called from the ancient custom of washing the feet of the poor on this day, which was taken to be the fulfillment of the “new commandment,” John xiii. 5, 34.] (Eccl.) The Thursday in Passion week, or next before Good Friday.

maurist.c: Maurist Maur"ist (?), n. [From Maurus, the favorite disciple of St. Benedict.] A member of the Congregation of Saint Maur, an offshoot of the Benedictines, originating in France in the early part of the seventeenth century. The Maurists have been distinguished for their interest in literature.

mausolean.c: Mausolean Mau`so*le"an (?), a. [L. Mausoleus. See Mausoleum.] Pertaining to a mausoleum; monumental.

mausoleum.c: Mausoleum Mau`so*le"um (?), n.; pl. E. Mausoleums (#), L. -lea (#). [L. mausoleum, Gr.?, fr.? Mausolus, king of Caria, to whom Artemisia, his widow, erected a stately monument, one of the wonders of the ancient world.] A magnificent tomb, or stately sepulchral monument.

mauther.c: Mauther Mau"ther (mä"thẽr), n. [Cf. AS. maegþ a maid.] [Also spelled mawther, mother.] A girl; esp., a great, awkward girl; a wench. [Prov. Eng.]

mauvaniline.c: Mauvaniline Mauv`an"i*line (?), n. (Chem.) See Mauve aniline, under Mauve.

mauve.c: Mauve Mauve (mōv), n. [F., mallow, L. malva. So named from the similarity of the color to that of the petals of common mallow, Malva sylvestris. See Mallow.] A color of a delicate purple, violet, or lilac.

mauveine.c: mauveine mauve"ïne (?), n. (Chem.) An artificial organic base, obtained by oxidizing a mixture of aniline and toluidine, and valuable for the dyestuffs it forms. [Written also mauvine.]

maverick.c: Maverick Mav"er*ick (?), n. In the southwestern part of the united States, a bullock or heifer that has not been branded, and is unclaimed or wild; -- said to be from Maverick, the name of a cattle owner in Texas who neglected to brand his cattle.
Maverick Mav"er*ick (?), v. t. To take a maverick. [Western U. S.]
Maverick brand Maverick brand. A brand originated by a dishonest cattleman, who, without owning any stock, gradually accumulates a herd by finding mavericks. [Western U. S.]

mavis.c: Mavis Ma"vis (mā"vĭs), n. [F. mauvis, Arm. milvid, milfid, milc'hhouid, Corn. melhuez.] (Zool.) The European throstle or song thrush (Turdus musicus).

mavourneen.c: Mavourneen Mavournin { Ma*vour"nin, Ma*vour"neen } (mȧ*vōor"nēn), n. [Ir. mo mhuirnin my darling; mo my + mhuirnin darling.] My darling; -- an Irish term of endearment for a girl or woman. “Erin mavournin.” Campbell.

maw.c: Maw Maw (mä), n. [See Mew a gull.] (Zool.) A gull.

Maw Maw, n. [OE. mawe, AS. maga stomach; akin to D. maag, OHG. mago, G. magen, Icel. magi, Sw. mage, Dan. mave. √103.] 1. A stomach; the receptacle into which food is taken by swallowing; in birds, the craw; -- now used only of the lower animals, exept humorously or in contempt. Chaucer.
Maw Maw, n. An old game at cards. Sir A. Weldon.

mawk.c: Mawk Mawk (mäk), n. [OE. mauk, maðek, Icel. maðkr; akin to Dan. maddik, and E. mad an earthworm. See Mad, n.]

mawkin.c: Mawkin Maw"kin (?), n. See Malkin, and Maukin.

mawkish.c: Mawkish Mawk"ish, a. [Orig., maggoty. See Mawk.] 1. Apt to cause satiety or loathing; nauseous; slightly nauseating; disgusting.

mawkishly.c: Mawkishly Mawk"ish*ly, adv. In a mawkish way.

mawkishness.c: Mawkishness Mawk"ish*ness, n. The quality or state of being mawkish. J. H. Newman.

mawks.c: Mawks Mawks (?), n. A slattern; a mawk. [Prov. Eng.]

mawmet.c: Mawmet Maw"met (?), n. [Contr. fr. Mahomet.] A puppet; a doll; originally, an idol, because in the Middle Ages it was generally but falsely believed that the Muslims worshiped images representing Mohammed. [Obs.] Wyclif. Beau. & Fl.

mawmetry.c: Mawmetry Maw"met*ry (?), n. The religion of Mohammed; also, idolatry. See Mawmet. [Obs.] Chaucer.

mawmish.c: Mawmish Maw"mish (?), a. [Prov. E. maum soft, mellow, rotten; cf. OD. molm rotten wood, G. mulm.] Nauseous. [Obs.] L' Estrange.

mawseed.c: Mawseed Maw"seed` (?), n. [Cf. G. magsamen.] (Bot.) The seed of the opium poppy.

mawworm.c: Mawworm Maw"worm` (?), n. [Maw the belly + worm.] (Zool.) (a) Any intestinal worm found in the stomach, esp. the common round worm (Ascaris lumbricoides), and allied species. (b) One of the larvae of botflies of horses; a bot.

maxilla.c: Maxilla ‖Max*il"la (?), n.; pl. Maxillae (#). [L., dim. of mala jaw, jawbone.] 1. (Anat.) (a) The bone of either the upper or the under jaw. (b) The bone, or principal bone, of the upper jaw, the bone of the lower jaw being the mandible. [Now commonly used in this restricted sense.]

maxillary.c: Maxillary Maxillar { Max"il*lar (?), Max"il*la*ry (?), } a. [L. maxillaris, fr. maxilla jawbone, jaw: cf. F. maxillaire.] 1. (Anat.) Pertaining to either the upper or the lower jaw, but now usually applied to the upper jaw only. -- n. The principal maxillary bone; the maxilla.

maxilliform.c: Maxilliform Max*il"li*form (?), a. [Maxilla + -form: cf. F. maxilliforme.] Having the form, or structure, of a maxilla.

maxilliped.c: Maxilliped Max*il"li*ped (?), n. [Maxilla + L. pes, pedis, foot.] (Zool.) One of the mouth appendages of Crustacea, situated next behind the maxillae. Crabs have three pairs, but many of the lower Crustacea have but one pair of them. Called also jawfoot, and foot jaw.

maxillomandibular.c: Maxillo-mandibular Max*il`lo-man*dib"u*lar (?), a. [Maxilla + mandibular.] (Anat.) Pertaining to the maxilla and mandible; as, the maxillo-mandibular nerve.

maxillopalatine.c: Maxillo-palatine Max*il`lo-pal"a*tine (?), a. [Maxilla + palatine.] (Anat.) Pertaining to the maxillary and palatine regions of the skull; as, the maxillo-palatine process of the maxilla. Also used as n.

maxilloturbinal.c: Maxilloturbinal Max*il`lo*tur`bi*nal (?), a. [Maxilla + turbinal.] (Anat.) Pertaining to the maxillary and turbinal regions of the skull. -- n. The maxillo-turbinal, or inferior turbinate, bone.

maxim.c: Maxim Max"im (?), n. [F. maxime, L. maxima (sc. sententia), the greatest sentence, proposition, or axiom, i. e., of the greatest weight or authority, fem. fr. maximus greatest, superl. of magnus great. See Magnitude, and cf. Maximum.]
Maxim gun Max"im gun` (?). A kind of machine gun; -- named after its inventor, Hiram S. Maxim.

maximilian.c: Maximilian Max`i*mil"ian (?), n. [From the proper name.] A gold coin of Bavaria, of the value of about 13s. 6d. sterling, or about three dollars and a quarter.

maximization.c: Maximization Max`i*mi*za"tion (?), n. The act or process of increasing to the highest degree. Bentham.

maximize.c: Maximize Max"i*mize (?), v. t. [L. maximus greatest.] To increase to the highest degree. Bentham.

maximum.c: Maximum Max"i*mum (?), n.; pl. Maxima (#). [L., neut. from maximus the greatest. See Maxim.] The greatest quantity or value attainable in a given case; or, the greatest value attained by a quantity which first increases and then begins to decrease; the highest point or degree; -- opposed to minimum.
Maximum Max"i*mum, a. Greatest in quantity or highest in degree attainable or attained; as, a maximum consumption of fuel; maximum pressure; maximum heat.

may.c: May May (mā), v. [imp. Might (mīt)] [AS. pres. maeg I am able, pret. meahte, mihte; akin to D. mogen, G. mögen, OHG. mugan, magan, Icel. mega, Goth. magan, Russ. moche. √103. Cf. Dismay, Main strength, Might. The old imp. mought is obsolete, except as a provincial word.] An auxiliary verb qualifying the meaning of another verb, by expressing: (a) Ability, competency, or possibility; -- now oftener expressed by can.
May May, n. [Cf. Icel. maer, Goth. mawi; akin to E. maiden. √103.] A maiden. [Obs.] Chaucer.

May May, n. [F. Mai, L. Maius; so named in honor of the goddess Maia (Gr. Mai^a), daughter of Atlas and mother of Mercury by Jupiter.] 1. The fifth month of the year, containing thirty-one days. Chaucer.
May laws May laws. 1. See Kulturkampf, above.

maya.c: Maya ‖Ma"ya (mä"yä), n. 1. (Hindu Philos.) The name (in Vedantic philosphy) for the doctrine of the unreality of matter, called, in English, idealism; hence, nothingness; vanity; illusion.

Maya Ma"ya (mä"yȧ), prop. n.; pl. Maya or Mayas. 1. the Indian people occupying the area of Veracruz, Chiapas, Tabasco, Campeche, and Yucatan, together with a part of Guatemala and a part of Salvador. The Maya peoples are dark, short, and brachycephalic, and at the time of the discovery had attained a higher grade of culture than any other American people. They cultivated a variety of crops, were expert in the manufacture and dyeing of cotton fabrics, used cacao as a medium of exchange, and were workers of gold, silver, and copper. Their architecture comprised elaborately carved temples and palaces, and they possessed a superior calendar, and a developed system of hieroglyphic writing, with records said to go back to about 700 a. d.
Maya arch Mayan arch { Mayan arch, Maya arch }. A form of corbel arch employing regular small corbels.

mayan.c: Mayan Ma"yan (mä"yain), a. 1. Designating, or pertaining to, an American Indian linguistic stock occupying the Mexican States of Veracruz, Chiapas, Tabasco, Campeche, and Yucatan, together with a part of Guatemala and a part of El Salvador. See 2nd Maya.

maybe.c: Maybe May"be (?), adv. [For it may be.] Perhaps; possibly; peradventure.
Maybe May"be, a. Possible; probable, but not sure. [R.]

maybird.c: Maybird May"bird` (?), n. (Zool.) (a) The whimbrel; -- called also May fowl, May curlew, and May whaap. (b) The knot. [Southern U. S.] (c) The bobolink.

mayduke.c: Mayduke May"duke` (?), n. [Corrupt. of Médoc, a province in France, where it is supposed to have originated.] A large dark-red cherry of excellent quality.

mayfish.c: Mayfish May"fish` (?), n. (Zool.) A common American minnow (Fundulus majalis). See Minnow.

mayflower.c: Mayflower May"flow`er (?), n. (Bot.) In England, the hawthorn; in New England, the trailing arbutus (see Arbutus); also, the blossom of these plants.

mayhap.c: Mayhap May"hap (?), adv. Perhaps; peradventure. [Prov. or Dialectic]

mayhem.c: mayhem may"hem (?), n. [The same as maim. See Maim.] 1. (Law) The maiming of a person by depriving him of the use of any of his members which are necessary for defense or protection. See Maim.

maying.c: Maying May"ing (?), n. The celebrating of May Day. “He met her once a-Maying.” Milton.

mayonnaise.c: mayonnaise ma`yon`naise" (?), n. [F.] A thick white sauce compounded of raw yolks of eggs beaten up with olive oil to the consistency near to that of a gel, and seasoned with vinegar, pepper, salt, etc.; -- used in dressing salads, fish, etc. Also, a dish dressed with this sauce.

mayor.c: mayor may"or (?), n. [OE. maire, F. maire, fr. L. major greater, higher, nobler, compar. of magnus great; cf. Sp. mayor. See Major, and cf. Merino.] The chief magistrate of a city or borough; the chief administrative officer of a municipal corporation. In some American cities there is a city court of which the major is chief judge. The post is usually elective, its holder chosen by the electorate of the entire city.

mayoral.c: Mayoral ‖May"or*al (?), n. [Sp., fr. mayor greater, L. major.] The conductor of a mule team; also, a head shepherd.

mayoralty.c: Mayoralty May"or*al*ty (?), n. The office, or the term of office, of a mayor.

mayoress.c: Mayoress May"or*ess (?), n. 1. The wife of a mayor.

mayorship.c: Mayorship May"or*ship, n. The office of a mayor.

maypole.c: Maypole May"pole` (?), n. A tall pole erected in an open place and wreathed with flowers, about which the rustic May-day sports were had.

maypop.c: Maypop May"pop (?), n. [Perh. corrupt. fr. maracock.] (Bot.) The edible fruit of a passion flower, especially that of the North American Passiflora incarnata, an oval yellowish berry as large as a small apple.

mayweed.c: Mayweed May"weed` (?), n. (Bot.) (a) A composite plant (Anthemis Cotula), having a strong odor; dog's fennel. It is a native of Europe, now common by the roadsides in the United States. (b) The feverfew.

mazame.c: Mazame Mazama { Ma*za"ma (?), Ma*za"me (?), } n. (Zool.) A goatlike antelope (Haplocerus montanus) which inhabits the Rocky Mountains, frequenting the highest parts; -- called also mountain goat.

mazard.c: Mazard Maz"ard (?), n. [Cf. F. merise a wild cherry.] (Bot.) A kind of small black cherry.
Mazard Maz"ard, n. [Prob. fr. mazer, the head being compared to a large goblet.] The jaw; the head or skull. [Obs.] Shak.
Mazard Maz"ard, v. t., To knock on the head. [Obs.]

mazarine.c: Mazarine Maz`a*rine" (?), a. Of or pertaining to Cardinal Mazarin, prime minister of France, 1643-1661.

mazdean.c: Mazdean Maz"de*an (?), a. Of or pertaining to Ahura-Mazda, or Ormuzd, the beneficent deity in the Zoroastrian dualistic system; hence, Zoroastrian.

maze.c: Maze Maze (māz), n. [OE. mase; cf. OE. masen to confuse, puzzle, Norweg. masast to fall into a slumber, masa to be continually busy, prate, chatter, Icel. masa to chatter, dial. Sw. masa to bask, be slow, work slowly and lazily, mas slow, lazy.] 1. A wild fancy; a confused notion. [Obs.] Chaucer.
Maze Maze (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Mazed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Mazing.] To perplex greatly; to bewilder; to astonish and confuse; to amaze. South.
Maze Maze, v. i. To be bewildered. [Obs.] Chaucer.

mazedness.c: Mazedness Maz"ed*ness (?), n. The condition of being mazed; confusion; astonishment. [Obs.] Chaucer.

mazeful.c: Mazeful Maze"ful (?), a. Mazy. [Obs.] Sir P. Sidney.

mazer.c: Mazer Maz"er (?), n. [OE. maser, akin to OD. maser an excrescence on a maple tree, OHG. masar, G. maser spot, Icel. mösurr maple.] A large drinking bowl; -- originally made of maple. [Obs.]

mazily.c: Mazily Ma"zi*ly (?), adv. In a mazy manner.

maziness.c: Maziness Ma"zi*ness, n. The state or quality of being mazy.

mazological.c: Mazological Maz`o*log"ic*al (?), a. Of or pertaining to mazology.

mazologist.c: Mazologist Ma*zol"o*gist (?), n. One versed in mazology or mastology.

mazology.c: Mazology Ma*zol"o*gy (?), n. [Gr. mazo`s the breast + -logy.] Same as Mastology.

mazurka.c: Mazurka Mazourka { Ma*zour"ka (?), Ma*zur"ka (?), } n. A Polish dance, or the music which accompanies it, usually in 3-4 or 3-8 measure, with a strong accent on the second beat.

mazy.c: Mazy Ma"zy (?), a. [From Maze.] Perplexed with turns and windings; winding; intricate; confusing; perplexing; embarrassing; as, mazy error. Milton.

me.c: Me Me (me), pron. One. See Men, pron. [Obs.] Chaucer.

Me Me (mē), pers. pron. [AS. mē, dat. & acc., mec, acc. only; akin to D. mij, G. mich, Icel. & Goth. mik, L. me, Gr. me`, 'eme`, Skr. mā, mām. √187. Cf. 2d Mine.] The person speaking, regarded as an object; myself; a pronoun of the first person used as the objective and dative case of the pronoum I; as, he struck me; he gave me the money, or he gave the money to me; he got me a hat, or he got a hat for me.

meach.c: Meach Meach (?), v. i. To skulk; to cower. See Mich.

meacock.c: Meacock Mea"cock (?), n. [Prob. fr. meek + cock.] An uxorious, effeminate, or spiritless man. [Obs.] Johnson.

mead.c: Mead Mead (mēd), n. [OE. mede, AS. meodo; akin to D. mede, G. met, meth, OHG. metu, mitu, Icel. mjöðr, Dan. miöd, Sw. mjöd, Russ. med', Lith. midus, W. medd, Gr. me`qy wine, Skr. madhu honey, a sweet drink, as adj., sweet. √270. Cf. Metheglin.] 1. A fermented drink made of water and honey with malt, yeast, etc.; metheglin; hydromel. Chaucer.
Mead Mead, n. [AS. mǣd. See Meadow.] A meadow.

meadow.c: Meadow Mead"ow (?), n. [AS. meady; akin to mǣd, and to G. matte; prob. also to E. mow. See Mow to cut (grass), and cf. 2d Mead.] 1. A tract of low or level land producing grass which is mown for hay; any field on which grass is grown for hay.
Meadow Mead"ow, a. Of or pertaining to a meadow; of the nature of a meadow; produced, growing, or living in, a meadow. “Fat meadow ground.” Milton.

meadow grass meadowgrass meadowgrass, meadow grass n. Any of various grasses that thrive in the presence of abundant moisture, especially those of the genus Poa, common in meadows, and of great value for hay and for pasture. See Grass.

meadow lark meadowlark meadowlark, meadow lark n. (Zool.), Any species of Sturnella, a genus of North American songbirds allied to the starlings. The common species (Sturnella magna) has a yellow breast with a black crescent.

meadowwort.c: Meadowwort Meadowsweet { Mead"ow*sweet` (?), Mead"ow*wort` (?), } n. (Bot.) The name of several plants of the genus Spiraea, especially the white- or pink-flowered Spiraea salicifolia, a low European and American shrub, and the herbaceous Spiraea Ulmaria, which has fragrant white flowers in compound cymes.

meadowy.c: Meadowy Mead"ow*y (?), a. Of or pertaining to meadows; resembling, or consisting of, meadow.

meagre.c: Meagre Meager { Mea"ger, Mea"gre } (?), a. [OE. merge, F. maigre, L. macer; akin to D. & G. mager, Icel. magr, and prob. to Gr. makro`s long. Cf. Emaciate, Maigre.]
Meagre Meager { Mea"ger, Mea"gre }, v. t. To make lean. [Obs.]
Meagre Mea"gre (?), n. [F. maigre.] (Zool.) A large European sciaenoid fish (Sciaena umbra or Sciaena aquila), having white bloodless flesh. It is valued as a food fish. [Written also maigre.]

meagrely.c: Meagrely Meagerly { Mea"ger*ly, Mea"gre*ly }, adv. Poorly; thinly.

meagreness.c: Meagreness Meagerness { Mea"ger*ness, Mea"gre*ness }, n. The state or quality of being meager; leanness; scantiness; barrenness.

meak.c: Meak Meak (?), n. [Cf. AS. mēce sword, OS. māki, Icel. maekir.] A hook with a long handle. [Obs.] Tusser.

meaking.c: Meaking Meak"ing, n. [See Meak.] (Naut.) The process of picking out the oakum from the seams of a vessel which is to be recalked.

meal.c: Meal Meal (mēl), n. [OE. mele, AS. mǣl part, portion, portion of time; akin to E. meal a repast. Cf. Piecemeal.] A part; a fragment; a portion. [Obs.]

Meal Meal, n. [OE. mel; akin to E. meal a part, and to D. maal time, meal, G. mal time, mahl meal, Icel. māl measure, time, meal, Goth. mēl time, and to E. measure. See Measure.] The portion of food taken at a particular time for the satisfaction of appetite; the quantity usually taken at one time with the purpose of satisfying hunger; a repast; the act or time of eating a meal; as, the traveler has not eaten a good meal for a week; there was silence during the meal.

Meal Meal, n. [OE. mele, AS. melu, melo; akin to D. meel, G. mehl, OHG. melo, Icel. mjöl, SW. mjöl, Dan. meel, also to D. malen to grind, G. mahlen, OHG., OS., & Goth. malan, Icel. mala, W. malu, L. molere, Gr. my`lh mill, and E. mill. √108. Cf. Mill, Mold soil, Mole an animal, Immolate, Molar.]
Meal Meal, v. t. 1. To sprinkle with, or as with, meal. Shak.

mealies.c: Mealies Meal"ies (?), n. pl. [From Mealy.] (Bot.) Maize or Indian corn; -- the common name in South Africa.

mealiness.c: Mealiness Meal"i*ness (?), n. The quality or state of being mealy.

mealtime.c: Mealtime Meal"time` (mēl"tīm`), n. The usual time of eating a meal.

mealy.c: Mealy Meal"y (mēl"y̆), a. [Compar. Mealier (?); superl. Mealiest.] 1. Having the qualities of meal; resembling meal; soft, dry, and friable; easily reduced to a condition resembling meal; as, a mealy potato.

mealy bug mealybug meal"y*bug`, mealy bug (mēl"y̆*bŭg`), n. (Zool.), Any of several homopteran scale insects (as, Coccus adonidum, and related species of the families Pseudococcidae and Eriococcidae), that cover themselves with a white powderlike or cottony wax secretion. They are common plant-eating pests in hothouses and are also destructive of fruit trees.

mealymouthed.c: Mealy-mouthed Meal"y-mouthed` (?), a. Using soft words; not straightforward; plausible; affectedly or timidly delicate of speech; speaking deviously; unwilling to tell the truth in plain language. Opposite of frank or blunt. “Mealy-mouthed philanthropies.” Tennyson.

mean.c: Mean Mean (mēn), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Meant (mĕnt); p. pr. & vb. n. Meaning.] [OE. menen, AS. mǣnan to recite, tell, intend, wish; akin to OS. mēnian to have in mind, mean, D. meenen, G. meinen, OHG. meinan, Icel. meina, Sw. mena, Dan. mene, and to E. mind. √104. See Mind, and cf. Moan.] 1. To have in the mind, as a purpose, intention, etc.; to intend; to purpose; to design; as, what do you mean to do?
Mean Mean, v. i. To have a purpose or intention. [Rare, except in the phrase to mean well, or ill.] Shak.

Mean Mean (mēn), a. [Compar. Meaner (mēn"ẽr); superl. Meanest.] [OE. mene, AS. mǣne wicked; akin to mān, a., wicked, n., wickedness, OS. mēn wickedness, OHG. mein, G. meineid perjury, Icel. mein harm, hurt, and perh. to AS. gemǣne common, general, D. gemeen, G. gemein, Goth. gamáins, and L. communis. The AS. gemǣne prob. influenced the meaning.]

Mean Mean, a. [OE. mene, OF. meiien, F. moyen, fr. L. medianus that is in the middle, fr. medius; akin to E. mid. See Mid.] 1. Occupying a middle position; middle; being about midway between extremes.

Mean Mean, n. 1. That which is mean, or intermediate, between two extremes of place, time, or number; the middle point or place; middle rate or degree; mediocrity; medium; absence of extremes or excess; moderation; measure.

meander.c: Meander Me*an"der (?), n. [L. Maeander, orig., a river in Phrygia, proverbial for its many windings, Gr.?: cf. F. méandre.] 1. A winding, crooked, or involved course; as, the meanders of the veins and arteries. Sir M. Hale.
Meander Me*an"der, v. t. To wind, turn, or twist; to make flexuous. Dryton.
Meander Me*an"der, v. i. [imp. & p. p. Meandered (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Meandering.] To wind or turn in a course or passage; to be intricate.

meandrian.c: Meandrian Me*an"dri*an (?), a. [L. Maeandrius: cf. F. méandrien.] Winding; having many turns.

meandrina.c: Meandrina ‖Me`an*dri"na (?), n. [NL.: cf. F. méandrine.] (Zool.) A genus of corals with meandering grooves and ridges, including the brain corals.

meandry.c: Meandry Meandrous { Me*an"drous (?), Me*an"dry (?), } a. Winding; flexuous.

meaning.c: Meaning Mean"ing (?), n. 1. That which is meant or intended; intent; purpose; aim; object; as, a mischievous meaning was apparent.

meanly.c: Meanly Mean"ly, adv. [From Mean low.] In a mean manner; unworthily; basely; poorly; ungenerously.

meanness.c: Meanness Mean"ness, n. 1. The condition, or quality, of being mean; want of excellence; poorness; lowness; baseness; sordidness; stinginess.

meanspirited.c: mean-spirited meanspirited mean"spir`it*ed, mean"-spir`it*ed (?), a. 1. Of a mean spirit; petty; small-minded; base; groveling; -- of people. -- Mean"-spir`it*ed*ness, n.

meant.c: Meant Meant (?), imp. & p. p. of Mean.

meanwhile.c: Meanwhile Meantime { Mean"time` (?), Mean"while` (?), } n. The intervening time; as, in the meantime (or mean time).
Meanwhile Meantime { Mean"time`, Mean"while`, } adv. In the intervening time; during the interval.

mear.c: Mear Mear (?), n. A boundary. See Mere. [Obs.]

mease.c: Mease Mease (?), n. [Cf. G. mass measure.] Five hundred; as, a mease of herrings. [Prov. Eng.]

measelry.c: Measelry Mea"sel*ry (?), n. [OE. meselrie, OF. mesellerie. See 1st Measle.] Leprosy. [Obs.] R. of Brunne.

measle.c: Measle Mea"sle (?), n. [OE. mesel, OF. mesel, LL. misellus, L. misellus unfortunate, dim. of miser. See Miser.] A leper. [Obs.] [Written also meazel, and mesel.] Wyclif (Matt. x. 8.).
Measle Mea"sle, n. (Zool.) A tapeworm larva. See 2d Measles, 4.

measled.c: Measled Mea"sled (?), a. [See 2d Measles.] Infected or spotted with measles, as pork. -- Mea"sled*ness, n.

measles.c: Measles Mea"sles (?), n. [From 1st Measle.] Leprosy; also, a leper. [Obs.]
Measles Mea"sles, n.; pl. in form, but used as singular in senses 1, 2, & 3. [D. mazelen; akin to G. masern, pl., and E. mazer, and orig. meaning, little spots. See Mazer.]

measurable.c: Measurable Meas"ur*a*ble (?), a. [F. mesurable, L. mensurabilis. See Measure, and cf. Mensurable.]

measure.c: measure meas"ure (mĕzh"ur; 135), n. [OE. mesure, F. mesure, L. mensura, fr. metiri, mensus, to measure; akin to metrum poetical measure, Gr. me`tron, E. meter. Cf. Immense, Mensuration, Mete to measure.] 1. A standard of dimension; a fixed unit of quantity or extent; an extent or quantity in the fractions or multiples of which anything is estimated and stated; hence, a rule by which anything is adjusted or judged.

Measure Meas"ure, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Measured (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Measuring.] [F. mesurer, L. mensurare. See Measure, n.] 1. To ascertain by use of a measuring instrument; to compute or ascertain the extent, quantity, dimensions, or capacity of, by a certain rule or standard; to take the dimensions of; hence, to estimate; to judge of; to value; to appraise.
Measure Meas"ure (?), v. i. 1. To make a measurement or measurements.

measured.c: Measured Meas"ured (?), a. Regulated or determined by a standard; hence, equal; uniform; graduated; limited; moderated; as, he walked with measured steps; he expressed himself in no measured terms. -- Meas"ured*ly, adv.

measureless.c: Measureless Meas"ure*less (?), a. Without measure; unlimited; immeasurable. -- Meas"ure*less*ness, n.

measurement.c: Measurement Meas"ure*ment (?), n. 1. The act or result of measuring; mensuration; as, measurement is required.

measurer.c: Measurer Meas"ur*er (?), n. One who measures; one whose occupation or duty is to measure commondities in market.

measuring.c: Measuring Meas"ur*ing, a. Used in, or adapted for, ascertaining measurements, or dividing by measure.

meat.c: Meat Meat (mēt), n. [OE. mete, AS. mete; akin to OS. mat, meti, D. met hashed meat, G. mettwurst sausage, OHG. maz food, Icel. matr, Sw. mat, Dan. mad, Goth. mats. Cf. Mast fruit, Mush.] 1. Food, in general; anything eaten for nourishment, either by man or beast. Hence, the edible part of anything; as, the meat of a lobster, a nut, or an egg. Chaucer.
Meat Meat, v. t. To supply with food. [Obs.] Tusser.

meatal.c: Meatal Me*a"tal (?), a. Of or pertaining to a meatus; resembling a meatus. Owen.

meathe.c: Meathe Meath { Meath, Meathe (?) }, n. [See Mead.] A sweet liquor; mead. [Obs.] Chaucer. Milton.

meatiness.c: Meatiness Meat"i*ness (?), n. Quality of being meaty.

meatless.c: Meatless Meat"less, a. Having no meat; without food.

meatoscope.c: Meatoscope Me*at"o*scope (?), n. [Meatus + -scope.] (Med.) A speculum for examining a natural passage, as the urethra.

meatotome.c: Meatotome Me*at"o*tome (?), n. [Meatus + Gr.? to cut.] (Surg.) An instrument for cutting into the urethra so as to enlarge its orifice.

meatus.c: Meatus ‖Me*a"tus (?), n. sing. & pl.; E. pl. Meatuses (?). [L., a going, passage, fr. meare to go.] (Anat.) A natural passage or canal; as, the external auditory meatus. See Illust. of Ear.

meaw.c: Meaw Meaw (?), n. The sea mew. [Obs.] Spenser.
Meaw Meaw, v. i. See Mew, to cry as a cat.

meawl.c: Meawl Meawl (?), v. i. See Mewl, and Miaul.

meazling.c: Meazling Meaz"ling (?), a. Falling in small drops; mistling; mizzing. [Obs.] Arbuthnot.

mecate.c: Mecate ‖Me*ca"te (?), n. [Sp.] A rope of hair or of maguey fiber, for tying horses, etc. [Southwestern U. S.]

meccawee.c: Meccawee Mec`ca*wee" (?), prop. a. Of or pertaining to Mecca, in Arabia. -- n. A native or inhabitant of Mecca.

mechanic.c: Mechanic Me*chan"ic (?), n. [F. mécanique mechanics. See Mechanic, a.] 1. The art of the application of the laws of motion or force to construction. [Obs.]

Mechanic Me*chan"ic (me*kăn"ĭk), a. [F. mécanique, L. mechanicus, Gr. mhchaniko`s, fr. mhchanh` a machine. See Machine.] 1. Having to do with the application of the laws of motion in the art of constructing or making things; of or pertaining to mechanics; mechanical; as, the mechanic arts. “These mechanic philosophers.” Ray.

mechanicalize.c: Mechanicalize Me*chan"ic*al*ize (?), v. t. To cause to become mechanical.

mechanically.c: Mechanically Me*chan"ic*al*ly, adv. In a mechanical manner.

mechanicalness.c: Mechanicalness Me*chan"ic*al*ness, n. The state or quality of being mechanical.

mechanician.c: Mechanician Mech`a*ni"cian (?), n. [Cf. F. mécanicien. See Mechanic.] One skilled in the theory or construction of machines; a machinist. Boyle.

mechanicochemical.c: Mechanico-chemical Me*chan`i*co-chem"ic*al (?), a. Pertaining to, connected with, or dependent upon, both mechanics and chemistry; -- said especially of those sciences which treat of such phenomena as seem to depend on the laws both of mechanics and chemistry, as electricity and magnetism.

mechanics.c: Mechanics Me*chan"ics (?), n. [Cf. F. mécanique.] That science, or branch of applied mathematics, which treats of the action of forces on bodies.

mechanism.c: Mechanism Mech"an*ism (?), n. [Cf. F. mécanisme, L. mechanisma. See Mechanic.] 1. The arrangement or relation of the parts of a machine; the parts of a machine, taken collectively; the arrangement or relation of the parts of anything as adapted to produce an effect; as, the mechanism of a watch; the mechanism of a sewing machine; the mechanism of a seed pod.

mechanist.c: Mechanist Mech"an*ist, n. 1. A maker of machines; one skilled in mechanics.

mechanize.c: Mechanize Mech"an*ize (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Mechanized (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Mechanizing (?).] [Cf. F. méchaniser.] 1. To cause to be mechanical. Shelley.

mechanograph.c: Mechanograph Mech"an*o*graph (?), n. [Gr. mhchanh` machine + -graph.] One of a number of copies of anything multiplied mechanically.

mechanographist.c: Mechanographist Mech`an*og"ra*phist (mĕk`ain*ŏg"rȧ*fĭst), n. An artist who, by mechanical means, multiplies copies of works of art.

mechanography.c: Mechanography Mech`an*og"ra*phy (?), n. The art of mechanically multiplying copies of a writing, or any work of art.

mechanurgy.c: Mechanurgy Mech"an*ur`gy (?), n. [Gr. mhchanh` machine + the root of? work.] That branch of science which treats of moving machines.

mechitarist.c: Mechitarist Mech"i*tar*ist (?), n. [From Mechitar, an Armenian., who founded the congregation in the early part of the eighteenth century.] (Eccl. Hist.) One of a religious congregation of the Roman Catholic Church devoted to the improvement of Armenians.

mechlin.c: Mechlin Mech"lin (?), n. A kind of lace made at, or originating in, Mechlin, in Belgium.

mechoacan.c: Mechoacan Me*cho"a*can (?), n. A species of jalap, of very feeble properties, said to be obtained from the root of a species of Convolvulus (Convolvulus Mechoacan); -- so called from Michoacan, in Mexico, whence it is obtained.

meckelian.c: Meckelian Meck*e"li*an (?), a. (Anat.) Pertaining to, or discovered by, J. F. Meckel, a German anatomist.

meconate.c: Meconate Mec"o*nate (?), n. [Cf. F. méconate.] (Chem.) A salt of meconic acid.

meconic.c: Meconic Me*con"ic (?), a. [Gr.? belonging to the poppy, fr.? the poppy: cf. F. méconique.] Pertaining to, or obtained from, the poppy or opium; specif. (Chem.), designating an acid related to aconitic acid, found in opium and extracted as a white crystalline substance.

meconidine.c: Meconidine Me*con"i*dine (?), n. (Chem) An alkaloid found in opium, and extracted as a yellow amorphous substance which is easily decomposed.

meconidium.c: Meconidium ‖Mec`o*nid"i*um (?), n. [NL., dim. of Gr.? a poppy. So called in allusion to the shape of the seed capsules of the poppy.] (Zool.) A kind of gonophore produced by hydroids of the genus Gonothyraea. It has tentacles, and otherwise resembles a free medusa, but remains attached by a pedicel.

meconin.c: Meconin Mec"o*nin (?), n. [Cf. F. méconine.] (Chem.) A substance regarded as an anhydride of meconinic acid, existing in opium and extracted as a white crystalline substance. Also erroneously called meconina, meconia, etc., as though it were an alkaloid.

meconinic.c: Meconinic Mec`o*nin"ic (?), a. (Chem.) Pertaining to, or designating, an acid which occurs in opium, and which may be obtained by oxidizing narcotine.

meconium.c: Meconium ‖Me*co"ni*um (?), n. [L., fr. Gr.?, fr.? poppy.] (Med.) (a) Opium. [Obs.] (b) The contents of the fetal intestine; hence, first excrement.

medal.c: Medal Med"al (?), n. [F. médaille, It. medaglia, fr. L. metallum metal, through (assumed) LL. metalleus made of metal. See Metal, and cf. Mail a piece of money.] A piece of metal in the form of a coin, struck with a device, and intended to preserve the remembrance of a notable event or an illustrious person, or to serve as a reward.
Medal Med"al, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Medaled (?), or Medalled; p. pr. & vb. n. Medaling or Medalling.] To honor or reward with a medal. “Medaled by the king.” Thackeray.
Medal play Med"al play`. (Golf) Play in which the score is reckoned by counting the number of strokes.

medalist.c: Medalist Med"al*ist, n. [Cf. F. médailliste, It. medaglista.] [Written also medallist.]

medallic.c: Medallic Me*dal"lic (?), a. Of or pertaining to a medal, or to medals. “Our medallic history.” Walpole.

medallion.c: Medallion Me*dal"lion (?), n. [F. médaillion, It. medaglione, augm. of medaglia. See Medal.]

medalurgy.c: Medalurgy Med"al*ur`gy (?), n. [Medal + the root of Gr.? work.] The art of making and striking medals and coins. [Written also medallurgy.]

meddle.c: Meddle Med"dle` (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Meddled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Meddling (?).] [OE. medlen to mix, OF. medler, mesler, F. mêler, LL. misculare, a dim. fr. L. miscere to mix. √271. See Mix, and cf. Medley, Mellay.]
Meddle Med"dle, v. t. To mix; to mingle. [Obs.] Chaucer.

meddler.c: Meddler Med"dler (?), n. One who meddles; one who interferes or busies himself with things in which he has no concern; an officious person; a busybody.

meddlesome.c: Meddlesome Med"dle*some (?), a. Given to meddling; apt to interpose in the affairs of others; officiously intrusive. -- Med"dle*some*ness, n.

meddlingly.c: Meddlingly Med"dling*ly, adv. In a meddling manner.

mede.c: Mede Mede (?), prop. n. A native or inhabitant of Media in Asia. “according to the law of the Medes and Persians, which altereth not” Daniel 6: 8.
Mede Mede, n. See 1st & 2d Mead, and Meed. [Obs.]

media.c: media me"di*a (mē"dĭ*ȧ), n. sing. & pl., 1. The latinic plural form of medium, sometimes used as a singular noun with the same meaning as medium; as, (Computers) place your installation media into the device which will read it; (Microbiology) the tuberculosis bacterium will only grow in a special media.

Media ‖Me"di*a, n.; pl. Mediae (-ē). [NL., fr. L. medius middle.] 1. (Phonetics) One of the sonant mutes β, δ, γ (b, d, g), in Greek, or of their equivalents in other languages, so named as intermediate between the tenues, π, τ, κ (p, t, k), and the aspiratae (aspirates) φ, θ, χ (ph or f, th, ch). Also called middle mute, or medial, and sometimes soft mute.

mediacy.c: Mediacy Me"di*a*cy (mē"dĭ*ȧ*sy̆), n. The state or quality of being mediate. Sir W. Hamilton.

mediaeval.c: Mediaeval Me`di*ae"val (mē`dĭ*ē"vail; 277), a. [L. medius middle + aevum age. See Middle, and Age.] Of or relating to the Middle Ages; as, mediaeval architecture. [Written also medieval.]

mediaevalism.c: Mediaevalism Me`di*ae"val*ism (mē`dĭ*ē"vail*ĭz'm), n. The method or spirit of the Middle Ages; devotion to the institutions and practices of the Middle Ages; a survival from the Middle Ages. [Written also medievalism.]

mediaevalist.c: Mediaevalist Me`di*ae"val*ist (mē`dĭ*ē"vail*ĭst), n. One who has a taste for, or is versed in, the history of the Middle Ages; one in sympathy with the spirit or forms of the Middle Ages. [Written also medievalist.]

mediaevally.c: Mediaevally Me`di*ae"val*ly (mē`dĭ*ē"vail*ly̆), adv. In the manner of the Middle Ages; in accordance with mediaevalism.

mediaevals.c: Mediaevals Me`di*ae"vals (mē`dĭ*ē"vailz), n. pl. The people who lived in the Middle Ages. Ruskin.

medial.c: Medial Me"di*al (mē"dĭ*ail), a. [L. medialis, fr. medius middle: cf. F. médial. See Middle.] Of or pertaining to a mean or average; mean; as, medial alligation.

medialuna.c: Medialuna ‖Me"di*a*lu"na (?), n. [Sp. media luna half-moon.] (Zool.) See Half-moon.

median.c: Median Me"di*an (mē"dĭ*ain), a. [L. medianus, fr. medius middle. See Medial.] 1. Being in the middle; running through the middle; as, a median groove.
Median Me"di*an, n. (Geom.) A median line or point.

mediant.c: Mediant Me"di*ant (?), n. [L. medians, p. p. of mediare to halve: cf. It. mediante, F. médiante.] (Mus.) The third above the keynote; -- so called because it divides the interval between the tonic and dominant into two thirds.

mediastinal.c: Mediastinal Me`di*as*ti"nal (?), a. (Anat.) Of or pertaining to a mediastinum.

mediastinum.c: Mediastinum Mediastine { Me`di*as"tine (?), ‖Me`di*as*ti"num (?), } n. [NL. mediastinum, fr. L. medius middle; cf. mediastinus helper, a menial servant, LL. mediastinus equiv. to medius: cf F. médiastin.] (Anat.) A partition; a septum; specifically, the folds of the pleura (and the space included between them) which divide the thorax into a right and left cavity. The space included between these folds of the pleura, called the mediastinal space, contains the heart and gives passage to the esophagus and great blood vessels.

mediate.c: Mediate Me"di*ate (?), a. [L. mediatus, p. p. of mediare, v. t., to halve, v. i., to be in the middle. See Mid, and cf. Moiety.] 1. Being between the two extremes; middle; interposed; intervening; intermediate. Prior.
Mediate Me"di*ate (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Mediated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Mediating.] [LL. mediatus, p. p. of mediare to mediate. See Mediate, a.]
Mediate Me"di*ate, v. t. 1. To effect by mediation or interposition; to bring about as a mediator, instrument, or means; as, to mediate a peace.

mediately.c: Mediately Me"di*ate*ly (?), adv. In a mediate manner; by a secondary cause or agent; not directly or primarily; by means; -- opposed to immediately.

mediateness.c: Mediateness Me"di*ate*ness, n. The state of being mediate.

mediation.c: Mediation Me`di*a"tion (?), n. [OE. mediacioun, F. médiation. See Mediate, a.] 1. The act of mediating; action or relation of anything interposed; action as a necessary condition, means, or instrument; interposition; intervention.

mediative.c: Mediative Me"di*a*tive (?), a. Pertaining to mediation; used in mediation; as, mediative efforts. Beaconsfield.

mediatization.c: Mediatization Me`di*at`i*za"tion (?), n. [Cf. F. médiatisation.] The act of mediatizing.

mediatize.c: Mediatize Me"di*a*tize (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Mediatized (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Mediatizing.] [Cf. F. médiatiser.] To cause to act through an agent or to hold a subordinate position; to annex; -- specifically applied to the annexation during the former German empire of a smaller German state to a larger, while allowing it a nominal sovereignty, and its prince his rank.

mediator.c: Mediator Me"di*a`tor (?), n. [L. mediator: cf. E. médiateur.] One who mediates; especially, one who interposes between parties at variance for the purpose of reconciling them; hence, an intercessor.

mediatorial.c: Mediatorial Me`di*a*to"ri*al (?), a. Of or pertaining to a mediator, or to mediation; mediatory; as, a mediatorial office. -- Me`di*a*to"ri*al*ly, adv.

mediatorship.c: Mediatorship Me"di*a`tor*ship (?), n. The office or character of a mediator.

mediatrix.c: Mediatrix Mediatress { Me`di*a"tress (?), Me`di*a*"trix (?), } n. [L. mediatrix, f. of mediator: cf. F. médiatrice.] A female mediator.

medic.c: Medic Med"ic (?), n. [L. medica, Gr.? (sc.?) a kind of clover introduced from Media, from? Median.] (Bot.) A leguminous plant of the genus Medicago. The black medic is the Medicago lupulina; the purple medic, or lucern, is Medicago sativa.

medicable.c: Medicable Med"i*ca*ble (?), a. [L. medicabilis, from medicare, medicari, to heal, fr. medicus physician. See Medical.] Capable of being medicated; admitting of being cured or healed.

medical.c: Medical Med"ic*al (?), a. [LL. medicalis, L. medicus belonging to healing, fr. mederi to heal; cf. Zend madha medical science, wisdom, Gr.? to learn, E. mind: cf. F. médical.]

medically.c: Medically Med"ic*al*ly, adv. In a medical manner; with reference to healing, or to the principles of the healing art.

medicament.c: Medicament Med"i*ca*ment (?), n. [L. medicamentum, fr. medicare, medicari, to heal: cf. F. médicament. See Medicable.] Anything used for healing diseases or wounds, especially a medicine; a medication; a healing application.

medicamental.c: Medicamental Med`ica*men"tal (?), a. Of or pertaining to medicaments or healing applications; having the qualities of medicaments. -- Med`ica*men"tal*ly, adv.

medicaster.c: Medicaster Med"i*cas`ter (?), n. [Cf. F. médicastre. See Medical.] A quack. [R.] Whitlock.

medicate.c: Medicate Med"i*cate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Medicated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Medicating (?).] [L. medicatus, p. p. of medicare, medicari. See Medicable.]

medication.c: Medication Med`i*ca"tion (?), [L. medicatio: cf. F. médication.] The act or process of medicating.

medicative.c: Medicative Med"i*ca*tive (?), a. Medicinal; acting like a medicine.

medicean.c: Medicean Med`i*ce"an (?), prop. a. Of or relating to the Medici, a noted Italian family; as, the Medicean Venus.

medicinable.c: Medicinable Me*dic"i*na*ble (?), a. Medicinal; having the power of healing. [Obs.] Shak.

medicinal.c: Medicinal Me*dic"i*nal (?), a. [L. medicinalis: cf. F. médicinal. See Medicine.] 1. Having curative or palliative properties; used for the cure or alleviation of bodily disorders; as, medicinal tinctures, plants, or springs.

medicinally.c: Medicinally Me*dic"i*nal*ly, adv. In a medicinal manner.

medicine.c: Medicine Med"i*cine (?), n. [L. medicina (sc. ars), fr. medicinus medical, fr. medicus: cf. F. médecine. See Medical.] 1. The science which relates to the prevention, cure, or alleviation of disease.
Medicine Med"i*cine, v. t. To give medicine to; to affect as a medicine does; to remedy; to cure. “Medicine thee to that sweet sleep.” Shak.

medicolegal.c: Medico-legal Med`i*co-le"gal (?), a. Of or pertaining to law as affected by medical facts.

medicommissure.c: Medicommissure Med`i*com"mis*sure (?), n. [L. medius middle + E. commissure.] (Anat.) A large transverse commissure in the third ventricle of the brain; the middle or soft commissure. B. G. Wildex.

medicornu.c: Medicornu ‖Med`i*cor"nu (?), n.; pl. Medicornua (#). [NL., fr. L. medius middle + cornu horn.] (Anat.) The middle or inferior horn of each lateral ventricle of the brain. B. G. Wilder.

mediety.c: Mediety Me*di"e*ty (?), n. [L. medietas.] The middle part; half; moiety. [Obs.] Sir T. Browne.

medievalist.c: Medievalist Medievalism Medieval { Me`di*e"val, Me`di*e"val*ism, Me`di*e"val*ist }. Same as Mediaeval, Mediaevalism, etc.

medina.c: Medina epoch Me*di"na ep"och (?). [From Medina in New York.] (Geol.) A subdivision of the Niagara period in the American upper Silurian, characterized by the formations known as the Oneida conglomerate, and the Medina sandstone. See the Chart of Geology.

mediocre.c: mediocre me`di*o"cre (mē`dĭ*ō"kẽr), a. [F. médiocre, L. mediocris, fr. medius middle. See Mid.] Of a middle quality; of but a moderate or low degree of excellence; indifferent; ordinary. “ A very mediocre poet.” Pope.
Mediocre Me"di*o`cre, n. 1. A mediocre person; a mediocrity. [R.]

mediostapedial.c: Mediostapedial Me`di*o*sta*pe"di*al (?), a. [L. medius middle + E. stapedial.] (Anat.) Pertaining to that part of the columella of the ear which, in some animals, connects the stapes with the other parts of the columella. -- n. The mediostapedial part of the columella.

medioxumous.c: Medioxumous Me`di*ox"u*mous (?), a. [L. medioxumus middlemost.] Intermediate. [Obs.] Dr. H. More.

meditate.c: Meditate Med"i*tate (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Meditated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Meditating.] [L. meditatus, p. p. of meditari to meditate; cf. Gr.? to learn, E. mind.] To keep the mind in a state of contemplation; to dwell on anything in thought; to think seriously; to muse; to cogitate; to reflect. Jer. Taylor.
Meditate Med"i*tate, v. t. 1. To contemplate; to keep the mind fixed upon; to study. “Blessed is the man that doth meditate good things.” Ecclus. xiv. 20.

meditation.c: Meditation Med`i*ta"tion (?), n. [OE. meditacioun, F. méditation, fr. L. meditatio.] 1. The act of meditating; close or continued thought; the turning or revolving of a subject in the mind; serious contemplation; reflection; musing.

meditatist.c: Meditatist Med"i*ta`tist, n. One who is given to meditation.

meditative.c: Meditative Med"i*ta*tive (?), a. [L. meditativus: cf. F. méditatif.] Disposed to meditate, or to meditation; as, a meditative man; a meditative mood. -- Med"i*ta*tive*ly, adv. -- Med"i*ta*tive*ness, n.

mediterranean.c: Mediterranean Med`i*ter*ra"ne*an (?), a. [L. mediterraneus; medius middle + terra land. See Mid, and Terrace.]

mediterraneous.c: Mediterraneous Med`i*ter*ra"ne*ous (?), a. Inland. Sir T. Browne.

medium.c: Medium Me"di*um (?), n.; pl. L. Media (#), E. Mediums (#). [L. medium the middle, fr. medius middle. See Mid, and cf. Medius.] 1. That which lies in the middle, or between other things; intervening body or quantity. Hence, specifically: (a) Middle place or degree; mean.
Medium Me"di*um, a. Having a middle position or degree; mean; intermediate; medial; as, a horse of medium size; a decoction of medium strength.

mediumsized.c: Medium-sized Me"di*um-sized` (?), a. Having a medium size; as, a medium-sized man.

medius.c: Medius ‖Me"di*us (?), n.; pl. Medii (#). [NL., fr. L. medius middle. See Medium.] (Anat.) The third or middle finger; the third digit, or that which corresponds to it.

medjidieh.c: Medjidieh Medjidie { Me*dji"di*e, Me*dji"di*eh } (?), n. [Turk. majīdieh (prop. fem. a., fr. Ar. mejīd glorious); -- so called after the sultan Abdul Mejid, lit., “servant of the Glorious One,” i.e., of God.] 1. (a) A silver coin of Turkey formerly rated at twenty, but since 1880 at nineteen, piasters (about 83 cents). (b) A gold coin of Turkey equal (in 1913) to one hundred piastres ($4.396 or 18s. ¾d.); a lira, or Turkish pound.

medlar.c: Medlar Med"lar (?), n. [OE. medler medlar tree, OF. meslier, F. néflier, L. mespilum, mespilus, Gr.?,?. Cf. Naseberry.] A tree of the genus Mespilus (Mespilus Germanica); also, the fruit of the tree. The fruit is something like a small apple, but has a bony endocarp. When first gathered the flesh is hard and austere, and it is not eaten until it has begun to decay.

medle.c: Medle Med"le (?), v. t. [See Meddle.] To mix; to mingle; to meddle. [Written also medly.] [Obs.] Chaucer.

medley.c: Medley Med"ley (?), n.; pl. Medleys (#). [OE. medlee, OF. meslée, medlée, mellée, F. mêlée. See Meddle, and cf. Melée, Mellay.] 1. A mixture; a mingled and confused mass of ingredients, usually inharmonious; a jumble; a hodgepodge; -- often used contemptuously.
Medley Med"ley, a. 1. Mixed; of mixed material or color. [Obs.] “A medlé coat.” Chaucer.

medly.c: Medly Med"ly (?), v. t. See Medle. Johnson.

medoc.c: Medoc ‖Mé`doc" (?), n. [Cf. Mayduke.] A class of claret wines, including several varieties, from the district of Médoc in the department of Gironde.

medrick.c: Medrick Med"rick (?), n. [Etymol. uncertain.] (Zool.) A species of gull or tern. [Prov.] Lowell.

medulla.c: Medulla Me*dul"la (?), n. [L.] 1. Marrow; pith; hence, essence. [Obs.] Milton.

medullary.c: Medullary Med"ul*la*ry (?), a. [L. medullaris, fr. medulla marrow: cf. F. médullaire.] 1. (Anat.) (a) Pertaining to, consisting of, or resembling, marrow or medulla. (b) Pertaining to the medula oblongata.

medullated.c: Medullated Me*dul"la*ted (?), a. (Anat.) Furnished with a medulla or marrow, or with a medullary sheath; as, a medullated nerve fiber.

medullin.c: Medullin Me*dul"lin (?), n. [Cf. F. médulline.] (Bot. Chem.) A variety of lignin or cellulose found in the medulla, or pith, of certain plants. Cf. Lignin, and Cellulose.

medusa.c: Medusa ‖Me*du"sa (?), n. [L., fr. Gr.?.] 1. (Class. Myth.) The Gorgon; or one of the Gorgons whose hair was changed into serpents, after which all who looked upon her were turned into stone.

medusiform.c: Medusiform Me*du"si*form (?), a. [Medusa + -form.] (Zool.) Resembling a medusa in shape or structure.

medusoid.c: Medusoid Me*du"soid (?), a. [Medusa + -oid.] (Zool.) Like a medusa; having the fundamental structure of a medusa, but without a locomotive disk; -- said of the sessile gonophores of hydroids. -- n. A sessile gonophore. See Illust. under Gonosome.

meech.c: Meech Meech (mēch), v. i. See Mich. [Obs. or Colloq.]

meed.c: Meed Meed (mēd), n. [OE. mede, AS. mēd, meord; akin to OS. mēda, OHG. miata, mieta, G. miethe hire, Goth. mizdō reward, Bohem. & Russ. mzda, Gr. misqo`s, Skr. mīdha. √276.] 1. That which is bestowed or rendered in consideration of merit; reward; recompense.
Meed Meed, v. t. 1. To reward; to repay. [Obs.] Waytt.

meedful.c: Meedful Meed"ful (?), a. Worthy of meed, reward, or recompense; meritorious. “Meedful works.” Wiclif.

meedfully.c: Meedfully Meed"ful*ly, adv. According to merit; suitably.

meek.c: Meek Meek (mēk), a. [Compar. Meeker (mēk"ẽr); superl. Meekest.] [OE. mek, meoc; akin to Icel. mjūkr mild, soft, Sw. mjuk, Dan. myg, D. muik, Goth. mukamōdei gentleness.] 1. Mild of temper; not easily provoked or orritated; patient under injuries; not vain, or haughty, or resentful; forbearing; submissive.

meeken.c: Meeken Meek { Meek, Meek"en (-'n) }, v. t. To make meek; to nurture in gentleness and humility. [Obs.] Chaucer.

meekly.c: Meekly Meek"ly, adv. In a meek manner. Spenser.

meekness.c: Meekness Meek"ness, n. The quality or state of being meek.

meer.c: Meer Meer (mēr), a. Simple; unmixed. See Mere, a. [Obs.]
Meer Meer, n. See Mere, a lake.
Meer Meer, n. A boundary. See Mere.

meerkat.c: Meerkat ‖Meer"kat (mēr"kăt), n. [D.] (Zool.) A South African carnivore (Suricata suricata, formerly Cynictis penicillata), allied to the ichneumons, having a lemurlike face and only four toes; called also yellow mongoose and suricate. [Also spelled mierkat.]

meerschaum.c: Meerschaum Meer"schaum (mēr"shäm; 277), n. [G., lit., sea foam; meer sea + schaum foam; but it perh. is a corruption of the Tartaric name myrsen. Cf. Mere a lake, and Scum.] 1. (Min.) A fine white claylike mineral, soft, and light enough when in dry masses to float in water. It is a hydrous silicate of magnesia, and is obtained chiefly in Asia Minor. It is manufacturd into tobacco pipes, cigar holders, etc. Also called sepiolite.

meet.c: Meet Meet (mēt), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Met (mĕt); p. pr. & vb. n. Meeting.] [OE. meten, AS. mētan, fr. mōt, gemōt, a meeting; akin to OS. mōtian to meet, Icel. maeta, Goth. gamōtjan. See Moot, v. t.] 1. To join, or come in contact with; esp., to come in contact with by approach from an opposite direction; to come upon or against, front to front, as distinguished from contact by following and overtaking.

Meet Meet, v. t. 1. To come together by mutual approach; esp., to come in contact, or into proximity, by approach from opposite directions; to join; to come face to face; to come in close relationship; as, we met in the street; two lines meet so as to form an angle.
Meet Meet, n. An assembling together; esp., the assembling of huntsmen for the hunt; also, the persons who so assemble, and the place of meeting.

Meet Meet, a. [OE. mete fitting, moderate, scanty, AS. mǣte moderate; akin to gemet fit, meet, metan to mete, and G. mässig moderate, gemäss fitting. See Mete.] Suitable; fit; proper; appropriate; qualified; convenient.

meeten.c: Meeten Meet"en (mēt'n), v. t. To render fit. [R.]

meeth.c: Meeth Meeth (mēth), n. Mead. See Meathe. [Obs.] Chaucer.

meeting.c: Meeting Meet"ing (mēt"ĭng), n. 1. A coming together; an assembling; as, the meeting of Congress.

meetinghouse.c: Meetinghouse Meet"ing*house` (?), n. A house used as a place of worship; a church; -- in England, applied only to a house so used by Dissenters.

megalo.c: Megalo- Mega Meg- { Meg- (mĕg-), Meg"a (mĕg"ȧ-), Meg"a*lo- (mĕg"ȧ*lo-) }. [Gr. me`gas, gen. mega`loy, great.] Combining forms signifying: (a) Great, extended, powerful; as, megascope, megacosm. (b) (Metric System, Elec., Mech., etc.) A million times, a million of; as, megabyte, a million butes; megawatt, a million watts; megameter, a million meters; megafarad, a million farads; megohm, a million ohms.

megacephalous.c: Megacephalous Megacephalic { Meg`a*ce*phal"ic (mĕg`ȧ*se*făl"ĭk), Meg`a*ceph"a*lous (mĕg`ȧ*sĕf"ȧ*lŭs) }, a. [Mega- + Gr. kefalh` head.] (Biol.) Large headed; -- applied to animals, and to plants when they have large flower heads.

megaceros.c: Megaceros ‖Me*gac"e*ros (me*găs"e*rŏs), n. [NL., fr. Gr. me`gas great + ke`ras horn.] (Paleon.) The Irish elk.

megachile.c: Megachile Meg"a*chile (?), n. [Mega- + Gr.? lip.] (Zool.) A leaf-cutting bee of the genus Megachilus. See Leaf cutter, under Leaf.

megacosm.c: Megacosm Meg"a*cosm (?), n. [Mega- + Gr.? world.] See Macrocosm. Croft.

megacoulomb.c: Megacoulomb Meg`a*cou`lomb" (?), n. [Mega- + coulomb.] (Elec.) A million coulombs.

megaderm.c: Megaderm Meg"a*derm (?), n. [Mega- + Gr.? skin.] (Zool.) Any one of several species of Old World blood-sucking bats of the genus Megaderma.

megadyne.c: Megadyne Meg"a*dyne (?), n. [Mega- + dyne.] (Physics) One of the larger measures of force, amounting to one million dynes.

megafarad.c: Megafarad Meg"a*far`ad (?), n. [Mega- + farad.] (Elec.) One of the larger measures of electrical capacitance, amounting to one million farads; a macrofarad.

megalerg.c: Megalerg Meg"a*lerg (?), n. [Megalo- + erg.] (Physics) A million ergs; a megerg.

megalesian.c: Megalesian Meg`a*le"sian (?), a. [L. Megalesius, fr. Gr. Mega`lh the Great, a surname of Cybele, the Magna Mater.] Pertaining to, or in honor of, Cybele; as, the Megalesian games at Rome.

megalethoscope.c: Megalethoscope Meg`a*leth"o*scope (?), n. [Mega- + alethoscope.] An optical apparatus in which pictures are viewed through a large lens with stereoptical effects. It is often combined with the stereoscope.

megalith.c: Megalith Meg"a*lith (?), n. [Mega- + -lith; cf. F. mégalithe.] A large stone; especially, a large stone used in constructing ancient monuments. -- Meg`a*lith"ic (#), a.

megalocephaly.c: Megalocephaly Megalocephalia { ‖Meg`a*lo*ce*pha"li*a (?), Meg`a*lo*ceph"a*ly (?) }, n. [NL. megalocephalia, fr. Gr.? having a large head.] (Med.) The condition of having an abnormally large head; called also megacephaly. -- Meg`a*lo*ce*phal"ic (#), a.

megalocyte.c: Megalocyte Meg"a*lo*cyte (?), n. [Megalo- + Gr.? a hollow vessel.] (Physiol.) A large, flattened red blood cell corpuscle having no nucleus, twice the diameter of the ordinary red corpuscle, found in considerable numbers in the blood in profound anaemia.
