microchemistry.c: micro-chemistry microchemistry mi`cro*chem"is*try, mi`cro-chem"is*try (?), n. [Micro- + chemistry.] The application of chemical tests to minute objects or portions of matter, usually assisted by sensitive instruments; -- distinguished from macro-chemistry.

microcline.c: Microcline Mi"cro*cline (?), n. [Micro- + Gr.? to incline.] (Min.) A mineral of the feldspar group, like orthoclase or common feldspar in composition, but triclinic in form.

micrococcal.c: Micrococcal Mi`cro*coc"cal (?), a. Of or pertaining to micrococci; caused by micrococci. Nature.

micrococcus.c: Micrococcus ‖Mi`cro*coc"cus (?), n.; pl. Micrococci (#). [NL. See Micro-, and Coccus.] (Biol.) A genus of Spherobacteria, in the form of very small globular or oval cells, forming, by transverse division, filaments, or chains of cells, or in some cases single organisms shaped like dumb-bells (Diplococcus), all without the power of motion. See Illust. of Ascoccus.

microcosm.c: Microcosm Mi"cro*cosm (?), n. [F. microcosme, L. microcosmus, fr. Gr. mikro`s small + ko`smos the world.] 1. A little world; a miniature universe. Hence (so called by Paracelsus), a man, as a supposed epitome of the exterior universe or great world. Opposed to macrocosm. Shak.

microcosmical.c: Microcosmical Microcosmic { Mi`cro*cos"mic (?), Mi`cro*cos"mic*al (?), } a. [Cf. F. microcosmique.] Of or pertaining to the microcosm.

microcosmography.c: Microcosmography Mi`cro*cos*mog"ra*phy (?), n. [Microcosm + -graphy.] Description of man as a microcosm.

microcoulomb.c: Microcoulomb Mi`cro*cou`lomb" (?), n. [Micro- + coulomb.] (Elec.) A measure of electrical quantity; the millionth part of one coulomb.

microcoustic.c: Microcoustic Mi`cro*cous"tic (?), a. [Micro- + acoustic: cf. F. microcoustique, micracoustique.] Pertaining, or suited, to the audition of small sounds; fitted to assist hearing.
Microcoustic Mi`cro*cous"tic, n. An instrument for making faint sounds audible, as to a partially deaf person.

microcrith.c: Microcrith Mi`cro*crith" (?), n. [Micro- + crith.] (Chem.) The weight of the half hydrogen molecule, or of the hydrogen atom, at one time taken as the standard in comparing the atomic weights of the elements; thus, an atom of oxygen weighs sixteen microcriths. This unit is no longer used, and has been replaced by the Dalton, which is of approximately the same value. See molecular weight and Crith. J. P. Cooke.

microcrystalline.c: Microcrystalline Mi`cro*crys"tal*line (?), a. [Micro- + crystalline.] (Crystallog.) Crystalline on a fine, or microscopic, scale; consisting of fine crystals; as, the ground mass of certain porphyrics is microcrystalline.

microcyte.c: Microcyte Mi"cro*cyte (?), n. [Micro- + Gr.? a hollow vessel.] (Physiol.) One of the elementary granules found in blood. They are much smaller than an ordinary corpuscle, and are particularly noticeable in disease, as in anaemia.

microdont.c: Microdont Mic"ro*dont (?), a. [Micr- + Gr. 'odoy`s, 'odo`ntos, a tooth.] (Anat.) Having small teeth.

microfarad.c: Microfarad Mi`cro*far"ad (?), n. [Micro- + farad.] (Elec.) The millionth part of a farad.

microform.c: Microform Mi"cro*form (?), n. [Micro- + form, n.] (Biol.) A microscopic form of life; an animal or vegetable organism of microscopic size.

microgeological.c: Micro-geological Mi`cro-ge`o*log"ic*al (?), a. Of or pertaining to micro-geology.

microgeology.c: Micro-geology Mi`cro-ge*ol"o*gy (?), n. [Micro- + geology.] The part of geology relating to structure and organisms which require to be studied with a microscope.

micrograph.c: Micrograph Mi"cro*graph (?), n. [See Micrography.] 1. An instrument for executing minute writing or engraving.

micrographic.c: Micrographic Mi`cro*graph"ic (?), a. Of or pertaining to micrography.

micrography.c: Micrography Mi*crog"ra*phy (?), n. [Micro- + -graphy: cf. F. micrographie.] 1. The description of microscopic objects.

microhm.c: Microhm Mi*crohm" (?), n. [Micr- + ohm.] (Elec.) The millionth part of an ohm.

microlepidoptera.c: Microlepidoptera ‖Mi`cro*lep`i*dop"te*ra (?), n. pl. [NL. See Micro-, and Lepidoptera.] (Zool.) A tribe of Lepidoptera, including a vast number of minute species, as the plume moth, clothes moth, etc.

microlestes.c: Microlestes ‖Mi`cro*les"tes (?), n. [NL., from Gr. mikro`s small +? a robber.] (Paleon.) An extinct genus of small Triassic mammals, the oldest yet found in European strata.

microlith.c: Microlith Mi"cro*lith (?), n. [Micro- + lith.] (Min.) Same as Microlite, 2.

microlithic.c: Microlithic Mi`cro*lith"ic (?), a. Formed of small stones.

micrological.c: Micrological Micrologic { Mi`cro*log"ic (?), Mi`cro*log"ic*al (?), } a. Of or pertaining to micrology; very minute; as, micrologic examination. -- Mi`cro*log"ic*al*ly, adv.

micrology.c: Micrology Mi*crol"o*gy (?), n. [Micro- + -logy.] 1. That part of science which treats of microscopic objects, or depends on microscopic observation.

micromere.c: Micromere Mi"cro*mere (?), n. [Micro- + -mere.] (Biol.) One of the smaller cells, or blastomeres, resulting from the complete segmentation of a telolecithal ovum.

micrometer.c: Micrometer Mi*crom"e*ter (?), n. [Micro- + -meter: cf. F. micromètre.] An instrument, used with a telescope or microscope, for measuring minute distances, or the apparent diameters of objects which subtend minute angles. The measurement given directly is that of the image of the object formed at the focus of the object glass.

micrometrical.c: Micrometrical Micrometric { Mi`cro*met"ric (?), Mi`cro*met"ric*al (?), } a. [Cf. F. micrométrique.] Belonging to micrometry; made by the micrometer. -- Mi`cro*met"ric*al*ly, adv.

micrometry.c: Micrometry Mi*crom"e*try (?), n. The art of measuring with a micrometer.

micromillimeter.c: Micromillimeter Mi`cro*mil"li*me`ter (?), n. [Micro- + millimeter.] The millionth part of a meter.

micron.c: micron mic"ron (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr. mikro`s small.] (Physics) A measure of length; the thousandth part of one millimeter; the millionth part of a meter.

micronesian.c: Micronesian Mi"cro*ne"sian (?), a. [From Micronesia, fr. Gr. mikro`s small + nh^sos an island.] Of or pertaining to Micronesia, a collective designation of the islands in the western part of the Pacific Ocean, embracing the Marshall and Gilbert groups, the Ladrones, the Carolines, etc.

micronesians.c: Micronesians Mi`cro*ne"sians (?), n. pl.; sing. Micronesian. (Ethnol.) A dark race inhabiting the Micronesian Islands. They are supposed to be a mixed race, derived from Polynesians and Papuans.

micronometer.c: Micronometer Mi`cro*nom"e*ter (?), n. [Micro- + chronometer.] An instrument for noting minute portions of time.

microorganism.c: Microorganism Mi`cro*or"gan*ism (?), n. [Micro- + organism.] (Biol.) Any microscopic form of life; a form of life too small to be seen by the naked eye; -- particularly applied to bacteria, protozoa, yeasts, and similar organisms, esp. such are supposed to cause infectious diseases.

micropantograph.c: Micropantograph Mi`cro*pan"to*graph (?), n. [Micro- + pantograph.] A kind of pantograph which produces copies microscopically minute.

microparasite.c: Microparasite Mi`cro*par"a*site (?), n. A parasitic microorganism. -- Mi`cro*par`a*sit"ic (#), a.

micropegmatite.c: Micropegmatite Mi`cro*peg"ma*tite (?), n. [Micro- + pegmatite.] (Min.) A rock showing under the microscope the structure of a graphic granite (pegmatite). -- Mi`cro*peg`ma*tit"ic (#), a.

microphone.c: microphone mi"cro*phone (mī"kro*fōn), n. [Micro- + Gr. fwnh` sound, voice: cf. F. microphone.] (Physics) An instrument for converting sounds into electrical signals, for the purpose of recording or amplifying the sounds. It produces its effects in various ways, as for example by the changes of intensity in an electric current, occasioned by the variations in the contact resistance of conducting bodies, especially of imperfect conductors, under the action of acoustic vibrations. Other forms of microphone may use changes in capacitance or other phenomena to transduce the sounds into electrical signals.

microphonic.c: microphonic mi`cro*phon"ic (mī`kro*fŏn"ĭk), a. Of or pertaining to a microphone; serving to intensify weak sounds.

microphonics.c: microphonics mi`cro*phon"ics (mī`kro*fŏn"ĭks), n. [See Microphone.] The science which treats of the means of increasing the intensity of low or weak sounds, or of the microphone.

microphonous.c: microphonous mi*croph"o*nous (mi*krŏf"o*nŭs or mĭ*krŏf"o*nŭs), a. Serving to augment the intensity of weak sounds; microcoustic.

microphotography.c: Microphotography Mi`cro*pho*tog"ra*phy (?), n. The art of making microphotographs.

microphthalmy.c: Microphthalmy Microphthalmia { Mi`croph*thal"mi*a (?), Mi`croph*thal"my (?), } n. [Micro- + Gr. 'ofqalmo`s eye.] An unnatural smallness of the eyes, occurring as the result of disease or of imperfect development.

microphyllous.c: Microphyllous Mi*croph"yl*lous (?), a. [Micro- + Gr. fy`llon leaf.] (Bot.) Small-leaved.

microphytal.c: Microphytal Mi*croph"y*tal (?), a. (Bot.) Pertaining to, or of the nature of, microphytes.

microphyte.c: Microphyte Mi"cro*phyte (?), n. [Micro- + Gr.? a plant: cf. F. microphyte.] (Bot.) A very minute plant, one of certain unicellular algae, such as the germs of various infectious diseases are believed to be.

micropyle.c: Micropyle Mi"cro*pyle (?), n. [Micro- + Gr.? gate, orifice: cf. F. micropyle.] (Biol.) (a) An opening in the membranes surrounding the ovum, by which nutrition is assisted and the entrance of the spermatozoa permitted. (b) An opening in the outer coat of a seed, through which the fecundating pollen enters the ovule. -- Mi*crop"y*lar (#), a.

microscopal.c: Microscopal Mi*cros"co*pal (?), a. Pertaining to microscopy, or to the use of the microscope. Huxley.

microscope.c: Microscope Mi"cro*scope (?), n. [Micro- + -scope.] An optical instrument, consisting of a lens, or combination of lenses, for making an enlarged image of an object which is too minute to be viewed by the naked eye.

microscopical.c: Microscopical Microscopic { Mi`cro*scop"ic (?), Mi`cro*scop"ic*al (?), } a. [Cf. F. microscopique.]

microscopically.c: Microscopically Mi`cro*scop"ic*al*ly, adv. By the microscope; with minute inspection; in a microscopic manner.

microscopist.c: Microscopist Mi*cros"co*pist (?; 277), n. One skilled in, or given to, microscopy.

microscopy.c: Microscopy Mi*cros"co*py (?), n. The use of the microscope; investigation with the microscope.

microseism.c: Microseism Mi"cro*seism (?), n. [Micro- + Gr.? an earthquake, fr.? to shake.] A feeble earth tremor not directly perceptible, but detected only by means of specially constructed apparatus. -- Mi`cro*seis"mic (#), Mi`cro*seis"mic*al (#), a.

microseismograph.c: Microseismograph Mi`cro*seis"mo*graph (?), n. [Microseiem + -graph.] A microseismometer; specif., a microseismometer producing a graphic record.

microseismology.c: Microseismology Mi`cro*seis*mol"o*gy (?), n. [Microseiem + -logy.] Science or study of microseisms.

microseismometer.c: Microseismometer Mi`cro*seis*mom"e*ter (?), n. [Microseism + -meter.] A seismometer for measuring amplitudes or periods, or both, of microseisms. -- Mi`cro*seis*mom"e*try (#), n.

microseme.c: Microseme Mi"cro*seme (?), a. [Micro- + Gr.? sign, mark: cf. F. microsème.] (Anat.) Having the orbital index relatively small; having the orbits broad transversely; -- opposed to megaseme.

microspectroscope.c: Microspectroscope Mi`cro*spec"tro*scope (mī`kro*spĕk"tro*skōp or mĭ`kro*spĕk"tro*skōp), n. [Micro- + spectroscope.] (Physics) A spectroscope arranged for attachment to a microscope, for observation of the spectrum of light from minute portions of any substance.

microsporangium.c: Microsporangium ‖Mi`cro*spo*ran"gi*um (?), n. [NL. See Micro-, and Sporangium.] (Bot.) A sporangium or conceptacle containing only very minute spores. Cf. Macrosporangium.

microspore.c: Microspore Mi"cro*spore (mī"kro*spōr), n. [Micro- + spore.] (Bot.) One of the exceedingly minute spores found in certain flowerless plants, as Selaginella and Isoetes, which bear two kinds of spores, one very much smaller than the other. Cf. Macrospore.

microsporic.c: Microsporic Mi`cro*spor"ic (?), a. (Bot.) Of or pertaining to microspores.

microsthene.c: Microsthene Mi"cro*sthene (mī"kro*sthēn), n. [Micro- + Gr. sqe`nos might, strength.] (Zool.) One of a group of mammals having a small size as a typical characteristic. It includes the lower orders, as the Insectivora, Cheiroptera, Rodentia, and Edentata.

microsthenic.c: Microsthenic Mi`cro*sthen"ic (?), a. (Zool.) Having a typically small size; of or pertaining to the microsthenes.

microtasimeter.c: Microtasimeter Mi`cro*ta*sim"e*ter (?), n. [Micro- + tasimeter.] (Physics) A tasimeter, especially when arranged for measuring very small extensions. See Tasimeter.

microtome.c: Microtome Mi"cro*tome (mī"kro*tōm), n. [Micro- + Gr. te`mnein to cut.] An instrument for making very thin sections for microscopical examination.

microtomical.c: Microtomical Microtomic { Mi`cro*tom"ic (?), Mi`cro*tom"ic*al (?) }, a. Of or pert. to the microtome or microtomy; cutting thin slices.

microtomist.c: Microtomist Mi*crot"o*mist (?), n. One who is skilled in or practices microtomy.

microtomy.c: Microtomy Mi*crot"o*my (?), n. The art of using the microtome; investigation carried on with the microtome.

microvolt.c: Microvolt Mi`cro*volt" (mī"kro*vōlt`), n. [Micro- + volt.] (Elec.) A measure of electro-motive force; the millionth part of one volt.

microweber.c: Microweber Mi`cro*we"ber (mī`kro*vā"bẽr), n. [Micro- + weber.] (Elec.) The millionth part of one weber.

microzoa.c: Microzoa ‖Mi`cro*zo"a (mī`kro*zō"ȧ), n. pl. [NL., fr. Gr. mikro`s small + zw^,on an animal.] (Zool.) The Infusoria.

microzo0spore.c: Microzo0spore Mi`cro*zo"o*spore (mī`kro*zō"o*spōr), n. [Micro- + zoospore.] (Bot.) A small motile spore furnished with two vibratile cilia, found in certain green algae.

microzyme.c: Microzyme Mi"cro*zyme (?), n. [Micro- + Gr. zy`mh leaven.] (Biol.) A microorganism which is supposed to act like a ferment in causing or propagating certain infectious or contagious diseases; a pathogenic bacterial organism. [obsolete]

micturition.c: Micturition Mic`tu*ri"tion (?), n. [L. micturire to desire to make water, v. desid. fr. mingere, mictum, to make water.] The act of voiding urine; urination; also, a morbidly frequent passing of the urine, in consequence of disease.

mid.c: Mid Mid (mĭd), a. [Compar. wanting; superl. Midmost.] [AS. midd; akin to OS. middi, D. mid (in comp.), OHG. mitti, Icel. miðr, Goth. midjis, L. medius, Gr. me`sos, Skr. madhya. √271. Cf. Amid, Middle, Midst, Mean, Mediate, Meridian, Mizzen, Moiety.]

mida.c: Mida Mi"da (?), n. [Gr.? a destructive insect in pulse.] (Zool.) The larva of the bean fly.

midas.c: Midas Mi"das (?), n. [So called from L. Midas, a man fabled to have had ass's ears.] (Zool.) A genus of longeared South American monkeys, including numerous species of marmosets. See Marmoset.

midass.c: Midas's ear Mi"das's ear" (?). [See Midas.] (Zool.) A pulmonate mollusk (Auricula aurismidae or Ellobium aurismidae); -- so called from resemblance to a human ear.

midbrain.c: Midbrain Mid"brain` (?), n. [Mid, a. + brain.] (Anat.) The middle segment of the brain; the mesencephalon. See Brain.

midday.c: Midday Mid"day` (?), n. [AS. middaeg. See Mid, a., and Day.] The middle part of the day; noon.
Midday Mid"day`, a. Of or pertaining to noon; meridional; as, the midday sun.

midden.c: Midden Mid"den (?), n. [Also midding.] [Cf. Dan. mögdynge, E. muck, and dung.]
Midden crow Mid"den crow" (?). (Zool.) The common European crow. [Prov. Eng.]

middest.c: Middest Mid"dest (?), a.; superl. of Mid. [See Midst.] Situated most nearly in the middle; middlemost; midmost. [Obs.] “ 'Mongst the middest crowd.” Spenser.

middle.c: Middle Mid"dle (mĭd"d'l), a. [OE. middel, AS. middel; akin to D. middel, OHG. muttil, G. mittel. √271. See Mid, a.]

Middle Mid"dle (?), n. [AS. middel. See Middle, a.] The point or part equally distant from the extremities or exterior limits, as of a line, a surface, or a solid; an intervening point or part in space, time, or order of series; the midst; central portion; specif., the waist. Chaucer. “The middle of the land.” Judg. ix. 37.

middleage.c: Middle-age Mid"dle-age` (?), [Middle + age. Cf. Mediaeval.] Of or pertaining to the Middle Ages; mediaeval.

middleaged.c: Middle-aged Mid"dle-aged` (?), a. Being about the middle of the ordinary age of man; early in the century, it was considered between 30 and 50 years old, but by the end of the 19th centruy it was considered as 40 to 60.

middleearth.c: Middle-earth Mid"dle-earth` (?), n. The world, considered as lying between heaven and hell. [Obs.] Shak.

middleground.c: Middle-ground Mid"dle-ground` (?), n. (Paint.) That part of a picture between the foreground and the background.

middlemost.c: Middlemost Mid"dle*most` (?), a. [Cf. Midmost.] Being in the middle, or nearest the middle; midmost.

middler.c: Middler Mid"dler (?), n. One of a middle or intermediate class in some schools and seminaries.

middling.c: Middling Mid"dling (?), a. Of middle rank, state, size, or quality; about equally distant from the extremes; medium; moderate; mediocre; ordinary. “A town of but middling size.” Hallam.

middlings.c: Middlings Mid"dlings (?), n. pl. 1. A combination of the coarser parts of ground wheat the finest bran, separated from the fine flour and coarse bran in bolting; -- formerly regarded as valuable only for feed; but now, after separation of the bran, used for making the best quality of flour. Middlings contain a large proportion of gluten.

middy.c: Middy Mid"dy (?), n.; pl. Middies (?). A colloquial abbreviation of midshipman.

midfeather.c: Midfeather Mid"feath`er (?), n. 1. (Steam Boilers) A vertical water space in a fire box or combustion chamber.

mithgarthr.c: Mithgarthr Midgarth Midgard { Mid"gard (mĭd"gärd), n. Also Mid"garth (-gärth), ‖Mith"garthr (Icel. meth"gärthr') }. [Icel. miðgarðr.] (Teut. Myth.) The middle space or region between heaven and hell, the abode of human beings; the earth.

midge.c: Midge Midge (?), n. [OE. migge, AS. mycge; akin to OS. muggia, D. mug, G. mücke, OHG. mucca, Icel. m?, Sw. mygga, mygg, Dan. myg; perh. named from its buzzing; cf. Gr.? to low, bellow.] (Zool.)

midget.c: Midget Midg"et (?), n. [Dim. of midge.] 1. (Zool.) A minute bloodsucking fly. [Local, U. S.]

midgut.c: Midgut Mid"gut` (?), n. [Mid, a. + gut.] (Anat.) The middle part of the alimentary canal from the stomach, or entrance of the bile duct, to, or including, the large intestine.

midheaven.c: Midheaven Mid"heav`en (?), n. 1. The midst or middle of heaven or the sky.

midland.c: Midland Mid"land (?), a. 1. Being in the interior country; distant from the coast or seashore; as, midland towns or inhabitants. Howell.
Midland Mid"land (?), n. The interior or central region of a country; -- usually in the plural. Drayton.

midmain.c: Midmain Mid"main` (?), n. The middle part of the main or sea. [Poetic] Chapman.

midmost.c: Midmost Mid"most` (?), a. [OE. middemiste. Cf. Foremost.] Middle; middlemost.

midnight.c: Midnight Mid"night` (?), n. [AS. midniht.] The middle of the night; twelve o'clock at night.
Midnight Mid"night`, a. Being in, or characteristic of, the middle of the night; as, midnight studies; midnight gloom. “Midnight shout and revelry.” Milton.
Midnight sun Mid"night` sun. The sun shining at midnight in the arctic or antarctic summer.

midrash.c: Midrash ‖Mid*rash" (?), n.; pl. Midrashim (#), Midrashoth (#). [Heb., explanation.] A talmudic exposition of the Hebrew law, or of some part of it.

midrib.c: Midrib Mid"rib` (?), n. (Bot.) A continuation of the petiole, extending from the base to the apex of the lamina of a leaf.

midriff.c: Midriff Mid"riff (mĭd"rĭf), n. [AS. midhrif; midd mid, middle + hrif bowels, womb; akin to OFries. midref midriff, rif, ref, belly, OHG. href body, and to L. corpus body. See Corpse.] (Anat.) 1. See Diaphragm, n., 2.

midsea.c: Mid-sea Mid sea { Mid" sea", or Mid"-sea" (?) } n. The middle part of the sea or ocean. Milton.

midship.c: Midship Mid"ship`, a. Of or pertaining to, or being in, the middle of a ship.

midships.c: Midships Mid"ships`, adv. [For amidships.] (Naut.) In the middle of a ship; -- properly amidships.
Midships Mid"ships`, n. pl. (Naut.) The timbers at the broadest part of the vessel. R. H. Dana, Jr.

midst.c: Midst Midst (?), n. [From middest, in the middest, for older in middes, where -s is adverbial (orig. forming a genitive), or still older a midde, a midden, on midden. See Mid, and cf. Amidst.]
Midst Midst, prep. In the midst of; amidst. Shak.
Midst Midst, adv. In the middle. [R.] Milton.

midsummer.c: Midsummer Mid"sum`mer (?), n. [AS. midsumor.] The middle of summer. Shak.

midward.c: Midward Mid"ward (?), a. Situated in the middle.
Midward Mid"ward, adv. In or toward the midst.

midway.c: Midway Mid"way` (?), n. The middle of the way or distance; a middle way or course. Shak.
Midway Mid"way`, a. Being in the middle of the way or distance; as, the midway air. Shak.
Midway Mid"way`, adv. In the middle of the way or distance; half way. “She met his glance midway.” Dryden.

midweek.c: Midweek Mid"week` (?), n. The middle of the week. Also used adjectively.

midwife.c: Midwife Mid"wife` (?), n.; pl. Midwives (#). [OE. midwif, fr. AS. mid with (akin to Gr.?) +? woman, wife. Properly, the woman or wife who is attendant upon a woman in childbirth. See Meta-, and Wife.] A woman who assists other women in childbirth; a female practitioner of the obstetric art.
Midwife Mid"wife`, v. t. To assist in childbirth.
Midwife Mid"wife`, v. i. To perform the office of midwife.

midwifery.c: Midwifery Mid"wife`ry (?; 277), n. 1. The art or practice of assisting women in childbirth; obstetrics.

midwinter.c: Midwinter Mid"win`ter (?), n. [AS. midwinter.] The middle of winter. Dryden.

mien.c: Mien Mien (mēn), n. [F. mine; perh. from sane source as mener to lead; cf. E. demean, menace, mine, n.] Aspect; air; manner; demeanor; carriage; bearing.

miff.c: Miff Miff (mĭf), n. [Cf. Prov. G. muff sullenness, sulkiness, muffen to be silky, muffïg sullen, pouting.] A petty falling out; a tiff; a quarrel; offense. Fielding.
Miff Miff, v. t. To offend slightly. [Colloq.]

might.c: Might Might (mīt), imp. of May. [AS. meahte, mihte.]

Might Might, n. [AS. meaht, miht, from the root of magan to be able, E. may; akin to D. magt, OS. maht, G. macht, Icel. māttr, Goth. mahts. √103. See May, v.] Force or power of any kind, whether of body or mind; energy or intensity of purpose, feeling, or action; means or resources to effect an object; strength; force; power; ability; capacity.

mightily.c: Mightily Might"i*ly (?), adv. [From Mighty.] 1. In a mighty manner; with might; with great earnestness; vigorously; powerfully.

mightiness.c: Mightiness Might"i*ness, n. 1. The quality of being mighty; possession of might; power; greatness; high dignity.

mighty.c: Mighty Might"y (?), a. [Compar. Mightier (?); superl. Mightiest.] [AS. meahtig, mihtig; akin to G. mächtig, Goth. mahteigs. See Might, n.]
Mighty Might"y, n.; pl. Mighties (#). A warrior of great force and courage. [R. & Obs.] 1 Chron. xi. 12.
Mighty Might"y, adv. In a great degree; very. [Colloq.] “He was mighty methodical.” Jeffrey.

migniard.c: Migniard Mign"iard (?), a. [F. mignard, akin to mignon. See Minion.] Soft; dainty. [Obs.] B. Jonson.

migniardise.c: Migniardise Mign"iard*ise (?), n. [F. mignardise.] Delicate fondling. [Obs.] B. Jonson.

mignon.c: Mignon Mi"gnon, v. t. To flatter. [R. & Obs.] Danie?.

mignonette.c: Mignonette Mi`gnon*ette" (?), n. [F. mignonnette, dim. of mignon darling. See 2d Minion.] (Bot.) A plant (Reseda odorata) having greenish flowers with orange-colored stamens, and exhaling a delicious fragrance. In Africa it is a low shrub, but further north it is usually an annual herb.

migraine.c: migraine mi*graine" (?), n. [F. migraine, LL. hemigrania, L. hemicrania, hemicranium, Gr. "hmikrani`a; "hmi- half + krani`on skull. See Hemi- and Cranium, and cf. Hemicrania, Migraine.] 1. A kind of intense sick or nervous headache, usually periodical and confined to one side of the head; called also migraine headache. Same as megrim. -- Mi*grain"ous, a.

migrant.c: Migrant Mi"grant (?), a. [L. migrans, p. pr. of migrare. See Migrate.] Migratory. Sir T. Browne.
Migrant Mi"grant (?), n. 1. A migratory bird, person, or other animal.

migrate.c: Migrate Mi"grate (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Migrated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Migrating (?).] [L. migratus, p. p. of migrare to migrate, transfer.]

migration.c: Migration Mi*gra"tion (?), n. [L. migratio: cf. F. migration.] The act of migrating.

mikado.c: Mikado Mi*ka"do (?), n. [Jap.] The popular designation of the hereditary sovereign of Japan; the emperor of Japan.

milady.c: Milady Mi*la"dy (?), n. [F., fr. English.] Lit., my lady; hence (as used on the Continent), an English noblewoman or gentlewoman.

milanese.c: Milanese Mil`an*ese" (?), prop. a. Of or pertaining to Milan in Italy, or to its inhabitants. -- n. sing. & pl. A native or inhabitant of Milan; people of Milan.

milch.c: Milch Milch (?), a. [OE. milche; akin to G. melk, Icel. milkr, mjōlkr, and to E. milk. See Milk.]

mild.c: Mild Mild (mīld), a. [Compar. Milder (?); superl. Mildest.] [AS. milde; akin to OS. mildi, D. & G. mild, OHG. milti, Icel. mildr, Sw. & Dan. mild, Goth. milds; cf. Lith. melas dear, Gr.? gladdening gifts.] Gentle; pleasant; kind; soft; bland; clement; hence, moderate in degree or quality; -- the opposite of harsh, severe, irritating, violent, disagreeable, etc.; -- applied to persons and things; as, a mild disposition; a mild eye; a mild air; a mild medicine; a mild insanity.

milden.c: Milden Mild"en (?), v. t. To make mild, or milder. Lowell.

mildew.c: Mildew Mil"dew (?), n. [AS. meledeáw; akin to OHG. militou, G. mehlthau, mehltau; prob. orig. meaning, honeydew; cf. Goth. milip honey. See Mellifluous, and Dew.] (Bot.) A growth of minute powdery or webby fungi, whitish or of different colors, found on various diseased or decaying substances.
Mildew Mil"dew, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Mildewed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Mildewing.] To taint with mildew; as, mildewed clothing.
Mildew Mil"dew, v. i. To become tainted with mildew.

mildly.c: Mildly Mild"ly (?), adv. In a mild manner.

mildness.c: Mildness Mild"ness, n. The quality or state of being mild; as, mildness of temper; the mildness of the winter.

mile.c: Mile Mile (mīl), n. [AS. mīl, fr. L. millia, milia; pl. of mille a thousand, i. e., milia passuum a thousand paces. Cf. Mill the tenth of a cent, Million.] A certain measure of distance, being equivalent in England and the United States to 320 poles or rods, or 5,280 feet.

mileage.c: Mileage Mile"age (mīl"aj; 48), n. 1. An allowance for traveling expenses at a certain rate per mile.

milepost.c: Milepost Mile"post` (?), n. 1. A post, or one of a series of posts, set up to indicate spaces of a mile each or the distance in miles from a given place.

milesian.c: Milesian Mi*le"sian, n. 1. A native or inhabitant of Miletus.

milestone.c: Milestone Mile"stone` (?), n. 1. A stone serving the same purpose as a milepost.

milfoil.c: Milfoil Mil"foil (?), n. [F. mille-feuille, L. millefolium; mille thousand + folium leaf. See Foil a leaf.] (Bot.) A common composite herb (Achillea Millefolium) with white flowers and finely dissected leaves; yarrow.

miliaria.c: Miliaria ‖Mil`i*a"ri*a (?), n. [NL. See Miliary.] (Med.) A fever accompanied by an eruption of small, isolated, red pimples, resembling a millet seed in form or size; miliary fever.

miliary.c: Miliary Mil"ia*ry (?; 277), a. [L. miliarius, fr. milium millet: cf. F. miliaire.]
Miliary Mil"ia*ry, n. (Zool.) One of the small tubercles of Echini.

milieu.c: Milieu ‖Mi`lieu" (me*lyẽ"), n. [F., fr. mi middle (L. medius) + lieu place. See Demi-, Lieu.] Environment.

miliola.c: Miliola ‖Mil"i*o`la (?), n. [NL., dim. of L. milium millet. So named from its resemblance to millet seed.] (Zool.) A genus of Foraminifera, having a porcelanous shell with several longitudinal chambers.

miliolite.c: Miliolite Mil"i*o*lite (?), n. (Paleon.) A fossil shell of, or similar to, the genus Miliola.

miliolitic.c: Miliolitic Mil`i*o*lit"ic (?), a. Of or pertaining to the genus Miliola; containing miliolites.

militant.c: Militant Mil"i*tant (?), a. [L. militans, -antis, p. pr. of militare to be soldier: cf. F. militant. See Militate.] Engaged in warfare; fighting; combating; serving as a soldier. -- Mil"i*tant*ly, adv.

militarily.c: Militarily Mil"i*ta*ri*ly (?), adv. In a military manner.

militarist.c: Militarist Mil"i*ta*rist (?), n. 1. A military man. [Obs.] Shak.

military.c: Military Mil"i*ta*ry (?), a. [L. militaris, militarius, from miles, militis, soldier: cf. F. militaire.]
Military Mil"i*ta*ry, n. [Cf. F. militaire.] The whole body of soldiers; soldiery; militia; troops; the army.

militate.c: Militate Mil"i*tate (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Militated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Militating (?).] [L. militare, militatum, to be a soldier, fr. miles, militis, soldier.] To make war; to fight; to contend; -- usually followed by against and with.

militia.c: Militia Mi*li"tia (?), n. [L., military service, soldiery, fr. miles, militis, soldier: cf. F. milice.]

militiaman.c: Militiaman Mi*li"tia*man (?), n.; pl. Militiamen (?). One who belongs to the militia.

militiate.c: Militiate Mi*li"ti*ate (?), v. i. To carry on, or prepare for, war. [Obs.] Walpole.

milk.c: Milk Milk (mĭlk), n. [AS. meoluc, meoloc, meolc, milc; akin to OFries. meloc, D. melk, G. milch, OHG. miluh, Icel. mjōlk, Sw. mjölk, Dan. melk, Goth. miluks, G. melken to milk, OHG. melchan, Lith. milszti, L. mulgere, Gr. 'ame`lgein. √107. Cf. Milch, Emulsion, Milt soft roe of fishes.]
Milk Milk (mĭlk), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Milked (mĭlkt); p. pr. & vb. n. Milking.]
Milk Milk (?), v. i. 1. To draw or to yield milk.

Milk sickness Milk sickness. (Veter., Med.) A peculiar malignant disease, occurring in parts of the western United States, and affecting certain kinds of farm stock (esp. cows), and persons using the meat or dairy products of infected cattle. Its chief symptoms in man are uncontrollable vomiting, obstinate constipation, pain, and muscular tremors. Its origin in cattle has been variously ascribed to the presence of certain plants in their food, and to polluted water.
Milk vetch Milk" vetch` (?). (Bot.) A leguminous herb (Astragalus glycyphyllos) of Europe and Asia, supposed to increase the secretion of milk in goats.

milker.c: Milker Milk"er (?), n. 1. One who milks; also, a mechanical apparatus for milking cows.

milkful.c: Milkful Milk"ful (?), a. Full of milk; abounding with food. [R.] “Milkful vales.” Sylvester.

milkily.c: Milkily Milk"i*ly (?), adv. In a milky manner.

milkiness.c: Milkiness Milk"i*ness, n. State or quality of being milky.

milkmaid.c: Milkmaid Milk"maid` (?), n. A woman who milks cows or is employed in the dairy.

milkman.c: Milkman Milk"man (?), n.; pl. Milkmen (?). A man who sells milk or delivers it to customers.

milksop.c: Milksop Milk"sop` (?), n. A piece of bread sopped in milk; figuratively, an effeminate or weak-minded person. Shak.

milkweed.c: Milkweed Milk"weed` (?), n. (Bot.) Any plant of the genera Asclepias and Acerates, abounding in a milky juice, and having its seed attached to a long silky down; silkweed. The name is also applied to several other plants with a milky juice, as to several kinds of spurge. Its leaves are a favorite food source for the larvae of the monarch butterfly.

milkwort.c: Milkwort Milk"wort` (?), n. (Bot.) A genus of plants (Polygala) of many species. The common European Polygala vulgaris was supposed to have the power of producing a flow of milk in nurses.

milky.c: Milky Milk"y (?), a. 1. Consisting of, or containing, milk.

mill.c: Mill Mill (mĭl), n. [L. mille a thousand. Cf. Mile.] A money of account of the United States, having the value of the tenth of a cent, or the thousandth of a dollar.

Mill Mill, n. [OE. mille, melle, mulle, milne, AS. myln, mylen; akin to D. molen, G. mühle, OHG. mulī, mulīn, Icel. mylna; all prob. from L. molina, fr. mola millstone; prop., that which grinds, akin to molere to grind, Goth. malan, G. mahlen, and to E. meal. √108. See Meal flour, and cf. Moline.]
Mill Mill (mĭl), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Milled (mĭld); p. pr. & vb. n. Milling.] [See Mill, n., and cf. Muller.]
Mill Mill, v. i. (Zool.) To swim under water; -- said of air-breathing creatures.
Mill Mill, v. t. 1. (Mining) To fill (a winze or interior incline) with broken ore, to be drawn out at the bottom.

millboard.c: Millboard Mill"board` (mĭl"bōrd`), n. A kind of stout pasteboard.

millcake.c: Mill-cake Mill"-cake` (mĭl"kāk`), n. The incorporated materials for gunpowder, in the form of a dense mass or cake, ready to be subjected to the process of granulation.

milldam.c: Milldam Mill"dam` (mĭl"dăm), n. A dam or mound to obstruct a water course, and raise the water to a height sufficient to turn a mill wheel.

milled.c: Milled Milled (mĭld), a. 1. Having been subjected to some process of milling.

millefiore.c: Millefiore glass Mil`le*fi*o"re glass` (?). [It. mille thousand + fiore flower.] Slender rods or tubes of colored glass fused together and embedded in clear glass; -- used for paperweights and other small articles.

millenarian.c: Millenarian Mil`le*na"ri*an (?), a. [See Millenary.] Consisting of a thousand years; of or pertaining to the millennium, or to the Millenarians.
Millenarian Mil`le*na"ri*an, n. One who believes that Christ will personally reign on earth a thousand years; a Chiliast.

millenarism.c: Millenarism Millenarianism { Mil`le*na"ri*an*ism (?), Mil"le*na*rism (?), } n. The doctrine of Millenarians.

millenary.c: Millenary Mil"le*na*ry (?), a. [L. millenarius, fr. milleni a thousand each, fr. mille a thousand: cf. F. millénaire. See Mile.] Consisting of a thousand; millennial.
Millenary Mil"le*na*ry, n. The space of a thousand years; a millennium; also, a Millenarian.“During that millenary.” Hare.

millennial.c: Millennial Mil*len"ni*al (?), a. Of or pertaining to the millennium, or to a thousand years; as, a millennial period; millennial happiness.

millennialist.c: Millennialist Mil*len"ni*al*ist, n. One who believes that Christ will reign personally on earth a thousand years; a Chiliast; also, a believer in the universal prevalence of Christianity for a long period.

millenniarism.c: Millenniarism Millennianism { Mil*len"ni*an*ism (?), Mil*len"ni*a*rism (?), } n. Belief in, or expectation of, the millennium{2}; millenarianism.

millennist.c: Millennist Mil"len*nist (mĭl"lĕn*nĭst), n. One who believes in the millennium{2}. [Obs.] Johnson.

millennium.c: Millennium Mil*len"ni*um (mĭl*lĕn"nĭ*ŭm), n. [LL., fr. L. mille a thousand + annus a year. See Mile, and Annual.] 1. A period of one thousand years.

milleped.c: Milleped Mil"le*ped (mĭl"le*pĕdĭ), n. [L. millepeda; mille a thousand + pes, pedis, foot: cf. F. mille-pieds.] (Zool.) A myriapod with many legs, esp. a chilognath, as the galleyworm. [Written also millipede and milliped.]

millepora.c: Millepora ‖Mil*le*po"ra (mĭl*le*pō"rȧ), n. [NL.] (Zool.) A genus of Hydrocorallia, which includes the millipores.

millepore.c: Millepore Mil"le*pore (mĭl"le*pōr), n. [L. mille thousand + porus pore: cf. F. millépore.] (Zool.) Any coral of the genus Millepora, having the surface nearly smooth, and perforated with very minute unequal pores, or cells. The animals are hydroids, not Anthozoa. See Hydrocorallia.

miller.c: Miller Mill"er (mĭl"ẽr), n. 1. One who keeps or attends a flour mill or gristmill.

millerite.c: Millerite Mil"ler*ite (?), n. A believer in the doctrine of William Miller (d. 1849), who taught that the end of the world and the second coming of Christ were at hand.

Millerite Mil"ler*ite, n. [From W. H. Miller, of Cambridge, Eng.] (Min.) A sulphide of nickel, commonly occurring in delicate capillary crystals, also in incrustations of a bronze yellow; -- sometimes called hair pyrites.

millesimal.c: Millesimal Mil*les"i*mal (?), a. [L. millesimus, fr. mille a thousand.] Thousandth; consisting of thousandth parts; as, millesimal fractions.

millet.c: millet mil"let (mĭl"lĕt), n. [F., dim. of mil, L. milium; akin to Gr. meli`nh, AS. mil.] (Bot.) The name of several cereal and forage grasses which bear an abundance of small roundish grains. The common millets of Germany and Southern Europe are Panicum miliaceum, and Setaria Italica.

milli.c: Milli- Mil"li- (mĭl"lĭ-). [From L. mille a thousand.] (Metric System, Elec., Mech., etc.) A prefix denoting a thousandth part of; as, millimeter, milligram, milliampère.

milliampere.c: Milliampere Mil`li*am`père" (mĭl"lĭ*äN`pâr"), n. [Milli- + ampère.] (Elec.) The thousandth part of one ampere.

milliard.c: Milliard ‖Mil`liard" (F. mel`yȧr"; E. mĭl"lĭ*ärd), n. [F., from mille, mil, thousand, L. mille.] A thousand millions; -- usually called billion in the United States. See Billion.

milliary.c: Milliary Mil"li*a*ry (mĭl"lĭ*a*ry̆), a. [L. milliarius containing a thousand, fr. mille thousand: cf. F. milliaire milliary. See Mile.] Of or pertaining to a mile, or to distance by miles; denoting a mile or miles.
Milliary Mil"li*a*ry, n.; pl. Milliaries (#). [L. milliarium. See Milliary, a.] A milestone.

millier.c: Millier ‖Mil`lier" (?), n. [F., fr. mille thousand.] A weight of the metric system, being one million grams; a metric ton.

millifold.c: Millifold Mil"li*fold` (?), a. [L. mille thousand + E. fold times.] Thousandfold. [R.] Davies (Holy Roode).

milligramme.c: Milligramme Milligram { Mil"li*gram, Mil"li*gramme } (?), n. [F. milligramme; milli- milli- + gramme. See 3d Gram.] A measure of mass and weight, in the metric system, being the thousandth part of a gram, very nearly equal to the weight of a cubic millimeter of water, or.01543 of a grain avoirdupois.

millilitre.c: Millilitre Milliliter { Mil"li*li`ter, Mil"li*li`tre } (?), n. [F. millilitre; milli- milli- + litre. See Liter.] A measure of capacity in the metric system, containing the thousandth part of a liter. It is very nearly equal to a cubic centimeter, and is equal to.061025 of an English cubic inch, or to.033815 of an American fluid ounce.

millimetre.c: Millimetre Millimeter { Mil"li*me`ter, Mil"li*me`tre } (?), n. [F. millimètre; milli- milli- + mètre. See 3d Meter.] A lineal measure in the metric system, containing the thousandth part of a meter; equal to.03937 of an inch. See 3d Meter.

millimicron.c: Millimicron Mil"li*mi`cron (?), n. [Milli- + micron.] The thousandth part of a micron or the millionth part of a millimeter; one nanometer; -- a unit of length sometimes used in measuring light waves, etc.

milliner.c: Milliner Mil"li*ner (?), n. [From Milaner an inhabitant of Milan, in Italy; hence, a man from Milan who imported women's finery.]

millinery.c: Millinery Mil"li*ner*y (?), n. 1. The articles made or sold by milliners, as headdresses, hats or bonnets, laces, ribbons, and the like.

millinet.c: Millinet Mil`li*net" (?), n. A stiff cotton fabric used by milliners for lining bonnets.

milling.c: Milling Mill"ing (?), n. The act or employment of grinding or passing through a mill; the process of fulling; the process of making a raised or intented edge upon coin, etc.; the process of dressing surfaces of various shapes with rotary cutters. See Mill.

million.c: Million Mil"lion (mĭl"yŭn), n. [F., from LL. millio, fr. L. mille a thousand. See Mile.] 1. The number of ten hundred thousand, or a thousand thousand, -- written 1,000,000. See the Note under Hundred.

millionaire.c: Millionaire Mil`lion*aire" (?; 277), n. [F. millionnaire.] One whose wealth is counted by millions of francs, dollars, or pounds; a very rich person; a person worth a million or more. [Written also millionnaire.]

millionairess.c: Millionairess Mil`lion*air"ess, n. A woman who is a millionaire, or the wife of a millionaire. [Humorous] Holmes.

millionary.c: Millionary Mil"lion*a*ry (?), a. Of or pertaining to millions; consisting of millions; as, the millionary chronology of the pundits. Pinkerton.

millioned.c: Millioned Mil"lioned (?), a. Multiplied by millions; innumerable. [Obs.] Shak.

millionth.c: Millionth Mil"lionth (?), a. Being the last one of a million of units or objects counted in regular order from the first of a series or succession; being one of a million.
Millionth Mil"lionth, n. The quotient of a unit divided by one million; one of a million equal parts.

millistere.c: Millistere Mil"li*stere (?), n. [F. millistère, from milli- milli- + stère.] A liter, or cubic decimeter.

milliweber.c: Milliweber Mil`li*we"ber (?), n. [Milli- + weber.] (Physics) The thousandth part of one weber.

millreis.c: Millreis Millree Millrea { Mill"rea` (mĭl"rē`), Mill"ree`, Mill"reis` (mĭl"rēs`) }, n. See Milreis.

millrynd.c: Millrynd Millrind { Mill"rind` (mĭl"rīnd`), Mill"rynd` (mĭl"rīnd`) }, n. [Mill + rynd.] (Her.) A figure supposed to represent the iron which holds a millstone by being set into its center.

millsixpence.c: Mill-sixpence Mill"-sixpence (?), n. A milled sixpence; -- the sixpence being one of the first English coins milled (1561).

millstone.c: Millstone Mill"stone` (?), n. One of two circular stones used for grinding grain or other substance in a mill{1}.

millwork.c: Millwork Mill"work` (?), n. 1. The shafting, gearing, and other driving machinery of mills.

millwright.c: Millwright Mill"wright` (?), n. A mechanic whose occupation is to build mills, or to set up their machinery.

milord.c: Milord Mi*lord" (?), n. [F. (also It., Sp., Russ.), fr. E. my lord.] Lit., my lord; hence (as used on the Continent), an English nobleman or gentleman.

milreis.c: Milreis Mil"reis` (?), n. [Pg. mil reis, i. e., one thousand reis; mil a thousand + reis, pl. of real a rei.] A Portuguese money of account rated in the treasury department of the United States at one dollar and eight cents; also, a Brazilian money of account rated at fifty-four cents and six mills (1913).

milt.c: Milt Milt (?), n. [AS. milte; akin to D. milt, G. milz, OHG. milzi, Icel. milti, Dan. milt, Sw. mjälte, and prob. to E. malt, melt. √108. See Malt the grain.] (Anat.) The spleen.
Milt Milt, n. [Akin to Dan. melk, Sw. mjölke, G. milch, and E. milk. See Milk.] (Zool.) (a) The spermatic fluid of fishes. (b) The testes, or spermaries, of fishes when filled with spermatozoa.
Milt Milt, v. t. To impregnate (the roe of a fish) with milt.

milter.c: Milter Milt"er (?), n. [Cf. D. milter, G. milcher, milchner. See 2d Milt.] (Zool.) A male fish.

miltonic.c: Miltonic Mil*ton"ic (?), prop. a. Of, pertaining to, or resembling, Milton, or his writings; as, Miltonic prose.

miltwaste.c: Miltwaste Milt"waste` (?), [1st milt + waste.] (Bot.) A small European fern (Asplenium Ceterach) formerly used in medicine.

milvine.c: Milvine Mil"vine (?), a. [L. milvus kite.] (Zool.) Of or resembling birds of the kite kind.
Milvine Mil"vine, n. (Zool.) A bird related to the kite.

milvus.c: Milvus ‖Mil"vus (?), n. [L., a kite.] (Zool.) A genus of raptorial birds, including the European kite.

mime.c: Mime Mime (?), n. [L. mimus, Gr.?, akin to? to imitate, to mimic: cf. F. mime. Cf. Mimosa.] 1. A kind of drama in which real persons and events were generally represented in a ridiculous manner; an ancient Greek or Roman form of farce.
Mime Mime, v. i. To mimic. [Obs.] -- Mim"er (#), n.

mimeograph.c: Mimeograph Mim"e*o*graph (?), n. [Gr.? to imitate + -graph.] A copying device that uses a stencil through which ink is pressed; it was invented by Edison.

mimesis.c: Mimesis ‖Mi*me"sis (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr.? imitation.] (Rhet. & Biol.) Imitation; mimicry.

mimetical.c: Mimetical Mimetic { Mi*met"ic (?; 277), Mi*met"ic*al (?), }[Gr.?, fr.? to imitate.]

mimetism.c: Mimetism Mim"e*tism (?), n. [From Gr.? to mimic.] (Biol.) Same as Mimicry.

mimetite.c: Mimetite Mim"e*tite (?), n. [Gr.? an imitator. So called because it resembles pyromorphite.] (Min.) A mineral occurring in pale yellow or brownish hexagonal crystals. It is an arseniate of lead.

mimical.c: Mimical Mimic { Mim"ic (?), Mim"ic*al (?), } a. [L. mimicus, Gr.?, fr.? mime: cf. F. mimique. See Mime.]

mimic.c: Mimic Mim"ic, n. One who imitates or mimics, especially one who does so for sport; a copyist; a buffoon. Burke.
Mimic Mim"ic, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Mimicked (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Mimicking.]

mimically.c: Mimically Mim"ic*al*ly (?), adv. In an imitative manner.

mimicker.c: Mimicker Mim"ick*er (?), n. 1. One who mimics; a mimic.

mimicry.c: Mimicry Mim"ic*ry (?), n. 1. The act or practice of one who mimics; ludicrous imitation for sport or ridicule.

mimographer.c: Mimographer Mi*mog"ra*pher (?), n. [L. mimographus, Gr.?;? a mime +? to write: cf. F. mimographe.] A writer of mimes. Sir T. Herbert.

mimosa.c: Mimosa ‖Mi*mo"sa (?; 277), n. [NL., fr. Gr.? imitator. Cf. Mime.] (Bot.) A genus of leguminous plants, containing many species, and including the sensitive plants (Mimosa sensitiva, and Mimosa pudica).

mimotannic.c: Mimotannic Mi`mo*tan"nic (?), a. [Mimosa + tannic.] (Chem.) Pertaining to, or designating, a variety of tannin or tannic acid found in Acacia, Mimosa, etc.

mina.c: mina ‖mi"na (?), n.; pl. L. Minae (#), E. Minas (#). [L., fr. Gr.?.] An ancient weight or denomination of money, of varying value. The Attic mina was valued at a hundred drachmas.

minable.c: Minable Min"a*ble (?), a. Such as can be mined; as, minable earth. Sir T. North.

minacious.c: Minacious Mi*na"cious (?), a. [L. minax, -acis. See Menace.] Threatening; menacing. [R.]

minaret.c: Minaret Min"a*ret (?), n. [Sp. minarete, Ar. manārat lamp, lantern, lighthouse, turret, fr. nār to shine.] (Arch.) A slender, lofty tower attached to a mosque and surrounded by one or more projecting balconies, from which the summon to prayer is cried by the muezzin.

minargent.c: Minargent Min*ar"gent (?), n. [Prob. contr. from aluminium + L. argentum silver.] An alloy consisting of copper, nickel, tungsten, and aluminium; -- used by jewelers.

minatorily.c: Minatorily Minatorially { Min`a*to"ri*al*ly (?), Min"a*to*ri*ly (?) }, adv. In a minatory manner; with threats.

minatory.c: Minatory Min"a*to*ry (?), a. [L. minatorius, fr. minari to threaten. See Menace.] Threatening; menacing. Bacon.

mince.c: Mince Mince (mĭns), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Minced (mĭnst); p. pr. & vb. n. Minging (mĭn"sĭng).] [AS. minsian to grow less, dwindle, fr. min small; akin to G. minder less, Goth. minniza less, mins less, adv., L. minor, adj. (cf. Minor); or more likely fr. F. mincer to mince, prob. from (assumed) LL. minutiare. √101. See Minish.]
Mince Mince, v. i. 1. To walk with short steps; to walk in a prim, affected manner.
Mince Mince, n. A short, precise step; an affected manner.
Mince pie Mince" pie` (?). A pie made of mince-meat.

mincemeat.c: Mince-meat Mince"-meat` (?), n. Minced meat; meat chopped very fine; a mixture of boiled meat, suet, apples, etc., chopped very fine, to which spices and raisins are added; -- used in making mince pie.

mincing.c: Mincing Min"cing (?), a. That minces; characterized by primness or affected nicety.

mincingly.c: Mincingly Min"cing*ly, adv. In a mincing manner; not fully; with affected nicety.

mind.c: Mind Mind (mīnd), n. [AS. mynd, gemynd; akin to OHG. minna memory, love, G. minne love, Dan. minde mind, memory, remembrance, consent, vote, Sw. minne memory, Icel. minni, Goth. gamunds, L. mens, mentis, mind, Gr. me`nos, Skr. manas mind, man to think. √104, 278. Cf. Comment, Man, Mean, v., 3d Mental, Mignonette, Minion, Mnemonic, Money.]

Mind Mind (mīnd), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Minded; p. pr. & vb. n. Minding.] [AS. myndian, gemyndīan to remember. See Mind, n.] 1. To fix the mind or thoughts on; to regard with attention; to treat as of consequence; to consider; to heed; to mark; to note. “Mind not high things, but condescend to men of low estate.” Rom. xii. 16.
Mind Mind, v. i. To give attention or heed; to obey; as, the dog minds well.

minded.c: Minded Mind"ed, a. Disposed; inclined; having a mind.

minder.c: Minder Mind"er (?), n. 1. One who minds, tends, or watches something, as a child, a machine, or cattle; as, a minder of a loom.

mindful.c: Mindful Mind"ful (?), a. Bearing in mind; regardful; attentive; heedful; observant.

mindless.c: Mindless Mind"less, a. 1. Not indued with mind or intellectual powers; stupid; unthinking.

mine.c: Mine Mine (mīn), pron. & a. [OE. min, fr. AS. mīn; akin to D. mijn, OS., OFries., & OHG. mīn, G. mein, Sw. & Dan. min, Icel. minn, Goth. meins my, mine, meina of me, and E. me. √187. See Me, and cf. My.] Belonging to me; my. Used as a pronominal to me; my. Used as a pronominal adjective in the predicate; as, “Vengeance is mine; I will repay.” Rom. xii. 19. Also, in the old style, used attributively, instead of my, before a noun beginning with a vowel.

Mine Mine, v. i. [F. miner, L. minare to drive animals, in LL. also, to lead, conduct, dig a mine (cf. E. lode, and lead to conduct), akin to L. minari to threaten; cf. Sp. mina mine, conduit, subterraneous canal, a spring or source of water, It. mina. See Menace, and cf. Mien.]
Mine Mine, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Mined (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Mining.]
Mine Mine, n. [F., fr. LL. mina. See Mine, v. i.]

mineral.c: Mineral Min"er*al (?), n. [F. minéral, LL. minerale, fr. minera mine. See Mine, v. i.]
Mineral Min"er*al, a. 1. Of or pertaining to minerals; consisting of a mineral or of minerals; as, a mineral substance.

mineralist.c: Mineralist Min"er*al*ist, n. [Cf. F. minéraliste.] One versed in minerals; mineralogist. [R.]

mineralize.c: Mineralize Min"er*al*ize (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Mineralized (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Mineralizing (?).] [Cf. F. minéraliser.]
Mineralize Min"er*al*ize, v. i. To go on an excursion for observing and collecting minerals; to mineralogize.

mineralizer.c: Mineralizer Min"er*al*i`zer (?), n. An element which is combined with a metal, thus forming an ore. Thus, in galena, or lead ore, sulphur is a mineralizer; in hematite, oxygen is a mineralizer.

mineralogical.c: Mineralogical Min`er*al*og"ic*al (?), a. [Cf. F. minéralogique. See Mineralogy.] Of or pertaining to mineralogy; as, a mineralogical table.

mineralogically.c: Mineralogically Min`er*al*og"ic*al*ly, adv. According to the principles of, or with reference to, mineralogy.

mineralogize.c: Mineralogize Min`er*al"o*gize (?), v. i. To study mineralogy by collecting and examining minerals. Miss Edgeworth.

mineralogy.c: Mineralogy Min`er*al"o*gy (?), n.; pl. Mineralogies (#). [Mineral + -logy: cf. F. minéralogie.]

minerva.c: Minerva Mi*ner"va (?), n. [L.] (Rom. Myth.) The goddess of wisdom, of war, of the arts and sciences, of poetry, and of spinning and weaving; -- identified with the Grecian Pallas Athene.

minette.c: Minette Mi*nette" (?), n. The smallest of regular sizes of portrait photographs.

minge.c: Minge Minge (?), v. t. [AS. myngian; akin to E. mind.] To mingle; to mix. [Obs.]
Minge Minge, n. [Prob. corrupt. fr. midge.] (Zool.) A small biting fly; a midge. [Local, U. S.]

mingle.c: Mingle Min"gle (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Mingled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Mingling (?).] [From OE. mengen, AS. mengan; akin to D. & G. mengen, Icel. menga, also to E. among, and possibly to mix. Cf. Among, Mongrel.]
Mingle Min"gle, v. i. 1. To become mixed or blended.

mingleable.c: Mingleable Min"gle*a*ble (?), a. That can be mingled. Boyle.

minglemangle.c: Mingle-mangle Min"gle-man`gle (?), v. t. [Reduplicated fr. mingle.] To mix in a disorderly way; to make a mess of. [Obs.] Udall.

minglement.c: Minglement Min"gle*ment (?), n. The act of mingling, or the state of being mixed.

minglingly.c: Minglingly Min"gling*ly (?), adv. In a mingling manner.

minaceous.c: Minaceous Min`*a"ceous (?), a. Of the color of minium or red lead; miniate.

miniardize.c: Miniardize Min"iard*ize (?), v. t. To render delicate or dainty. [Obs.] Howell.

miniate.c: Miniate Min"i*ate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Miniated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Miniating (?).] [L. miniatus, p. p. of miniare. See Minium.] To paint or tinge with red lead or vermilion; also, to decorate with letters, or the like, painted red, as the page of a manuscript. T. Wharton.
Miniate Min"i*ate (?), a. Of or pertaining to the color of red lead or vermilion; painted with vermilion.

miniature.c: Miniature Min"i*a*ture (?; 277), n. [It. miniatura, fr. L. miniare. See Miniate, v.,Minium.]
Miniature Min"i*a*ture, a. Being on a small scale; much reduced from the reality; as, a miniature copy.
Miniature Min"i*a*ture, v. t. To represent or depict in a small compass, or on a small scale.

miniaturist.c: Miniaturist Min"i*a*tur`ist (?), n. A painter of miniatures.

minibus.c: Minibus Min"i*bus (?), n. [L. minor less + -bus, as in omnibus.] 1. A kind of light passenger vehicle, carrying four persons. [archaic]

minie.c: Minie ball Min"ie ball` (?). [From the inventor, Captain Minié, of France.] A conical rifle bullet, with a cavity in its base plugged with a piece of iron, which, by the explosion of the charge, is driven farther in, expanding the sides to fit closely the grooves of the barrel.
Minie rifle Min"ie ri"fle (?). A rifle adapted to minie balls.

minify.c: Minify Min"i*fy (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Minified (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Minifying (?).] [L. minor less + -fly.]

minikin.c: Minikin Min"i*kin (?), n. [OD. minneken a darling, dim. of minne love; akin to G. minne, and to E. mind.]

minim.c: Minim Min"im (?), n. [F. minime, L. minimus the least, smallest, a superl. of minor: cf. It. minima a note in music. See Minor, and cf. Minimum.]
Minim Min"im, a. Minute. “Minim forms.” J. R. Drake.

minimal.c: Minimal Min"i*mal (?), a. Of, pertaining to, or having a character of, a minim or minimum; least; smallest; as, a minimal amount or value.

miniment.c: Miniment Min"i*ment (?), n. [Prob. corrupt. of moniment.] A trifle; a trinket; a token. [Obs.] Spenser.

minimization.c: Minimization Min`i*mi*za"tion (?), n. The act or process of minimizing. Bentham.

minimize.c: minimize min"i*mize (mĭn"ĭ*mīz), v. t. [imp. & p. p. minimized (mĭn"ĭ*mīzd); p. pr. & vb. n. minimizing (mĭn"ĭ*mī*zĭng).] 1. To reduce to the smallest part or proportion possible; to reduce to a minimum. Bentham.

minimum.c: Minimum Min"i*mum (?), n.; pl. Minima (#). [L., fr. minimus. See Minim.] The least quantity assignable, admissible, or possible, in a given case; hence, a thing of small consequence; -- opposed to maximum.

minimus.c: Minimus ‖Min"i*mus (?), n.; pl. Minimi (#). [L. See Minim.] 1. A being of the smallest size. [Obs.] Shak.

mining.c: Mining Min"ing (?), n. [See Mine, v. i.] The act or business of making mines or of working them.
Mining Min"ing, a. Of or pertaining to mines; as, mining engineer; mining machinery; a mining region.

minion.c: Minion Min"ion, n. [F. mignon, fr. OHG. minni love, G. minne; akin to E. mind. See Mind, and cf. Mignonette.]
Minion Min"ion, a. [See 2d Minion.] Fine; trim; dainty. [Obs.] “Their... minion dancing.” Fryth.

minionette.c: Minionette Min`ion*ette" (?), a. Small; delicate. [Obs.] “His minionette face.” Walpole.
Minionette Min"ion*ette, n. (Print.) A size of type between nonpareil and minion; -- used in ornamental borders, etc.

minionly.c: Minionly Minionlike { Min"ion*like` (?), Min"ion*ly, } a. & adv. Like a minion; daintily. Camden.

minionship.c: Minionship Min"ion*ship, n. State of being a minion. [R.]

minious.c: Minious Min"ious (?), a. [L. minium red lead.] Of the color of red or vermilion. [Obs.] Sir T. Browne.

minish.c: Minish Min"ish (?), v. t. [OE. menusen, F. menuiser to make small, cut small, fr. (assumed) LL. minutiare, for minutare, fr. L. minutus small. See Minute, a., and cf. Diminish, Minge.] To diminish; to lessen.

minishment.c: Minishment Min"ish*ment (?), n. The act of diminishing, or the state of being diminished; diminution. [Obs.]

minister.c: Minister Min"is*ter (?), n. [OE. ministre, F. ministre, fr. L. minister, orig. a double comparative from the root of minor less, and hence meaning, an inferior, a servant. See 1st Minor, and cf. Master, Minstrel.]

Minister Min"is*ter, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Ministered (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Ministering.] [OE. ministren, OF. ministrer, fr. L. ministrare. See Minister, n.] To furnish or apply; to afford; to supply; to administer.
Minister Min"is*ter, v. i. 1. To act as a servant, attendant, or agent; to attend and serve; to perform service in any office, sacred or secular.

ministerial.c: Ministerial Min`is*te"ri*al (?), a. [L. ministerialis: cf. F. ministériel. See Minister, and cf. Minstrel.]

ministerialist.c: Ministerialist Min`is*te"ri*al*ist, n. A supporter of the ministers, or the party in power.

ministerially.c: Ministerially Min`is*te"ri*al*ly, adv. In a ministerial manner; in the character or capacity of a minister.

ministrant.c: Ministrant Min"is*trant (mĭn"ĭs*traint), a. [L. ministrans, -antis, of ministrare to minister.] Performing service as a minister; attendant on service; acting under command; subordinate. “Princedoms and dominations ministrant.” Milton. -- n. One who ministers.

ministration.c: Ministration Min`is*tra"tion (?), n. [L. ministratio, fr. ministrare.] The act of ministering; service; ministry. “The days of his ministration.” Luke i. 23.

ministrative.c: Ministrative Min"is*tra*tive (?), a. Serving to aid; ministering.

ministress.c: Ministress Min"is*tress (?), n. [Cf. L. ministrix.] A woman who ministers. Akenside.

ministry.c: Ministry Min"is*try (?), n.; pl. Ministries (#). [L. ministerium. See Minister, n., and cf. Mystery a trade.]

ministryship.c: Ministryship Min"is*try*ship, n. The office of a minister. Swift.

minium.c: minium min"i*um (?; 277), n. [L. minium, an Iberian word, the Romans getting all their cinnabar from Spain; cf. Basque armineá.] (Chem.) A heavy, brilliant red pigment, consisting of an oxide of lead, Pb3O4, obtained by exposing lead or massicot to a gentle and continued heat in the air. It is used as a cement, as a paint, and in the manufacture of flint glass. Called also red lead, lead tetroxide, lead orthoplumbate, mineral orange, mineral red, Paris red, Saturn red, and less definitively, lead oxide.

miniver.c: Miniver Min"i*ver (?), n. [See Meniver.] A fur esteemed in the Middle Ages as a part of costume. It is uncertain whether it was the fur of one animal only or of different animals.

minivet.c: Minivet Min"i*vet (?), n. (Zool.) A singing bird of India of the family Campephagidae.

mink.c: Mink Mink (mĭṉk), n. [Cf. 2d Minx.] 1. (Zool.) A carnivorous mammal of the genus Mustela (foremrly Putorius), allied to the weasel. The European mink is Mustela lutreola. The common American mink (Mustela vison) varies from yellowish brown to black. Its fur is highly valued. Called also minx, nurik, and vison.

minnesinger.c: Minnesinger Min"ne*sing`er (?), n. [G., fr. minne love + singen to sing.] A love-singer; specifically, one of a class of German poets and musicians who flourished from about the middle of the twelfth to the middle of the fourteenth century. They were chiefly of noble birth, and made love and beauty the subjects of their verses.

minnow.c: Minnow Min"now, n. [OE. menow, cf. AS. myne; also OE. menuse, OF. menuise small fish; akin to E. minish, minute.] [Written also minow.]

mino.c: Mino bird Mi"no bird" (mī"no bẽrd). [Hind. mainā.] (Zool.) An Asiatic bird (Gracula musica), allied to the starlings. It is black, with a white spot on the wings, and a pair of flat yellow wattles on the head. It is often tamed and taught to pronounce words. It is one of the birds called mynah bird.

minor.c: minor mi"nor (mī"nẽr), a. [L., a comparative with no positive; akin to AS. min small, G. minder less, OHG. minniro, a., min, adv., Icel. minni, a., minnr, adv., Goth. minniza, a., mins, adv., Ir. & Gael. min small, tender, L. minuere to lessen, Gr. miny`qein, Skr. mi to damage. Cf. Minish, Minister, Minus, Minute.]
Minor Mi"nor (?), n. 1. A person of either sex who has not attained the age at which full civil rights are accorded; an infant; in England and the United States, one under twenty-one years of age.

minorat.c: Minorat ‖Mi`no*rat" (?), n. [G. Cf. Minor, a.] (Law) A custom or right, analogous to borough-English in England, formerly existing in various parts of Europe, and surviving in parts of Germany and Austria, by which certain entailed estates, as a homestead and adjacent land, descend to the youngest male heir.

minorate.c: Minorate Mi"nor*ate (?), v. t. [L. minoratus; p. p. of minorare to diminish, fr. minor, a. See 1st Minor.] To diminish. [R.] Sir T. Browne.

minoration.c: Minoration Mi`nor*a"tion (?), n. [L. minoratio: cf. F. minoration.] A diminution. [R.] Sir T. Browne.

minoress.c: Minoress Mi"nor*ess (?), n. See Franciscan Nuns, under Franciscan, a.

minorite.c: Minorite Mi"nor*ite (?), n. [L. minor less. Cf. 2d Minor, 3.] A Franciscan friar.

minority.c: Minority Mi*nor"i*ty (?), n.; pl. Minorities (#). [Cf. F. minorité. See Minor, a. & n.]

minos.c: Minos Mi"nos (?), prop. n. [Gr.?.] (Class. Myth.) A king and lawgiver of Crete, fabled to be the son of Jupiter and Europa. After death he was made a judge in the Lower Regions.

minotaur.c: Minotaur Min"o*taur (mĭn"o*tär), n. [L. Minotaurus, Gr. Minw`tayros; Mi`nos, the husband of Pasiphae + tay^ros a bull, the Minotaur being the offspring of Pasiphae and a bull: cf. F. minotaure.] (Class. Myth.) A fabled monster, half man and half bull, confined in the labyrinth constructed by Daedalus in Crete.

minster.c: Minster Min"ster (?), n. [AS. mynster, fr. L. monasterium. See Monastery.] (Arch.) A church of a monastery. The name is often retained and applied to the church after the monastery has ceased to exist (as Beverly Minster, Southwell Minster, etc.), and is also improperly used for any large church.

minstrel.c: Minstrel Min"strel (?), n. [OE. minstrel, menestral, OF. menestrel, fr. LL. ministerialis servant, workman (cf. ministrellus harpist), fr. L. ministerium service. See Ministry, and cf. Ministerial.] In the Middle Ages, one of an order of men who subsisted by the arts of poetry and music, and sang verses to the accompaniment of a harp or other instrument; in modern times, a poet; a bard; a singer and harper; a musician. Chaucer.

minstrelsy.c: Minstrelsy Min"strel*sy (?), n. 1. The arts and occupation of minstrels; the singing and playing of a minstrel.

mint.c: Mint Mint (mĭnt), n. [AS. minte, fr. L. mentha, Gr. mi`nqa, mi`nqh.] (Bot.) The name of several aromatic labiate plants, mostly of the genus Mentha, yielding odoriferous essential oils by distillation. See Mentha.

Mint Mint, n. [AS. mynet money, coin, fr. L. moneta the mint, coined money, fr. Moneta, a surname of Juno, in whose at Rome money was coined; akin to monere to warn, admonish, AS. manian, and to E. mind. See Mind, and cf. Money, Monition.] 1. A place where money is coined by public authority.
Mint Mint, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Minted; p. pr. & vb. n. Minting.] [AS. mynetian.]
Mint sauce Mint sauce. 1. A sauce of vinegar and sugar flavored with spearmint leaves.

mintage.c: Mintage Mint"age (?), n. 1. The coin, or other production, made in a mint.

mintman.c: Mintman Mint"man (?), n.; pl. Mintmen (?). One skilled in coining, or in coins; a coiner.

mintmaster.c: Mint-master Mint"-mas`ter (?), n. The master or superintendent of a mint. Also used figuratively.

minuend.c: minuend min"u*end (?), n. [L. minuendus to be diminished, fr. minuere to lessen, diminish. See Minish.] (Arith.) In the process of subtraction{2}, the number from which another number (the subtrahend) is to be subtracted, to find the difference.

minuet.c: Minuet Min"u*et (?), n. [F., fr. menu small, L. minutus small. So called on account of the short steps of the dance. See 4th Minute.]

minus.c: Minus Mi"nus (mī"nŭs), a. [L. See Minor, and cf. Mis- pref. from the French.] (Math.) Less; requiring to be subtracted; negative; as, a minus quantity.

minuscule.c: Minuscule Mi*nus"cule (?), n. [L. minusculus rather small, fr. minus less: cf. F. minuscule.]
minuscule minuscule adj. a. Of or relating to a minuscule{2} or of a script written in minuscules{2}; of the size and style of minuscules{2}; written in minuscules{2}; minuscular.

minutary.c: Minutary Min"u*ta*ry (?), a. Pertaining to, or consisting of, minutes. [Obs.] Fuller.

minute.c: Minute Min"ute (?; 277), n. [LL. minuta a small portion, small coin, fr. L. minutus small: cf. F. minute. See 4th Minute.]
Minute Min"ute, a. Of or pertaining to a minute or minutes; occurring at or marking successive minutes.
Minute Min"ute, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Minuted; p. pr. & vb. n. Minuting.] To set down a short sketch or note of; to jot down; to make a minute or a brief summary of.
Minute Mi*nute" (mī*nūt" or mĭ*nūt"), a. [L. minutus, p. p. of minuere to lessen. See Minish, Minor, and cf. Menu, Minuet.]

minutejack.c: Minute-jack Mi*nute"-jack` (?), n. 1. A figure which strikes the hour on the bell of some fanciful clocks; -- called also jack of the clock house.

minutely.c: Minutely Mi*nute"ly (?), adv. [From 4th Minute.] In a minute manner; with minuteness; exactly; nicely.
Minutely Min"ute*ly (?), a. [From 1st Minute.] Happening every minute; continuing; unceasing. [Obs.]
Minutely Min"ute*ly, adv. At intervals of a minute; very often and regularly. J. Philips.

minuteman.c: Minuteman Min"ute*man (?), n.; pl. Minutemen (?). A militiaman who was to be ready to march at a moment's notice; -- a term used in the American Revolution.

minuteness.c: Minuteness Mi*nute"ness (?), n. The quality of being minute.

minutia.c: Minutia ‖Mi*nu"ti*a, n.; pl. Minutiae (-ē). [L., fr. minutus small, minute. See 4th Minute.] A minute particular; a small or minor detail; -- used chiefly in the plural.

minx.c: Minx Minx (mĭṉks), n. [Prob. of Low German origin; cf. LG. minsk wench, jade, hussy, D. mensch; prop. the same word as D. & G. mensch man, human being, OHG. mennisco, AS. mennisc, fr. man. See Man.] 1. A pert or a wanton girl. Shak.
Minx Minx, n. [See Mink.] (Zool.) The mink; -- called also minx otter. [Obs.]

miny.c: Miny Min"y (mīn"y̆), a. Abounding with mines; like a mine. “Miny caverns.” Thomson.

minyan.c: Minyan Min*yan" (men*yän"), n. (Jewish Relig.) A quorum, or number necessary, for conducting public worship.

miocene.c: Miocene Mi"o*cene (mī"o*sēn), prop. a. [Gr. mei`wn less + kaino`s new, fresh, recent.] (Geol.) Of or pertaining to the middle division of the Tertiary. -- n. The Miocene period. See Chart of Geology.

miohippus.c: Miohippus ‖Mi`o*hip"pus (mī`o*hĭp"pŭs), n. [NL., fr. Gr. mei`wn less + "ippo`s horse.] (Paleon.) An extinct Miocene mammal of the Horse family, closely related to the genus Anhithecrium, and having three usable hoofs on each foot.

miquelet.c: Miquelet Miq"ue*let (mĭk"we*lĕt), n. [Sp. miquelete.] (Mil.) An irregular or partisan soldier; a bandit.

mir.c: Mir Mir (mēr), n. [Russ. mir'.] A Russian village community. D. M. Wallace.
Mir Mir, n. [Per. mīr.] Same as Emir.

mira.c: Mira ‖Mi"ra (?), n. [NL., from L. mirus wonderful.] (Astron.) A remarkable variable star in the constellation Cetus (ο Ceti).

mirabilary.c: Mirabilary Mi*rab"i*la*ry (?), n.; pl. Mirabilaries (?). One who, or a work which, narrates wonderful things; one who writes of wonders. [Obs.] Bacon.

mirabilis.c: Mirabilis ‖Mi*rab"i*lis (?), prop. n. [L., wonderful.] (Bot.) A genus of plants. See Four-o'clock.

mirabilite.c: Mirabilite Mi*rab"i*lite (?), n. (Min.) Native sodium sulphate; Glauber's salt.

mirable.c: Mirable Mi"ra*ble (?), a. [L. mirabilis, fr. mirari to wonder: cf. OF. mirable. See Marvel.] Wonderful; admirable. [Obs.] Shak.

miracle.c: Miracle Mir"a*cle (?), n. [F., fr. L. miraculum, fr. mirari to wonder. See Marvel, and cf. Mirror.]
Miracle Mir"a*cle, v. t. To make wonderful. [Obs.] Shak.

miraculize.c: Miraculize Mi*rac"u*lize (?), v. t. To cause to seem to be a miracle. [R.] Shaftesbury.

mirador.c: Mirador Mir`a*dor" (?), n. [Sp., fr. mirar to behold, view. See Mirror.] (Arch.) Same as Belvedere.

mirage.c: Mirage Mi`rage" (?), n. [F., fr. mirer to look at carefully, to aim, se mirer to look at one's self in a glass, to reflect, to be reflected, LL. mirare to look at. See Mirror.] An optical effect, sometimes seen on the ocean, but more frequently in deserts, due to total reflection of light at the surface common to two strata of air differently heated. The reflected image is seen, commonly in an inverted position, while the real object may or may not be in sight. When the surface is horizontal, and below the eye, the appearance is that of a sheet of water in which the object is seen reflected; when the reflecting surface is above the eye, the image is seen projected against the sky. The fata Morgana and looming are species of mirage.

mire.c: Mire Mire (mīr), n. [AS. mīre, mȳre; akin to D. mier, Icel. maurr, Dan. myre, Sw. myra; cf. also Ir. moirbh, Gr. my`rmhx.] An ant. [Obs.] See Pismire.
Mire Mire, n. [OE. mire, myre; akin to Icel. m?rr swamp, Sw. myra marshy ground, and perh. to E. moss.] Deep mud; wet, spongy earth. Chaucer.
Mire Mire, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Mired (mīrd); p. pr. & vb. n. Miring.]
Mire Mire, v. i. To stick in mire. Shak.

mirifical.c: Mirifical Mirific { Mi*rif"ic (?), Mi*rif"ic*al (?), } a. [L. mirificus; mirus wonderful + -ficare (in comp.) to make. See -fy.] Working wonders; wonderful.

miriness.c: Miriness Mir"i*ness (?), n. The quality of being miry.

mirk.c: Mirk Mirk (?), a. [See Murky.] Dark; gloomy; murky. Spenser. Mrs. Browning.
Mirk Mirk, n. Darkness; gloom; murk. “In mirk and mire.” Longfellow.

mirksome.c: Mirksome Mirk"some (?), a. Dark; gloomy; murky. [Archaic] Spenser. -- Mirk"some*ness, n. [Archaic]

mirky.c: Mirky Mirk"y (?), a. Dark; gloomy. See Murky.

mirliton.c: Mirliton Mir"li*ton (?), n. [F.] 1. A kind of musical toy into which one sings, hums, or speaks, producing a coarse, reedy sound. It is also called a kazoo.

mirror.c: Mirror Mir"ror (?), n. [OE. mirour, F. miroir, OF. also mireor, fr. (assumed) LL. miratorium, fr. mirare to look at, L. mirari to wonder. See Marvel, and cf. Miracle, Mirador.]
Mirror Mir"ror (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Mirrored (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Mirroring.] 1. To reflect, as in a mirror.

mirth.c: Mirth Mirth (?), n. [OE. mirthe, murthe, merthe, AS. myrð, myrgð, merhð, mirhð. See Merry.]

mirthful.c: Mirthful Mirth"ful (?), a. 1. Full of mirth or merriment; merry; as, mirthful children.

mirthless.c: Mirthless Mirth"less, a. Without mirth. -- Mirth"less*ness, n.

miry.c: Miry Mir"y (?), a. [From 2d Mire.] Abounding with deep mud; full of mire; muddy; as, a miry road.

miryachit.c: Miryachit Mir"ya*chit` (?), n. [Written also myriachit.] [Yakoot merjäk epileptic, fr. imerek jerk, rage.] (Med.) A nervous disease in which the patient involuntarily imitates the words or action of another.

mirza.c: Mirza Mir"za (?), n. [Per. mīrzā, abbrev. fr. mīrzādeh son of the prince; mīr prince (Ar. amīr, emīr) + zādeh son.] The common title of honor in Persia, prefixed to the surname of an individual. When appended to the surname, it signifies Prince.

mis.c: Mis- Mis- (mĭs-). [In words of Teutonic origin, fr. AS. mis-; akin to D. mis-, G. miss-, OHG. missa-, missi-, Icel. & Dan. mis-, Sw. miss-, Goth. missa-; orig., a p. p. from the root of G. meiden to shun, OHG. mīdan, AS. mīðan (√100. Cf. Miss to fail of). In words from the French, fr. OF. mes-, F. mé-, mes-, fr. L. minus less (see Minus). In present usage these two prefixes are commonly confounded.] A prefix used adjectively and adverbially in the sense of amiss, wrong, ill, wrongly, unsuitably; as, misdeed, mislead, mischief, miscreant.
Mis Mis (mĭs), a. & adv. [See Amiss.] Wrong; amiss. [Obs.] “To correcten that [which] is mis.” Chaucer.

misacceptation.c: Misacceptation Mis*ac`cep*ta"tion (?), n. Wrong acceptation; understanding in a wrong sense.

misaccompt.c: Misaccompt Mis`ac*compt" (?), v. t. To account or reckon wrongly. [Obs.] Chaucer.

misadjust.c: Misadjust Mis`ad*just" (?), v. t. To adjust wrongly of unsuitably; to throw out of adjustment. I. Taylor.

misadjustment.c: Misadjustment Mis`ad*just"ment (?), n. Wrong adjustment; unsuitable arrangement.

misadventure.c: Misadventure Mis`ad*ven"ture (?; 135), n. [OE. mesaventure, F. mésaventure.] Mischance; misfortune; ill luck; unlucky accident; ill adventure. Chaucer.

misadvise.c: Misadvise Mis`ad*vise" (?), v. t. To give bad counsel to.

misadvised.c: Misadvised Mis`ad*vised" (?), a. Ill advised. -- Mis`ad*vis"ed*ly (#), adv.

misaffection.c: misaffection mis`af*fec"tion (mĭs`ăf*fĕk"shŭn), n. An evil or wrong affection; the state of being ill affected. [Obs.] Bp. Hall.

misaffirm.c: misaffirm mis`af*firm" (mĭs`ăf*fẽrm"), v. t. To affirm incorrectly.

misaimed.c: misaimed mis*aimed" (mĭs*āmd"), a. Not rightly aimed. Spenser.

misallegation.c: misallegation mis*al`le*ga"tion (?), n. A erroneous statement or allegation. Bp. Hall.

misallege.c: misallege mis`al*lege" (?), v. t. To state erroneously.

misalliance.c: Misalliance Mis`al*li"ance (?), n. [F. mésalliance.] A marriage with a person of inferior rank or social station; an improper alliance; a mesalliance.

misallied.c: Misallied Mis`al*lied" (?), a. Wrongly allied or associated.

misalter.c: Misalter Mis*al"ter (?), v. t. To alter wrongly; esp., to alter for the worse. Bp. Hall.

misanthrope.c: misanthrope mis"an*thrope (mĭs"ăn*thrōp), n. [Gr. misa`nqrwpos; misei^n to hate + 'a`nqrwpos a man; cf. F. misanthrope. Cf. Miser.] A hater of mankind; a misanthropist.

misanthropical.c: Misanthropical Misanthropic { Mis`an*throp"ic (?), Mis`an*throp"ic*al (?), } a. [Cf. F. misanthropique.] Hating or disliking mankind.

misanthropos.c: Misanthropos Mis*an"thro*pos (?), n. [NL. See Misanthrope.] A misanthrope. [Obs.] Shak.

misanthropy.c: Misanthropy Mis*an"thro*py (?), n. [Gr.?: cf. F. misanthropie.] Hatred of, or dislike to, mankind; -- opposed to philanthropy. Orrery.

misapplication.c: Misapplication Mis*ap`pli*ca"tion (?), n. A wrong application. Sir T. Browne.

misapply.c: Misapply Mis`ap*ply" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Misapplied (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Misapplying.] To apply wrongly; to use for a wrong purpose; as, to misapply a name or title; to misapply public money.

misapprehend.c: Misapprehend Mis*ap`pre*hend" (?), v. t. To take in a wrong sense; to misunderstand. Locke.

misapprehension.c: Misapprehension Mis*ap`pre*hen"sion (?), n. A mistaking or mistake; wrong apprehension of one's meaning of a fact; misconception; misunderstanding.

misapprehensively.c: Misapprehensively Mis*ap`pre*hen"sive*ly (?), adv. By, or with, misapprehension.

misappropriate.c: Misappropriate Mis`ap*pro"pri*ate (?), v. t. To appropriate wrongly; to use for a wrong purpose.

misappropriation.c: Misappropriation Mis`ap*pro`pri*a"tion (?), n. Wrong appropriation; wrongful use.

misarrange.c: Misarrange Mis`ar*range" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Misarranged (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Misarranging (?).] To place in a wrong order, or improper manner.

misarcribe.c: Misarcribe Mis`ar*cribe" (?), v. t. To ascribe wrongly.

misassay.c: Misassay Mis`as*say" (?), v. t. To assay, or attempt, improperly or unsuccessfully. [Obs.] W. Browne.

misassign.c: Misassign Mis`as*sign" (?), v. t. To assign wrongly.

misattend.c: Misattend Mis`at*tend" (?), v. t. To misunderstand; to disregard. [Obs.] Milton.

misbear.c: Misbear Mis*bear" (?), v. t. To carry improperly; to carry (one's self) wrongly; to misbehave. [Obs.] Chaucer.

misbecome.c: Misbecome Mis`be*come" (?), v. t. Not to become; to suit ill; not to befit or be adapted to. Macaulay.

misbecoming.c: Misbecoming Mis`be*com"ing, a. Unbecoming. Milton. -- Mis`be*com"ing*ly, adv. -- Mis`be*com"ing*ness, n. Boyle.

misbede.c: Misbede Mis*bede" (?), v. t. [imp. Misbode (?); p. p. Misboden (?).] [AS. mis-beôdan.] To wrong; to do injury to. [Obs.]

misbegotten.c: Misbegotten Misbegot { Mis`be*got" (?), Mis`be*got"ten (?), } p. a. 1. Unlawfully or irregularly begotten; of bad or disreputable origin; pernicious. “Valor misbegot.” Shak.

misbehave.c: Misbehave Mis`be*have" (?), v. t. & i. [imp. & p. p. Misbehaved (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Misbehaving.] To behave ill; to conduct one's self improperly; -- often used with a reciprocal pronoun.

misbehaved.c: Misbehaved Mis`be*haved" (?), a. Guilty of ill behavior; illbred; rude. “A misbehaved and sullen wench.” Shak.

misbehavior.c: Misbehavior Mis`be*hav"ior (?), n. Improper, rude, or uncivil behavior; ill conduct. Addison.

misbelief.c: Misbelief Mis`be*lief" (?), n. Erroneous or false belief.

misbelieve.c: Misbelieve Mis`be*lieve" (?), v. i. To believe erroneously, or in a false religion. “That misbelieving Moor.” Shak.

misbeliever.c: Misbeliever Mis`be*liev"er (?), n. One who believes wrongly; one who holds a false religion. Shak.

misbeseem.c: Misbeseem Mis`be*seem" (?), v. t. To suit ill.

misbestow.c: Misbestow Mis`be*stow" (?), v. t. To bestow improperly.

misbestowal.c: Misbestowal Mis`be*stow"al (?), n. The act of misbestowing.

misbileve.c: Misbileve Mis`bi*leve" (?), n. Misbelief; unbelief; suspicion. [Obs.] Chaucer.

misborn.c: Misborn Mis"born` (?), a. Born to misfortune. Spenser.

miscalculate.c: Miscalculate Mis*cal"cu*late (?), v. t. & i. 1. To calculate erroneously.

miscall.c: Miscall Mis*call" (?), v. t. 1. To call by a wrong name; to name improperly.

miscarriage.c: Miscarriage Mis*car"riage (?), n. 1. Unfortunate event or issue of an undertaking; failure to attain a proper or desired result or reach a destination; as, a serious miscarriage of justice.

miscarriageable.c: Miscarriageable Mis*car"riage*a*ble (?), a. Capable of miscarrying; liable to fail. [R.] Bp. Hall.

miscarry.c: Miscarry Mis*car"ry (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Miscarried (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Miscarrying.]

miscast.c: Miscast Mis*cast" (?), v. t. To cast or reckon wrongly.
Miscast Mis*cast", n. An erroneous cast or reckoning.

miscegenation.c: Miscegenation Mis`ce*ge*na"tion (?), n. [L. miscere to mix + the root of genus race.] A mixing of races; amalgamation, as by intermarriage of black and white.

miscellanarian.c: Miscellanarian Mis`cel*la*na"ri*an (?), a. [See Miscellany.] Of or pertaining to miscellanies. Shaftesbury. -- n. A writer of miscellanies.

miscellane.c: Miscellane Mis"cel*lane (?), n. [See Miscellaneous, and cf. Maslin.] A mixture of two or more sorts of grain; -- now called maslin and meslin. Bacon.

miscellanea.c: Miscellanea ‖Mis"cel*la"ne*a (?), n. pl. [L. See Miscellany.] A collection of miscellaneous matters; matters of various kinds.

miscellaneous.c: Miscellaneous Mis`cel*la"ne*ous (?), a. [L. miscellaneus mixed, miscellaneous, fr. miscellus mixed, fr. miscere to mix. See Mix, and cf. Miscellany.] Mixed; mingled; consisting of several things; of diverse sorts; promiscuous; heterogeneous; as, a miscellaneous collection. “A miscellaneous rabble.” Milton. -- Mis`cel*la"ne*ous*ly, adv. -- Mis`cel*la"ne*ous*ness, n.

miscellanist.c: Miscellanist Mis"cel*la*nist (?), n. A writer of miscellanies; miscellanarian.

miscellany.c: Miscellany Mis"cel*la*ny (?), n.; pl. Miscellanies (#). [L. miscellanea, neut. pl. of. miscellaneus: cf. F. miscellanée, pl. miscellanées. See Miscellaneous.] A mass or mixture of various things; a medley; esp., a collection of compositions on various subjects.

miscensure.c: Miscensure Mis*cen"sure (?), v. t. To misjudge. [Obs.] Daniel. -- n. Erroneous judgment. [Obs.] Sylvester.

mischance.c: Mischance Mis*chance" (?), n. [OE. meschance, OF. mescheance.] Ill luck; ill fortune; mishap. Chaucer.
Mischance Mis*chance", v. i. To happen by mischance. Spenser.

mischaracterize.c: Mischaracterize Mis*char"ac*ter*ize (?), v. t. To characterize falsely or erroneously; to give a wrong character to.

mischarge.c: Mischarge Mis*charge" (?), v. t. To charge erroneously, as in an account. -- n. A mistake in charging.
