mischief.c: Mischief Mis"chief (mĭs"chĭf), n. [OE. meschef bad result, OF. meschief; pref. mes- (L. minus less) + chief end, head, F. chef chief. See Minus, and Chief.]
Mischief Mis"chief, v. t. To do harm to. [Obs.] Milton.

mischiefmaker.c: Mischief-maker Mis"chief-mak`er (?), n. One who makes mischief; one who excites or instigates quarrels or enmity.

mischiefmaking.c: Mischief-making Mis"chief-mak`ing, a. Causing harm; exciting enmity or quarrels. Rowe. -- n. The act or practice of making mischief, inciting quarrels, etc.

mischievous.c: Mischievous Mis"chie*vous (mĭs"che*vŭs), a. Causing mischief; harmful; hurtful; -- now often applied where the evil is done carelessly or in sport; as, a mischievous child. “Most mischievous foul sin.” Shak.

mischoose.c: Mischoose Mis*choose" (?), v. t. [imp. Mischose (?); p. p. Mischosen (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Mischoosing.] To choose wrongly. Milton.
Mischoose Mis*choose", v. i. To make a wrong choice.

mischristen.c: Mischristen Mis*chris"ten (?), v. t. To christen wrongly.

miscibility.c: Miscibility Mis`ci*bil"i*ty (?), n. [Cf. F. miscibilité.] Capability of being mixed.

miscible.c: Miscible Mis"ci*ble (?), a. [Cf. F. miscible, fr. L. miscere to mix.] Capable of being mixed; mixable. Burke.

miscite.c: Miscite Mis*cite", v. t. To cite erroneously.

miscognizant.c: Miscognizant Mis*cog"ni*zant (?), a. (Law) Not cognizant; ignorant; not knowing.

miscognize.c: Miscognize Mis*cog"nize (?), v. t. To fail to apprehend; to misunderstand. [Obs.] Holland.

miscollocation.c: Miscollocation Mis*col`lo*ca"tion (?), n. Wrong collocation. De Quincey.

miscolor.c: Miscolor Mis*col"or (?), v. t. To give a wrong color to.

miscomprehend.c: Miscomprehend Mis*com`pre*hend" (?), v. t. To get a wrong idea of or about; to misunderstand.

miscomputation.c: Miscomputation Mis*com`pu*ta"tion (?), n. Erroneous computation; false reckoning.

miscompute.c: Miscompute Mis`com*pute" (?), v. t. [Cf. Miscount.] To compute erroneously. Sir T. Browne.

misconceive.c: Misconceive Mis`con*ceive" (?), v. t. & i. [imp. & p. p. Misconceived (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Misconceiving.] To conceive wrongly; to interpret incorrectly; to receive a false notion of; to misunderstand; to misjudge; to misapprehend.

misconception.c: Misconception Mis`con*cep"tion (?), n. Erroneous conception; false opinion; wrong understanding. Harvey.

misconclusion.c: Misconclusion Mis`con*clu"sion (?), n. An erroneous inference or conclusion. Bp. Hall.

misconduct.c: Misconduct Mis*con"duct (?), n. 1. Wrong conduct; bad behavior; mismanagement. Addison.
Misconduct Mis`con*duct" (?), v. t. To conduct amiss; to mismanage. Johnson.
Misconduct Mis`con*duct", v. i. To behave amiss.

misconfident.c: Misconfident Mis*con"fi*dent (?), a. Having a mistaken confidence; wrongly trusting. [R.] Bp. Hall.

misconjecture.c: Misconjecture Mis`con*jec"ture (?; 135), n. A wrong conjecture or guess. Sir T. Browne.
Misconjecture Mis`con*jec"ture (?), v. t. & i. To conjecture wrongly.

misconsecrate.c: Misconsecrate Mis*con"se*crate (?), v. t. To consecrate amiss. “Misconsecrated flags.” Bp. Hall.

misconsequence.c: Misconsequence Mis*con"se*quence (?), n. A wrong consequence; a false deduction.

misconstruable.c: Misconstruable Mis*con"stru*a*ble (?), a. Such as can be misconstrued, as language or conduct. R. North.

misconstruct.c: Misconstruct Mis`con*struct" (?), v. t. To construct wrongly; to construe or interpret erroneously.

misconstruction.c: Misconstruction Mis`con*struc"tion (?), n. Erroneous construction; wrong interpretation. Bp. Stillingfleet.

misconstrue.c: Misconstrue Mis*con"strue (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Misconstrued (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Misconstruing.] To construe wrongly; to interpret erroneously.

miscontinuance.c: Miscontinuance Mis`con*tin"u*ance (?), n. (Law) Discontinuance; also, continuance by undue process.

miscopy.c: Miscopy Mis*copy" (?), v. t. To copy amiss.
Miscopy Mis*copy", n. A mistake in copying. North Am. Rev.

miscorrect.c: Miscorrect Mis`cor*rect" (?), v. t. To fail or err in attempting to correct. “Scaliger miscorrects his author.” Dryden.

miscounsel.c: Miscounsel Mis*coun"sel (?), v. t. To counsel or advise wrongly.

miscount.c: Miscount Mis*count" (?), v. t. & i. [Cf. OF. mesconter, F. mécompter. Cf. Miscompute.] To count erroneously.
Miscount Mis*count", n. [Cf. F. mécompte error, OF. mesconte.] 1. An erroneous counting.

miscovet.c: Miscovet Mis*cov"et (?), v. t. To covet wrongfully. [Obs.]

miscreancy.c: Miscreancy Miscreance { Mis"cre*ance (?), Mis"cre*an*cy (?), } n. [OF. mescreance, F. mécréance incredulity.] The quality of being miscreant; adherence to a false religion; false faith. [Obs.] Ayliffe.

miscreant.c: Miscreant Mis"cre*ant (?), n. [OF. mescreant, F. mécréant; pref. mes- (L. minus less) + p. pr. fr. L. credere to believe. See Creed.]
Miscreant Mis"cre*ant, a. 1. Holding a false religious faith.

miscreate.c: Miscreate Mis`cre*ate" (?), a. Miscreated; illegitimate; forged; as, miscreate titles. [Obs. or Poet.] Shak.
Miscreate Mis`cre*ate" (?), v. t. To create badly or amiss.

miscreated.c: Miscreated Mis`cre*at"ed (?), a. Formed unnaturally or illegitimately; deformed. Spenser. Milton.

miscredent.c: Miscredent Mis*cre"dent (?), n. [Pref. mis- + credent. Cf. Miscreant.] A miscreant, or believer in a false religious doctrine. [Obs.] Holinshed.

miscredulity.c: Miscredulity Mis`cre*du"li*ty (?), n. Wrong credulity or belief; misbelief. Bp. Hall.

miscue.c: Miscue Mis*cue" (?), n. 1. (Billiards) A false stroke with a billiard cue, the cue slipping from the ball struck without impelling it as desired.

misdate.c: Misdate Mis*date", v. t. [imp. & p. p. Misdated; p. pr. & vb. n. Misdating.] 1. To put a false or erroneous date on (a document). Young.

misdeal.c: Misdeal Mis*deal" (?), v. t. & i. [imp. & p. p. Misdealt (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Misdealing.] To deal or distribute wrongly, as cards; to make a wrong distribution.
Misdeal Mis*deal", n. The act of misdealing; a wrong distribution of cards to the players.

misdeed.c: Misdeed Mis*deed" (?), n. [AS. misdǣd. See Deed, n.] An evil deed; a wicked action.

misdeem.c: Misdeem Mis*deem" (?), v. t. To misjudge. [Obs.] Milton.

misdemean.c: Misdemean Mis`de*mean" (?), v. t. To behave ill; -- with a reflexive pronoun; as, to misdemean one's self.

misdemeanant.c: Misdemeanant Mis`de*mean"ant (?), n. One guilty of a misdemeanor. Sydney Smith.

misdemeanor.c: Misdemeanor Mis`de*mean"or (?), n. 1. Ill behavior; evil conduct; fault. Shak.

misdempt.c: Misdempt Mis*dempt" (?), obs. p. p. of Misdeem. Spenser.

misdepart.c: Misdepart Mis`de*part" (?), v. t. To distribute wrongly. [Obs.]

misderive.c: Misderive Mis`de*rive" (?), v. t. 1. To turn or divert improperly; to misdirect. [Obs.] Bp. Hall.

misdescribe.c: Misdescribe Mis`de*scribe" (?), v. t. To describe wrongly.

misdiet.c: Misdiet Mis*di"et, v. t. To diet improperly.

misdight.c: Misdight Mis*dight" (?), a. Arrayed, prepared, or furnished, unsuitably. [Archaic] Bp. Hall.

misdirect.c: Misdirect Mis`di*rect" (?), v. t. To give a wrong direction to; as, to misdirect a passenger, or a letter; to misdirect one's energies. Shenstone.

misdirection.c: Misdirection Mis`di*rec"tion (?), n. 1. The act of directing wrongly, or the state of being so directed.

misdisposition.c: Misdisposition Mis*dis`po*si"tion (?), n. Erroneous disposal or application. Bp. Hall.

misdistinguish.c: Misdistinguish Mis`dis*tin"guish (?), v. t. To make wrong distinctions in or concerning. Hooker.

misdivide.c: Misdivide Mis`di*vide" (?), v. t. To divide wrongly.

misdo.c: Misdo Mis*do" (mĭs*dōo"), v. t. [imp. Misdid (?); p. p. Misdone (mĭs*dŭn"); p. pr. & vb. n. Misdoing.] [AS. misdōn. See Do, v.]
Misdo Mis*do", v. i. To do wrong; to commit a fault.

misdoing.c: Misdoing Mis*do"ing, n. A wrong done; a fault or crime; an offense; as, it was my misdoing.

misdoubt.c: Misdoubt Mis*doubt" (?), v. t. & i. To be suspicious of; to have suspicion. [Obs.]

misdoubtful.c: Misdoubtful Mis*doubt"ful (?), a Misgiving; hesitating. [Obs.] “Her misdoubtful mind.” Spenser.

mise.c: Mise Mise (?), n. [F. mise a putting, setting, expense, fr. mis, mise, p. p. of mettre to put, lay, fr. LL. mittere to send.]

misease.c: Misease Mis*ease" (?), n. [OE. mesaise, OF. mesaise.] Want of ease; discomfort; misery. [Obs.] Chaucer.

miseased.c: Miseased Mis*eased" (?), a. Having discomfort or misery; troubled. [Obs.] Chaucer.

misedition.c: Misedition Mis`e*di"tion (?), n. An incorrect or spurious edition. [Obs.] Bp. Hall.

miseducate.c: Miseducate Mis*ed"u*cate (?; 135), v. t. To educate in a wrong manner.

misemploy.c: Misemploy Mis`em*ploy" (?), v. t. To employ amiss; as, to misemploy time, advantages, talents, etc.

misemployment.c: Misemployment Mis`em*ploy"ment (?), n. Wrong or mistaken employment. Johnson.

misenter.c: Misenter Mis*en"ter (?), v. t. To enter or insert wrongly, as a charge in an account.

misentreat.c: Misentreat Mis`en*treat" (?), v. t. To treat wrongfully. [Obs.] Grafton.

misentry.c: Misentry Mis*en"try (?), n. An erroneous entry or charge, as of an account.

miser.c: Miser Mi"ser (mī"zẽr), n. [L. miser wretched, miserable; cf. Gr. mi^sos hate, misei^n to hate: cf. It. & Sp. misero wretched, avaricious.]

miserable.c: Miserable Mis"er*a*ble (?), a. [F. misérable, L. miserabilis, fr. miserari to lament, pity, fr. miser wretched. See Miser.]
Miserable Mis"er*a*ble, n. A miserable person. [Obs.] Sterne.

miserableness.c: Miserableness Mis"er*a*ble*ness, n. The state or quality of being miserable.

miserably.c: Miserably Mis"er*a*bly, adv. In a miserable; unhappily; calamitously; wretchedly; meanly.

miserere.c: Miserere ‖Mis`e*re"re (?), n. [L., have mercy, fr. misereri to have mercy, fr. miser. See Miser.]

misericordia.c: Misericordia ‖Mis`e*ri*cor"di*a (?), n. [L., mercy, compassion; miser wretched + cor, cordis, heart.]

miserly.c: Miserly Mi"ser*ly (mī"zẽr*ly̆), a. [From Miser.] Like a miser; very covetous; avaricious; stingy; sordid; niggardly.

misery.c: Misery Mi"ser*y (?), n.; pl. Miseries (#). [OE. miserie, L. miseria, fr. miser wretched: cf. F. misère, OF. also, miserie.]

misesteem.c: Misesteem Mis`es*teem" (?), n. [Cf. F. mésestime.] Want of esteem; disrespect. Johnson.

misestimate.c: Misestimate Mis*es"ti*mate (?), v. t. To estimate erroneously. J. S. Mill.

misexpound.c: Misexpound Mis`ex*pound" (?), v. t. To expound erroneously.

misfaith.c: Misfaith Mis*faith" (?), n. Want of faith; distrust. “[Anger] born of your misfaith.” Tennyson.

misfall.c: Misfall Mis*fall" (?), v. t. [imp. Misfell; p. p. Misfallen (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Misfalling.] To befall, as ill luck; to happen to unluckily. [Obs.] Chaucer.

misfare.c: Misfare Mis*fare" (?), v. i. [AS. misfaran.] To fare ill. [Obs.] -- n. Misfortune. [Obs.] Spenser.

misfashion.c: Misfashion Mis*fash"ion (?), v. t. To form wrongly.

misfeasance.c: Misfeasance Mis*fea"sance (?), n. [OF. pref. mes- wrong (L. minus less) + faisance doing, fr. faire to do, L. facere. Cf. Malfeasance.] (Law) A trespass; a wrong arising from an overt act; the improper doing of an act which a person might lawfully do. Bouvier. Wharton.

misfeign.c: Misfeign Mis*feign" (?), v. i. To feign with an evil design. [Obs.] Spenser.

misfit.c: Misfit Mis*fit" (?), n. 1. The act or the state of fitting badly; as, a misfit in making a coat; a ludicrous misfit.

misform.c: Misform Mis*form" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Misformed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Misforming.] To make in an ill form. Spenser.

misfortune.c: Misfortune Mis*for"tune (?), n. Bad fortune or luck; calamity; an evil accident; disaster; mishap; mischance.
Misfortune Mis*for"tune, v. i. To happen unluckily or unfortunately; to miscarry; to fail. [Obs.] Stow.

misframe.c: Misframe Mis*frame" (?), v. t. To frame wrongly.

misget.c: Misget Mis*get" (?), v. t. To get wrongfully. [Obs.]

misgive.c: Misgive Mis*give" (?), v. t. [imp. Misgave (?); p. p. Misgiven (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Misgiving.]
Misgive Mis*give", v. i. To give out doubt and apprehension; to be fearful or irresolute. “My mind misgives.” Shak.

misgiving.c: misgiving mis*giv"ing, n. Evil premonition; doubt; distrust; a feeling of apprehension; -- used commonly in the plural. “Suspicious and misgivings.” South.

misgo.c: Misgo Mis*go" (mĭs*gō"), v. i. To go astray. Spenser.

misgovern.c: Misgovern Mis*gov"ern (?), v. t. To govern badly; as, to misgovern a country. Knolles.

misgovernance.c: Misgovernance Mis*gov"ern*ance (?), n. Misgovernment; misconduct; misbehavior. [Obs.] Chaucer. Spenser.

misgoverned.c: Misgoverned Mis*gov"erned (?), a. Ill governed, as a people; ill directed. “Rude, misgoverned hands.” Shak.

misgovernment.c: Misgovernment Mis*gov"ern*ment (?), n. Bad government; want of government. Shak.

misgraff.c: Misgraff Mis*graff" (?), v. t. To misgraft. [Obs.] Shak.

misgraft.c: Misgraft Mis*graft" (?), v. t. To graft wrongly.

misground.c: Misground Mis*ground" (?), v. t. To found erroneously. “Misgrounded conceit.” Bp. Hall.

misgrowth.c: Misgrowth Mis*growth" (?), n. Bad growth; an unnatural or abnormal growth.

misguess.c: Misguess Mis*guess" (?), v. t. & i. To guess wrongly.

misguide.c: Misguide Mis*guide" (?), v. t. To guide wrongly; to lead astray; as, to misguide the understanding.

mishandle.c: Mishandle Mis*han"dle (?), v. t. To handle ill or wrongly; to maltreat.

mishap.c: Mishap Mis*hap" (?), n. Evil accident; ill luck; misfortune; mischance. Chaucer.
Mishap Mis*hap" (?), v. i. To happen unluckily; -- used impersonally. [Obs.] “If that me mishap.” Chaucer.

mishappen.c: Mishappen Mis*hap"pen (?), v. i. To happen ill or unluckily. Spenser.

mishcup.c: Mishcup Mish*cup" (?), n. [See Scup.] (Zool.) The scup. [Local, U. S.]

mishear.c: Mishear Mis*hear" (?), v. t. & i. To hear incorrectly.

mishmash.c: Mishmash Mish"mash` (?), n. [Cf. G. mish-mash, fr. mischen to mix.] A hodgepodge or hotchpotch; a confused jumble. [Also spelled mishmosh.] Sir T. Herbert.

mishna.c: Mishna Mish"na (?), n. [NHeb. mishnāh, i. e., repetition, doubling, explanation (of the divine law), fr. Heb. shānāh to change, to repeat.] A collection or digest of Jewish traditions and explanations of Scripture, forming the text of the Talmud. [Written also Mischna.]

mishnic.c: Mishnic Mish"nic (?), a. Of or pertaining to the Mishna.

misimagination.c: Misimagination Mis`im*ag`i*na"tion (?), n. Wrong imagination; delusion. Bp. Hall.

misimprove.c: Misimprove Mis`im*prove" (?), v. t. To use for a bad purpose; to abuse; to misuse; as, to misimprove time, talents, advantages, etc. South.

misimprovement.c: Misimprovement Mis`im*prove"ment (?), n. Ill use or employment; use for a bad purpose.

misincline.c: Misincline Mis"in*cline" (?), v. t. To cause to have a wrong inclination or tendency; to affect wrongly.

misinfer.c: Misinfer Mis`in*fer" (?), v. t. To infer incorrectly.

misinform.c: Misinform Mis`in*form" (?), v. t. To give untrue information to; to inform wrongly.
Misinform Mis`in*form", v. i. To give untrue information; (with against) to calumniate. [R.] Bp. Montagu.

misinformation.c: Misinformation Mis*in`for*ma"tion (?), n. Untrue or incorrect information. Bacon.

misinformer.c: Misinformer Mis`in*form"er (?), n. One who gives untrue or incorrect information.

misinstruct.c: Misinstruct Mis`in*struct" (?), v. t. To instruct amiss.

misinstruction.c: Misinstruction Mis`in*struc"tion (?), n. Wrong or improper instruction.

misintend.c: Misintend Mis`in*tend" (?), v. t. To aim amiss. [Obs.]

misinterpret.c: Misinterpret Mis`in*ter"pret (?), v. t. To interpret erroneously; to understand or to explain in a wrong sense.

misinterpretable.c: Misinterpretable Mis`in*ter"pret*a*ble (?), a. Capable of being misinterpreted; liable to be misunderstood.

misinterpretation.c: Misinterpretation Mis`in*ter"pre*ta"tion (?), n. The act of interpreting erroneously; a mistaken interpretation.

misinterpreter.c: Misinterpreter Mis`in*ter"pret*er (?), n. One who interprets erroneously.

misjoin.c: Misjoin Mis*join" (?), v. t. To join unfitly or improperly.

misjoinder.c: Misjoinder Mis*join"der (?), n. (Law) An incorrect union of parties or of causes of action in a procedure, criminal or civil. Wharton.

misjudge.c: Misjudge Mis*judge" (?), v. t. & i. To judge erroneously or unjustly; to err in judgment; to misconstrue.

misjudgment.c: Misjudgment Mis*judg"ment (?), n. [Written also misjudgement.] A wrong or unjust judgment.

miskeep.c: Miskeep Mis*keep" (?), v. t. To keep wrongly. Chaucer.

misken.c: Misken Mis*ken" (?), v. t. Not to know. [Obs.]

miskin.c: Miskin Mis"kin (?), n. [Prob. for music + -kin.] (Mus.) A little bagpipe. [Obs.] Drayton.

miskindle.c: Miskindle Mis*kin"dle (?), v. t. To kindle amiss; to inflame to a bad purpose; to excite wrongly.

misknow.c: Misknow Mis*know" (?), v. t. To have a mistaken notion of or about. [Obs.] Bp. Hall.

mislactation.c: Mislactation Mis`lac*ta"tion (?), n. (Med.) Defective flow or vitiated condition of the milk.

mislay.c: Mislay Mis*lay" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Mislaid (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Mislaying.]

misle.c: Misle Mi"sle (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Misled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Misling (?).] [Prop. mistle, fr. mist. Cf. Mistle, Mizzle.] To rain in very fine drops, like a thick mist; to mizzle; to drizzle. [archaic]
Misle Mi"sle, n. A fine rain; a thick mist; a mizzle; a drizzle.

mislead.c: Mislead Mis*lead" (mĭs*lēd"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Misled (mĭs*lĕd"); p. pr. & vb. n. Misleading.] [AS. mislǣdan. See Mis-, and Lead to conduct.] To lead into a wrong way or path; to lead astray; to guide into error; to cause to mistake; to deceive.

misleader.c: Misleader Mis*lead"er (?), n. One who leads into error.

mislearn.c: Mislearn Mis*learn" (?), v. t. To learn wrongly.

misled.c: Misled Mis*led" (?), imp. & p. p. of Mislead.

mislight.c: Mislight Mis*light" (?), v. t. To deceive or lead astray with a false light. Herrick.

mislike.c: Mislike Mis*like" (mĭs*līk"), v. t. & i. [imp. & p. p. Misliked (mĭs*līkt"); p. pr. & vb. n. Misliking.] [AS. mislīcian to displease. See Like, v.] To dislike; to disapprove of; to have aversion to; as, to mislike a man.

mislive.c: Mislive Mis*live" (?), v. i. To live amiss.

mislodge.c: Mislodge Mis*lodge" (?), v. t. To lodge amiss. [Obs.]

misly.c: Misly Mis"ly (?), a. Raining in very small drops; drizzling. [archaic]

mismake.c: Mismake Mis*make" (mĭs*māk"), v. t. To make or form amiss; to spoil in making. “Limping possibilities of mismade human nature.” Mrs. Browning.

mismanage.c: Mismanage Mis*man"age (?), v. t. & i. To manage ill or improperly; as, to mismanage public affairs.

mismanagement.c: Mismanagement Mis*man"age*ment (?), n. Wrong or bad management; as, he failed through mismagement.

mismanager.c: Mismanager Mis*man"a*ger (?), n. One who manages ill.

mismark.c: Mismark Mis*mark" (?), v. t. To mark wrongly.

mismatch.c: Mismatch Mis*match" (?), v. t. To match unsuitably.

mismate.c: Mismate Mis*mate" (?), v. t. To mate wrongly or unsuitably; to mismatch; as, to mismate gloves or shoes; a mismated couple.

mismeasure.c: Mismeasure Mis*meas"ure (?; 135), v. t. To measure or estimate incorrectly.

mismeter.c: Mismeter Mis*me"ter (?), v. t. To give the wrong meter to, as to a line of verse. [R.] Chaucer.

misname.c: Misname Mis*name" (?), v. t. To call by the wrong name; to give a wrong or inappropriate name to.

misnomer.c: Misnomer Mis*no"mer (?), n. [OF. pref. mes- amiss, wrong (L. minus less) + F. nommer to name, L. nominare, fr. nomen name. See Name.] The misnaming of a person in a legal instrument, as in a complaint or indictment; any misnaming of a person or thing; a wrong or inapplicable name or title.

misnumber.c: Misnumber Mis*num"ber (?), v. t. To number wrongly.

misnurture.c: Misnurture Mis*nur"ture (?; 135), v. t. To nurture or train wrongly; as, to misnurture children. Bp. Hall.

misobedience.c: Misobedience Mis`o*be"di*ence (?), n. Mistaken obedience; disobedience. [Obs.] Milton.

misobserve.c: Misobserve Mis`ob*serve" (?), v. t. To observe inaccurately; to mistake in observing. Locke.

misobserver.c: Misobserver Mis`ob*serv"er (?), n. One who misobserves; one who fails to observe properly.

misogamist.c: Misogamist Mi*sog"a*mist (?), n. [Gr. misei^n to hate +? marriage.] A hater of marriage.

misogamy.c: Misogamy Mi*sog"a*my (?), n. [Cf. F. misogamie.] Hatred of marriage.

misogynist.c: Misogynist Mi*sog"y*nist (mĭ*sŏj"ĭ*nĭst), n. [Gr. misogy`nhs, misogy`naios; misei^n to hate + gynh` woman: cf. F. misogyne.] A woman hater. Contrast misandrist. Fuller.

misogynous.c: Misogynous Mi*sog"y*nous (mĭ*sŏj"ĭ*nŭs), a. Hating women; having deep-seated distrust of women; -- used of men.

misogyny.c: Misogyny Mi*sog"y*ny (mĭ*sŏj"ĭ*ny̆; 277), n. [Gr. misogyni`a: cf. F. misogynie.] Hatred of women. Contrast misandry. Johnson.

misology.c: Misology Mi*sol"o*gy (mĭ*sŏl"o*jy̆), n. [Gr. misologi`a; misei^n to hate + lo`gos discourse.] Hatred of argument or discussion; hatred of enlightenment. G. H. Lewes.

misorder.c: Misorder Mis*or"der (?), v. t. To order ill; to manage erroneously; to conduct badly. [Obs.] Shak.

misotheism.c: Misotheism Mis"o*the`ism (?), n. [Gr. misei^n to hate + qeo`s god.] Hatred of God. De Quincey.

mispaint.c: Mispaint Mis*paint" (?), v. t. To paint ill, or wrongly.

mispassion.c: Mispassion Mis*pas"sion (?), n. Wrong passion or feeling. [Obs.]

mispay.c: Mispay Mis*pay" (?), v. t. [Cf. Appay.] To dissatisfy. [Obs.]

mispend.c: Mispend Mispell Mis*pell" (?), v. t., Mis*pend" (?), v. t., etc. See Misspell, Misspend, etc.

mispense.c: Mispense Mis*pense" (?), n. See Misspense. Bp. Hall.

mispersuade.c: Mispersuade Mis`per*suade" (?), v. t. To persuade amiss.

mispersuasion.c: Mispersuasion Mis`per*sua"sion (?), n. A false persuasion; wrong notion or opinion. Dr. H. More.

mispickel.c: Mispickel Mis*pick"el (?), n. [G.] (Min.) Arsenical iron pyrites; arsenopyrite.

misplace.c: Misplace Mis*place" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Misplaced (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Misplacing (?).] 1. To put in a wrong place; to set or place on an improper or unworthy object; as, he misplaced his confidence.

misplacement.c: Misplacement Mis*place"ment (?), n. The act of misplacing, or the state of being misplaced.

misplead.c: Misplead Mis*plead" (?), v. i. To err in pleading.

mispleading.c: Mispleading Mis*plead"ing, n. (Law) An error in pleading.

mispoint.c: Mispoint Mis*point" (?), v. t. To point improperly; to punctuate wrongly.

mispraise.c: Mispraise Mis*praise" (?), v. t. To praise amiss.

misprint.c: Misprint Mis*print" (mĭs*prĭnt"), v. t. To print wrongly; to make a mistake in printing.

misprint mis"print (mĭs"prĭnt), n. A mistake in printing; a deviation from the copy; as, a book full of misprints. Misprints are sometimes noted and corrected in a list of corrigenda distributed with a book.

misprise.c: Misprise Mis*prise" (?), v. t. See Misprize. [Obs.] Shak.

Misprise Mis*prise", v. t. [OF. mesprise mistake, F. méprise, fr. mespris, masc., mesprise, fem., p. p. of mesprendre to mistake; F. méprendre; pref. mes- amiss + prendre to take, L. prehendere.] To mistake. [Obs.] Shak.

misprision.c: Misprision Mis*pri"sion (?), n. [LL. misprisio, or OF. mesprison, prop., a mistaking, but confused with OF. mespris contempt, F. mépris. See 2d Misprise, Misprize, Prison.]

misprize.c: Misprize Mis*prize" (mĭs*prīz"), v. t. [OF. mesprisier to deprise, F. mépriser; pref. amiss, wrong (L. minus less + LL. pretium price. See price, Prize, v.] To slight or undervalue.

misproceeding.c: Misproceeding Mis`pro*ceed"ing (?), n. Wrong or irregular proceding.

misprofess.c: Misprofess Mis`pro*fess" (?), v. i. To make a false profession; to make pretensions to skill which is not possessed.
Misprofess Mis`pro*fess", v. t. To make a false profession of.

mispronounce.c: Mispronounce Mis`pro*nounce" (?), v. t. & i. [imp. & p. p. Mispronounced (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Mispronouncing (?).] To pronounce incorrectly.

mispronunciation.c: Mispronunciation Mis`pro*nun`ci*a"tion (? or?), n. Wrong or improper pronunciation.

misproportion.c: Misproportion Mis`pro*por"tion (?), v. t. To give wrong or unesthetic proportions to; to join without due proportion; as, the legs were misrpoportioned to the body.

mispunctuate.c: Mispunctuate Mis*punc"tu*ate (?; 135), v. t. To punctuate wrongly or incorrectly.

misquotation.c: Misquotation Mis`quo*ta"tion (?), n. Erroneous or inaccurate quotation.

misquote.c: Misquote Mis*quote" (?), v. t. & i. To quote erroneously or incorrectly. Shak.

misraise.c: Misraise Mis*raise" (?), v. t. To raise or excite unreasonable. “Misraised fury.” Bp. Hall.

misrate.c: Misrate Mis*rate" (?), v. t. To rate erroneously.

misread.c: Misread Mis*read" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Misread (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Misreading (?).] To read amiss; to misunderstand in reading.

misreceive.c: Misreceive Mis`re*ceive" (?), v. t. To receive wrongly.

misrecite.c: Misrecite Mis`re*cite" (?), v. t. & i. To recite erroneously.

misreckon.c: Misreckon Mis*reck"on (?), v. t. & i. To reckon wrongly; to miscalculate. Swift.

misrecollect.c: Misrecollect Mis*rec`ol*lect" (?), v. t. & i. To have an erroneous remembrance of; to suppose erroneously that one recollects. Hitchcock.

misrecollection.c: Misrecollection Mis*rec`ol*lec"tion (?), n. Erroneous or inaccurate recollection.

misreform.c: Misreform Mis`re*form" (?), v. t. To reform wrongly or imperfectly.

misregard.c: Misregard Mis`re*gard" (?), n. Wrong understanding; misconstruction. [Obs.] Spenser.

misregulate.c: Misregulate Mis*reg"u*late (?), v. t. To regulate wrongly or imperfectly; to fail to regulate.

misrehearse.c: Misrehearse Mis`re*hearse" (?), v. t. To rehearse or quote incorrectly. Sir T. More.

misrelate.c: Misrelate Mis`re*late" (?), v. t. To relate inaccurately.

misrelation.c: Misrelation Mis`re*la"tion (?), n. Erroneous relation or narration. Abp. Bramhall.

misremember.c: Misremember Mis`re*mem"ber (?), v. t. & i. To mistake in remembering; not to remember correctly. Sir T. More.

misrender.c: Misrender Mis*ren"der (?), v. t. To render wrongly; to translate or recite wrongly. Boyle.

misrepeat.c: Misrepeat Mis`re*peat" (?), v. t. To repeat wrongly; to give a wrong version of. Gov. Winthrop.

misreport.c: Misreport Mis`re*port" (?), v. t. & i. To report erroneously; to give an incorrect account of. Locke.
Misreport Mis`re*port", n. An erroneous report; a false or incorrect account given. Denham. South.

misrepresent.c: Misrepresent Mis*rep`re*sent" (?), v. t. To represent incorrectly (almost always, unfavorably); to give a false or erroneous representation of, either maliciously, ignorantly, or carelessly. Swift.
Misrepresent Mis*rep`re*sent", v. i. To make an incorrect or untrue representation. Milton.

misrepresentation.c: Misrepresentation Mis*rep`re*sen*ta"tion (?), n. Untrue representation; false or incorrect statement or account; -- usually unfavorable to the thing represented; as, a misrepresentation of a person's motives. Sydney Smith.

misrepresentative.c: Misrepresentative Mis*rep`re*sent"a*tive (?), a. Tending to convey a wrong impression; misrepresenting.

misrepute.c: Misrepute Mis`re*pute" (?), v. t. To have in wrong estimation; to repute or estimate erroneously.

misrule.c: Misrule Mis*rule" (?), v. t. & i. To rule badly; to misgovern.
Misrule Mis*rule", n. 1. The act, or the result, of misruling.

miss.c: Miss Miss (mĭs), n.; pl. Misses (mĭs"sĕz). [Contr. fr. mistress.] 1. A title of courtesy prefixed to the name of a girl or a woman who has not been married. See Mistress, 5.

Miss Miss, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Missed (mĭst); p. pr. & vb. n. Missing.] [AS. missan; akin to D. & G. missen, OHG. missan, Icel. missa, Sw. mista, Dan. miste. √100. See Mis-, pref.] 1. To fail of hitting, reaching, getting, finding, seeing, hearing, etc.; as, to miss the mark one shoots at; to miss the train by being late; to miss opportunites of getting knowledge; to miss the point or meaning of something said.
Miss Miss (mĭs), v. i. 1. To fail to hit; to fly wide; to deviate from the true direction.
Miss Miss, n. 1. The act of missing; failure to hit, reach, find, obtain, etc.

missa.c: Missa ‖Mis"sa (?), n.; pl. Missae (#). [LL. See 1st Mass.] (R. C. Ch.) The service or sacrifice of the Mass.

missal.c: Missal Mis"sal (?), n. [LL. missale, liber missalis, from missa mass: cf. F. missel. See 1st Mass.] The book containing the service of the Mass for the entire year; a Mass book.
Missal Mis"sal, a. Of or pertaining to the Mass, or to a missal or Mass book. Bp. Hall.

missay.c: Missay Mis*say" (?), v. t. 1. To say wrongly.
Missay Mis*say", v. i. To speak ill. [Obs.] Spenser.

misseek.c: Misseek Mis*seek" (?), v. t. To seek for wrongly. [Obs.]

misseem.c: Misseem Mis*seem" (?), v. i. 1. To make a false appearance. [Obs.]

misseldine.c: Misseldine Mis"sel*dine (?), n. [See Mistletoe.] [Written also misselden.] The mistletoe. [Obs.] Baret.

missemblance.c: Missemblance Mis*sem"blance (?), n. False resemblance or semblance. [Obs.]

missend.c: Missend Mis*send" (?), v. t. To send amiss or incorrectly.

misserve.c: Misserve Mis*serve" (?), v. t. & i. To serve unfaithfully.

misset.c: Misset Mis*set" (mĭs*sĕt"), v. t. To set or place wrongly.

misshape.c: Misshape Mis*shape" (?), v. t. To shape ill; to give an ill or unnatural from to; to deform. “Figures monstrous and misshaped.” Pope.

misshapen.c: Misshapen Mis*shap"en (?), a. Having a bad or ugly form. “The mountains are misshapen.” Bentley.

missheathed.c: Missheathed Mis*sheathed" (?), a. Sheathed by mistake; wrongly sheathed; sheathed in a wrong place. Shak.

missificate.c: Missificate Mis*sif"i*cate (?), v. i. [LL. missa Mass + -ficare (in comp.) to make. See fy-.] To perform Mass. [Obs.] Milton.

missile.c: Missile Mis"sile (?), a. [L. missils, fr. mittere, missum, to cause to go, to send, to throw; cf. Lith. mesti to throw: cf. F. missile. Cf. Admit, Dismiss, Mass the religious service, Message, Mission.] Capable of being thrown; adapted for hurling or to be projected from the hand, or from any instrument or engine{2}, so as to strike an object at a distance.
Missile Mis"sile, n. [L. missile.] 1. A weapon thrown or projected or intended to be projected, as a lance, an arrow, or a bullet.

missing.c: Missing Miss"ing (?), a. [From Miss, v. i.] Absent from the place where it was expected to be found; lost; lacking; wanting; not present when called or looked for.

missingly.c: Missingly Miss"ing*ly, adv. With a sense of loss. [Obs.] Shak.

mission.c: Mission Mis"sion (?), n. [L. missio, fr. mittere, missum, to send: cf. F. mission. See Missile.] 1. The act of sending, or the state of being sent; a being sent or delegated by authority, with certain powers for transacting business; comission.
Mission Mis"sion (?), v. t. To send on a mission. [Mostly used in the form of the past participle.] Keats.

missionary.c: Missionary Mis"sion*ary (?), n.; pl. Missionaries (#). [Cf. F. missionnaire. See Mission, n.] One who is sent on a mission; especially, one sent to propagate religion. Swift.
Missionary Mis"sion*a*ry, a. Of or pertaining to missions; as, a missionary meeting; a missionary fund.

missioner.c: Missioner Mis"sion*er (?), n. A missionary; an envoy; one who conducts a mission. See Mission, n., 6. “Like mighty missioner you come.” Dryden.

missis.c: Missis Mis"sis (?), n. A mistress; a wife; -- so used by the illiterate. G. Eliot.

missish.c: Missish Miss"ish, a. Like a miss; prim; affected; sentimental.

missit.c: Missit Mis*sit" (?), v. t. To sit badly or imperfectly upon; to misbecome. [Obs.] Chaucer.

missive.c: Missive Mis"sive (?), a. [See Missive, n.] 1. Specially sent; intended or prepared to be sent; as, a letter missive. Ayliffe.
Missive Mis"sive, n. [F. lettre missive. See Mission, n.] 1. That which is sent; a writing containing a message.

missound.c: Missound Mis*sound" (?), v. t. To sound wrongly; to utter or pronounce incorrectly. E,Hall.

misspeak.c: Misspeak Mis*speak" (?), v. i. To err in speaking.
Misspeak Mis*speak", v. t. To utter wrongly.

misspell.c: Misspell Mis*spell" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Misspelled (?), or Misspelt (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Misspelling.] To spell incorrectly.

misspend.c: Misspend Mis*spend" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Misspent (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Misspending.] To spend amiss or for wrong purposes; to squander; to waste; as, to misspend time or money. J. Philips.

misspense.c: misspense mis*spense" (?), n. A spending improperly; a wasting. [Obs.] Barrow.

misspent.c: Misspent Mis*spent" (?), imp. & p. p. of Misspend.

misstate.c: Misstate Mis*state" (?), v. t. To state wrongly; as, to misstate a question in debate. Bp. Sanderson.

misstayed.c: Misstayed Mis*stayed" (?), a. (Naut.) Having missed stays; -- said of a ship.

misstep.c: Misstep Mis*step", n. A wrong step; an error of conduct.
Misstep Mis*step", v. i. To take a wrong step; to go astray.

missuggestion.c: Missuggestion Mis`sug*ges"tion (? or?), n. Wrong or evil suggestion. [Obs.] Bp. Hall.

misswear.c: Misswear Mis*swear" (?), v. i. To swear falsely.

missy.c: Missy Mis"sy, n. An affectionate, or contemptuous, form of miss; a young girl; a miss. -- a. Like a miss, or girl.

mist.c: mist mist (mĭst), n. [AS. mist; akin to D. & Sw. mist, Icel. mistr, G. mist dung, Goth. maíhstus, AS. mīgan to make water, Icel. mīga, Lith. migla mist, Russ. mgla, L. mingere, meiere, to make water, Gr. 'omichei^n to make water, 'omi`chlh mist, Skr. mih to make water, n., a mist mēgha cloud. √102. Cf. Misle, Mizzle, Mixen.] 1. Visible watery vapor suspended in the atmosphere, at or near the surface of the earth; fog.
Mist Mist, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Misted; p. pr. & vb. n. Misting.] To cloud; to cover with mist; to dim. Shak.
Mist Mist, v. i. To rain in very fine drops; as, it mists.

mistakable.c: Mistakable Mis*tak"a*ble (?), a. Liable to be mistaken; capable of being misconceived. Sir T. Browne.

mistake.c: Mistake Mis*take" (mĭs*tāk"), v. t. [imp. & obs. p. p. Mistook (mĭs*tŏok"); p. p. Mistaken (mĭs*tāk"'n); p. pr. & vb. n. Mistaking.] [Pref. mis- + take: cf. Icel. mistaka.] 1. To take or choose wrongly. [Obs. or R.] Shak.
Mistake Mis*take", v. i. To err in knowledge, perception, opinion, or judgment; to commit an unintentional error.
Mistake Mis*take" (mĭs*tāk"), n. 1. An apprehending wrongly; a misconception; a misunderstanding; a fault in opinion or judgment; an unintentional error of conduct.

mistaken.c: Mistaken Mis*tak"en (?), p.a. 1. Being in error; judging wrongly; having a wrong opinion or a misconception; as, a mistaken man; he is mistaken.

mistaking.c: Mistaking Mis*tak"ing, n. An error; a mistake. Shak.

mistaught.c: Mistaught Mis*taught" (mĭs*tät"), a. [See Misteach.] Wrongly taught; as, a mistaught youth. L'Estrange.

misteach.c: Misteach Mis*teach" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Mistaught (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Misteaching.] [AS. mistǣcan.] To teach wrongly; to instruct erroneously.

mistell.c: Mistell Mis*tell" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Mistold (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Mistelling.] To tell erroneously.

mistemper.c: Mistemper Mis*tem"per (?), v. t. To temper ill; to disorder; as, to mistemper one's head. Warner.

mister.c: Mister Mis"ter (?), n. [See Master, and cf. Mistress.] A title of courtesy prefixed to the name of a man or youth. It is usually written in the abbreviated form Mr.
Mister Mis"ter, v. t. To address or mention by the title Mr.; as, he mistered me in a formal way. [Colloq.]

Mister Mis"ter, n. [OF. mistier trade, office, ministry, need, F. métier trade, fr. L. ministerium service, office, ministry. See Ministry, Mystery trade.] [Written also mester.] 1. A trade, art, or occupation. [Obs.]
Mister Mis"ter, v. i. To be needful or of use. [Obs.]

misterm.c: Misterm Mis*term" (?), v. t. To call by a wrong name; to miscall.

mistery.c: Mistery Mis"ter*y (?), n. See Mystery, a trade.

mistful.c: Mistful Mist"ful (?), a. Clouded with, or as with, mist.

misthink.c: Misthink Mis*think" (?), v. i. [See Think.] To think wrongly. [Obs.] “Adam misthought of her.” Milton.
Misthink Mis*think", v. t. To have erroneous thoughts or judgment of; to think ill of. [Obs.] Shak.

misthought.c: Misthought Mis*thought" (?), n. Erroneous thought; mistaken opinion; error. [Obs.] Spenser.

misthrive.c: Misthrive Mis*thrive" (?), v. i. To thrive poorly; to be not thrifty or prosperous. [Obs.]

misthrow.c: Misthrow Mis*throw" (?), v. t. To throw wrongly.

mistico.c: Mistico Mistic { Mis"tic (?), Mis"ti*co (?), } n. [Sp. místico.] A kind of small sailing vessel used in the Mediterranean. It is rigged partly like a xebec, and partly like a felucca.

mistide.c: Mistide Mis*tide" (?), v. i. [AS. mistīdan. See Tide.] To happen or come to pass unfortunately; also, to suffer evil fortune. [Obs.]

mistigri.c: Mistigri Mistigris { ‖Mis`ti`gris" (?), ‖Mis`ti`gri" }, n. [F. mistigri.] A variety of the game of poker in which the joker is used, and called mistigris or mistigri.

mistily.c: Mistily Mist"i*ly, adv. With mist; darkly; obscurely.

mistime.c: Mistime Mis*time" (?), v. t. [AS. mistīmain to turn out ill.] To time wrongly; not to adapt to the time.

mistiness.c: Mistiness Mist"i*ness (?), n. State of being misty.

mistion.c: Mistion Mis"tion (?), n. [L. mistio, mixtio. See Mix, and cf. Mixtion.] Mixture. [Obs.]

mistitle.c: Mistitle Mis*ti"tle (?), v. t. To call by a wrong title.

mistle.c: Mistle Mis"tle (?), v. i. [Eng. mist. See Misle, and Mizzle.] To fall in very fine drops, as rain; to drizzle.

mistletoe.c: Mistletoe Mis"tle*toe (?), n. [AS. misteltān; mistel mistletoe + tān twig. AS. mistel is akin of D., G., Dan. & Sw. mistel, OHG. mistil, Icel. mistilteinn; and AS. tān to D. teen, OHG. zein, Icel. teinn, Goth. tains. Cf. Missel.] (Bot.) A parasitic evergreen plant of Europe (Viscum album), bearing a glutinous fruit. When found upon the oak, where it is rare, it was an object of superstitious regard among the Druids. A bird lime is prepared from its fruit. [Written also misletoe, misseltoe, and mistleto.] Lindley. Loudon.

mistonusk.c: Mistonusk ‖Mis"to*nusk (?), n. [From the Indian name.] (Zool.) The American badger.

mistook.c: Mistook Mis*took" (?), imp. & obs. p. p. of Mistake.

mistradition.c: Mistradition Mis`tra*di"tion (?), n. A wrong tradition. “Monsters of mistradition.” Tennyson.

mistrain.c: Mistrain Mis*train" (?), v. t. To train amiss.

mistral.c: Mistral Mis"tral (?), n. [F., fr. Provençal.] A violent and cold northwest wind experienced in the Mediterranean provinces of France, etc.

mistranslate.c: Mistranslate Mis`trans*late" (?), v. t. To translate erroneously.

mistransport.c: Mistransport Mis`trans*port" (?), v. t. To carry away or mislead wrongfully, as by passion. [Obs.] Bp. Hall.

mistreading.c: Mistreading Mis*tread"ing (?), n. Misstep; misbehavior. “To punish my mistreadings.” Shak.

mistreat.c: Mistreat Mis*treat" (?), v. t. To treat amiss; to abuse.

mistress.c: Mistress Mis"tress (?), n. [OE. maistress, OF. maistresse, F. maîtresse, LL. magistrissa, for L. magistra, fem. of magister. See Master, Mister, and cf. Miss a young woman.] 1. A woman having power, authority, or ownership; a woman who exercises authority, is chief, etc.; the female head of a family, a school, etc.
Mistress Mis"tress, v. i. To wait upon a mistress; to be courting. [Obs.] Donne.

mistressship.c: Mistressship Mis"tress*ship, n. 1. Female rule or dominion.

mistrial.c: Mistrial Mis*tri"al (?), n. (Law) A false or erroneous trial; a trial which has no result; a trial which comes to no conclusion, such as a criminal trial which does not produce a unanimous verdict of the jurors.

mistrist.c: Mistrist Mis*trist" (?), v. t. To mistrust. [Obs.] Chaucer.

mistrow.c: Mistrow Mis*trow" (?), v. i. To think wrongly. [Obs.]

mistrust.c: Mistrust Mis*trust" (?), n. Want of confidence or trust; suspicion; distrust. Milton.
Mistrust Mis*trust", v. t. 1. To regard with jealousy or suspicion; to suspect; to doubt the integrity of; to distrust.

mistrustful.c: Mistrustful Mis*trust"ful (?), a. Having or causing mistrust, suspicions, or forebodings.

mistrustingly.c: Mistrustingly Mis*trust"ing*ly, adv. With distrust or suspicion.

mistrustless.c: Mistrustless Mis*trust"less, a. Having no mistrust or suspicion.

mistune.c: Mistune Mis*tune" (?), v. t. To tune wrongly.

mistura.c: Mistura ‖Mis*tu"ra (?), n. [L. See Mixture.] (Med.) (a) A mingled compound in which different ingredients are contained in a liquid state; a mixture. See Mixture, n., 4. (b) Sometimes, a liquid medicine containing very active substances, and which can only be administered by drops. Dunglison.

misturn.c: Misturn Mis*turn" (?), v. t. To turn amiss; to pervert.

mistutor.c: Mistutor Mis*tu"tor (?), v. t. To instruct amiss.

misty.c: Misty Mist"y (mĭst"y̆), a. [Compar. Mistier (mĭst"ĭ*ẽr); superl. Mistiest.] [AS. mistig. See Mist. In some senses misty has been confused with mystic.] 1. Accompanied with mist; characterized by the presence of mist; obscured by, or overspread with, mist; as, a misty morning; misty weather; misty mountains; a misty atmosphere.

misunderstand.c: Misunderstand Mis*un`der*stand" (mĭs*ŭn`dẽr*stănd"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Misunderstood (mĭs*ŭn`dẽr*stŏod"); p. pr. & vb. n. Misunderstanding.] To misconceive; to mistake; to miscomprehend; to take in a wrong sense.

misunderstander.c: Misunderstander Mis*un`der*stand"er (mĭs*ŭn`dẽr*stănd"ẽr), n. One who misunderstands. Sir T. More.

misunderstanding.c: Misunderstanding Mis*un`der*stand"ing, n. 1. Mistake of the meaning; error; misconception. Bacon.

misurato.c: Misurato ‖Mi`su*ra"to (mē`sōo*rä"to), a. [It.] (Mus.) Measured; -- a direction to perform a passage in strict or measured time.

misusage.c: Misusage Mis*us"age (mĭs*ūz"aj), n. [Cf. F. mésusage.] Bad treatment; abuse. Spenser.

misuse.c: Misuse Mis*use" (mĭs*ūz"), v. t. [F. mésuser. See Mis-, prefix from French, and Use.] 1. To treat or use improperly; to use to a bad purpose; to misapply; as, to misuse one's talents. South.
Misuse Mis*use" (mĭs*ūs"), n. 1. Wrong use; misapplication; erroneous or improper use.

misuser.c: Misuser Mis*us"er (?), n. 1. One who misuses. “Wretched misusers of language.” Coleridge.

misvalue.c: Misvalue Mis*val"ue (?), v. t. To value wrongly or too little; to undervalue.

misvouch.c: Misvouch Mis*vouch" (?), v. t. To vouch falsely.

miswander.c: Miswander Mis*wan"der (?), v. i. To wander in a wrong path; to stray; to go astray. [Obs.] Chaucer.

misway.c: Misway Mis*way" (?), n. A wrong way. [Obs.] Chaucer.

miswear.c: Miswear Mis*wear" (?), v. t. To wear ill. [Obs.] Bacon.

miswed.c: Miswed Mis*wed" (?), v. t. To wed improperly.

misween.c: Misween Mis*ween" (?), v. i. To ween amiss; to misjudge; to distrust; to be mistaken. [Obs.] Spenser.

miswend.c: Miswend Mis*wend" (?), v. i. To go wrong; to go astray. [Obs.] “The world is miswent.” Gower.

misword.c: Misword Mis*word" (?), v. t. To word wrongly; as, to misword a message, or a sentence.
Misword Mis*word", n. A word wrongly spoken; a cross word. [Obs.] Sylvester. Breton.

misworship.c: Misworship Mis*wor"ship (?), n. Wrong or false worship; mistaken practices in religion. Bp. Hall.
Misworship Mis*wor"ship, v. t. To worship wrongly. Bp. Hall.

misworshiper.c: Misworshiper Mis*wor"ship*er (?), n. One who worships wrongly.

miswrite.c: Miswrite Mis*write" (?), v. t. To write incorrectly.

misy.c: Misy Mi"sy (?), n. [Cf. L. misy a mineral, perh. copperas, Gr.?.] (Min.) An impure yellow sulphate of iron; yellow copperas or copiapite.

misyoke.c: Misyoke Mis*yoke" (?), v. t. To yoke improperly.

mite.c: Mite Mite (mīt), n. [AS. mīte mite (in sense 1); akin to LG. mite, D. mijt, G. miete, OHG. mīza; cf. Goth. maitan to cut.] 1. (Zool.) A minute arachnid, of the order Acarina, of which there are many species; as, the dust mite, cheese mite, sugar mite, harvest mite, three-toed spider mite, etc. See Acarina.

mitre.c: Mitre Miter { Mi"ter, Mi"tre } (?), n. [F. mitre, fr. L. mitra headband, turban, Gr.?.] 1. A covering for the head, worn on solemn occasions by bishops and other church dignitaries. It has been made in many forms, the present form being a lofty cap with two points or peaks. Fairholt.
Mitre Miter { Mi"ter, Mi"tre }, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Mitered (?) or Mitred; p. pr. & vb. n. Mitering (?) or Mitring.] 1. To place a miter upon; to adorn with a miter. [wns=2] “Mitered locks.” Milton.
Mitre Miter { Mi"ter, Mi"tre }, v. i. To meet and match together, as two pieces of molding, on a line bisecting the angle of junction.

miterwort.c: Miterwort Mi"ter*wort` (?), n. (Bot.) Any plant of the genus Mitella, -- slender, perennial herbs with a pod slightly resembling a bishop's miter; bishop's cap.

mithras.c: Mithras Mithra Mi"thra, Mi"thras (?), prop. n. [L., from Gr.?.] The sun god of the ancient Persians; the god of light and truth.

mithridate.c: Mithridate Mith"ri*date (?), n. (Med.) An antidote against poison, or a composition in form of an electuary, supposed to serve either as a remedy or a preservative against poison; an alexipharmic; -- so called from King Mithridates, its reputed inventor.

mithridatic.c: Mithridatic Mith`ri*dat"ic (mĭth`rĭ*dăt"ĭk), a. Of or pertaining to King Mithridates, or to a mithridate.

mitigable.c: Mitigable Mit"i*ga*ble (?), a. Admitting of mitigation; that may be mitigated.

mitigant.c: Mitigant Mit"i*gant (?), a. [L. mitigans, p. pr. of mitigare. See Mitigate.] Tending to mitigate; mitigating; lenitive. Johnson.

mitigate.c: Mitigate Mit"i*gate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Mitigated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Mitigating.] [L. mitigatus, p. p. of mitigare to soften, mitigate; mitis mild, soft + the root of agere to do, drive.] 1. To make less severe, intense, harsh, rigorous, painful, etc.; to soften; to meliorate; to alleviate; to diminish; to lessen; as, to mitigate heat or cold; to mitigate grief.

mitigation.c: Mitigation Mit`i*ga"tion (?), n. [OE. mitigacioun, F. mitigation, fr. L. mitigatio.] The act of mitigating, or the state of being mitigated; abatement or diminution of anything painful, harsh, severe, afflictive, or calamitous; as, the mitigation of pain, grief, rigor, severity, punishment, or penalty.

mitigative.c: Mitigative Mit"i*ga*tive (?), a. [L. mitigativus: cf. F. mitigatif.] Tending to mitigate; alleviating.

mitigator.c: Mitigator Mit"i*ga`tor (?), n. One who, or that which, mitigates.

mitigatory.c: Mitigatory Mit"i*ga*to*ry (?), a. Tending to mitigate or alleviate; mitigative.

miting.c: Miting Mit"ing (?), n. [From Mite.] A little one; -- used as a term of endearment. [Obs.] Skelton.

mitis.c: Mitis casting Mi"tis cast`ing (?). [Perh. fr. L. mitis mild.] A process, invented by P. Ostberg, for producing malleable iron castings by melting wrought iron, to which from 0.05 to 0.1 per cent of aluminum is added to lower the melting point, usually in a petroleum furnace, keeping the molten metal at the bubbling point until it becomes quiet, and then pouring the molten metal into a mold lined with a special mixture consisting essentially of molasses and ground burnt fire clay; also, a casting made by this process; -- called also wrought-iron casting.
Mitis metal Mitis metal. The malleable iron produced by mitis casting; -- called also simply mitis.

mitome.c: Mitome Mi"tome (?), n. [Gr.? a thread.] (Biol.) The denser part of the protoplasm of a cell. [archaic]

mitosis.c: Mitosis ‖Mi*to"sis (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr.? a thread.] (Biol.) See Karyokinesis.

mitotic.c: Mitotic Mi*tot"ic (?), a. (Biol.) Of or pertaining to mitosis; karyokinetic; as, mitotic cell division; -- opposed to amitotic. -- Mi*tot"ic*al*ly (#), adv.

mitraille.c: Mitraille ‖Mi`traille" (?), n. [F. See Mitrailleur.] Shot or bits of iron used sometimes in loading cannon.

mitrailleur.c: Mitrailleur ‖Mi`tra`illeur" (?), n. [F.] 1. (Mil.) One who serves a mitrailleuse.

mitrailleuse.c: Mitrailleuse ‖Mi`tra`illeuse" (?), n. [F., fr. mitrailler to fire grapeshot, fr. mitraille old iron, grapeshot, dim. of OF. mite a mite.] (Mil.) A breech-loading machine gun consisting of a number of barrels fitted together, so arranged that the barrels can be fired simultaneously, or successively, and rapidly. [obsolescent]

mitral.c: Mitral Mi"tral (?), a. [Cf. F. mitral. See Miter.] Pertaining to a miter; resembling a miter; as, the mitral valve between the left auricle and left ventricle of the heart.

mitriform.c: Mitriform Mit"ri*form (?), a. [Miter + -form: cf. F. mitriforme.] Having the form of a miter, or a peaked cap; as, a mitriform calyptra. Gray.

mitt.c: Mitt Mitt (?), n. [Abbrev. fr. mitten.] 1. A mitten; also, a covering for the wrist and hand and not for the fingers, usually worn by women.

mitten.c: Mitten Mit"ten (?), n. [OE. mitaine, meteyn, F. mitaine, perh. of Celtic origin; cf. Ir. miotog, Gael. miotag, Ir. & Gael. mutan a muff, a thick glove. Cf. Mitt.] 1. A covering for the hand, worn to defend it from cold or injury. It differs from a glove in not having a separate sheath for each finger. Chaucer.

mittened.c: Mittened Mit"tened (?), a. Covered with a mitten or mittens. “Mittened hands.” Whittier.

mittent.c: Mittent Mit"tent (?), a. [L. mittens, p. pr. of mittere to send.] Sending forth; emitting. [Obs.] Wiseman.

mittimus.c: Mittimus ‖Mit"ti*mus (?), n. [L., we send, fr. mittere to send.] (Law) (a) A precept or warrant granted by a justice for committing to prison a party charged with crime; a warrant of commitment to prison. Burrill. (b) A writ for removing records from one court to another. Brande & C.

mittlers.c: Mittler's green Mit"tler's green` (?). (Chem.) A pigment of a green color, the chief constituent of which is oxide of chromium.

mitty.c: Mitty Mit"ty (?), n. The stormy petrel. [Prov. Eng.]

mitu.c: Mitu Mi"tu (mī"tu), n. [Braz. mitu poranga.] (Zool.) A South American curassow of the genus Mitua.

mity.c: Mity Mit"y (?), a. [From Mite.] Having, or abounding with, mites.

mix.c: Mix Mix (mĭks), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Mixed (mĭkst) (less properly Mixt); p. pr. & vb. n. Mixing.] [AS. miscan; akin to OHG. misken, G. mischen, Russ. mieshate, W. mysgu, Gael. measg, L. miscere, mixtum, Gr. mi`sgein, migny`nai, Skr. miçra mixed. The English word has been influenced by L. miscere, mixtum (cf. Mixture), and even the AS. miscan may have been borrowed fr. L. miscere. Cf. Admix, Mash to bruise, Meddle.] 1. To cause a promiscuous interpenetration of the parts of, as of two or more substances with each other, or of one substance with others; to unite or blend into one mass or compound, as by stirring together; to mingle; to blend; as, to mix flour and salt; to mix wines.
Mix Mix (?), v. i. 1. To become united into a compound; to be blended promiscuously together.

mixable.c: Mixable Mix"a*ble (?), a. Capable of being mixed.

mixed.c: Mixed Mixed (?), a. Formed by mixing; united; mingled; blended. See Mix, v. t. & i.

mixedly.c: Mixedly Mix"ed*ly (?), adv. In a mixed or mingled manner.

mixen.c: Mixen Mix"en (?), n. [AS. mixen, myxen, fr. meohx, meox, dung, filth; akin to E. mist. See Mist.] A compost heap; a dunghill. Chaucer. Tennyson.

mixer.c: Mixer Mix"er (?), n. 1. One who, or that which, mixes.

mixogamous.c: Mixogamous Mix*og"a*mous (?), a. [Gr.? a mixing +? marriage.] (Zool.) Pairing with several males; -- said of certain fishes of which several males accompany each female during spawning.

mixolydian.c: Mixolydian mode Mix`o*lyd"i*an mode` (?). [Gr.? a mixing + E. Lydian.] (Mus.) The seventh ecclesiastical mode, whose scale commences on G.

mixtilinear.c: Mixtilinear Mixtilineal { Mix`ti*lin"e*al (?), Mix`ti*lin"e*ar (?), } a. [L. mixtus mixed (p. p. of miscere to mix) + E. lineal, linear.] Containing, or consisting of, lines of different kinds, as straight, curved, and the like; as, a mixtilinear angle, that is, an angle contained by a straight line and a curve. [R.]

mixtion.c: Mixtion Mix"tion (?), n. [L. mixtio, mistio: cf. F. mixtion. See Mistion, Mix.] 1. Mixture. [Obs.]

mixtly.c: Mixtly Mixt"ly (?), adv. With mixture; in a mixed manner; mixedly. Bacon.

mixture.c: Mixture Mix"ture (?), n. [L. mixtura, fr. miscere, mixtum, to mix: cf. F. mixture. See Mix.] 1. The act of mixing, or the state of being mixed; as, made by a mixture of ingredients. Hooker.

mizmaze.c: Mizmaze Miz"maze` (?), n. A maze or labyrinth. [Obs.]

mizzen.c: Mizzen Miz"zen (?), a. [It. mezzana, fr. mezzano middle, fr. mezzo middle, half: cf. F. misaine foresail. See Mezzo.] (Naut.) Hindmost; nearest the stern; as, the mizzen shrouds, sails, etc.
Mizzen Miz"zen, n. (Naut.) The hindmost of the fore and aft sails of a three-masted vessel; also, the spanker.

mizzenmast.c: Mizzenmast Miz"zen*mast (?), n. (Naut.) the third mast from the bow in a vessel having three or more masts; the after and shorter mast of a yawl, ketch, or dandy.

mizzle.c: Mizzle Miz"zle (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Mizzled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Mizzling (?).] [See Misle, and cf. Mistle.] 1. To rain in very fine drops; to drizzle. Spenser.

mizzy.c: Mizzy Miz"zy (?), n. [Cf. F. moisi moldy, musty, p. p. of moisir to mold, fr. L. mucere to be moldy.] A bog or quagmire. [Obs.] Ainsworth.

mnaught.c: M'-Naught M'-Naught" (maik*nät"), v. t. (Steam Engines) To increase the power of (a single-cylinder beam engine) by adding a small high-pressure cylinder with a piston acting on the beam between the center and the flywheel end, using high-pressure steam and working as a compound engine, -- a plan introduced by M'Naught, a Scottish engineer, in 1845.

mnemonical.c: Mnemonical Mnemonic { Mne*mon"ic (ne*mŏn"ĭk), Mne*mon"ic*al (ne*mŏn"ĭ*kail), } a. [Gr. mnhmoniko`s, fr. mnh`mwn mindful, remembering, mnh`mh memory, mna^sqai to think on, remember; akin to E. mind.] Assisting in memory; helping to remember; as, a mnemonic device.

mnemonician.c: Mnemonician Mne`mo*ni"cian (?), n. One who instructs in the art of improving or using the memory.

mnemonics.c: Mnemonics Mne*mon"ics (?), n. [Gr. ta~ mnhmonika`: cf. F. mnémonique.] The art of memory; a method for improving the memory; a system of precepts and rules intended to assist the memory; artificial memory.

mnemosyne.c: Mnemosyne Mne*mos"y*ne (?), n. [L., fr. Gr. mnhmosy`nh remembrance, memory, and the goddess of memory. See Mnemonic.] (Class Myth.) The goddess of memory and the mother of the Muses.

mnemotechny.c: Mnemotechny Mne"mo*tech`ny (?), n. [Gr.? memory +? art: cf. F. mnémotechnie.] Mnemonics.

mo.c: Mo Mo (mō), a., adv., & n. [Written also moe.] [AS. mā. See More.] More; -- usually, more in number. [Obs.]

-mo -mo (?). A suffix added to the names of certain numerals or to the numerals themselves, to indicate the number of leaves made by folding a sheet of paper; as, sixteenmo or 16mo; eighteenmo or 18mo. It is taken from the Latin forms similarly used; as, duodecimo, sextodecimo, etc. A small circle, placed after the number and near its top, is often used for -mo; as, 16°, 18°, etc.

moa.c: moa mo"a (mō"ȧ), n. [Native name.] (Zool.) Any one of several very large extinct species of wingless birds belonging to Dinornis, and other related genera, of the suborder Dinornithes, found in New Zealand. They are allied to the apteryx and the ostrich. They were probably exterminated by the natives before New Zealand was discovered by Europeans. Some species were much larger than the ostrich.

moabite.c: Moabite Mo"ab*ite (?), n. One of the posterity of Moab, the son of Lot. (Gen. xix. 37.) Also used adjectively.

Moabite stone Mo"ab*ite stone (?). (Archaeol.) A block of black basalt, found at Dibon in Moab by Rev. F. A. Klein, Aug. 19, 1868, which bears an inscription of thirty-four lines, dating from the 9th century b. c., and written in the Moabite alphabet, the oldest Phoenician type of the Semitic alphabet. It records the victories of Mesha, king of Moab, esp. those over Israel (2 Kings iii. 4, 5, 27).

moabitess.c: Moabitess Mo"ab*i`tess (?), n. A female Moabite. Ruth i. 22.

moan.c: Moan Moan (mōn), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Moaned (mōnd); p. pr. & vb. n. Moaning.] [AS. mǣnan to moan, also, to mean; but in the latter sense perh. a different word. Cf. Mean to intend.] 1. To make a low prolonged sound of grief or pain, whether articulate or not; to groan softly and continuously.
Moan Moan, v. t. 1. To bewail audibly; to lament.
Moan Moan, n. [OE. mone. See Moan, v. i.] 1. A low prolonged sound, articulate or not, indicative of pain or of grief; a low groan.

moanful.c: Moanful Moan"ful (?), a. Full of moaning; expressing sorrow. -- Moan"ful*ly, adv.

moat.c: Moat Moat (?), n. [OF. mote hill, dike, bank, F. motte clod, turf: cf. Sp. & Pg. mota bank or mound of earth, It. motta clod, LL. mota, motta, a hill on which a fort is built, an eminence, a dike, Prov. G. mott bog earth heaped up; or perh. F. motte, and OF. mote, are from a LL. p. p. of L. movere to move (see Move). The name of moat, properly meaning, bank or mound, was transferred to the ditch adjoining: cf. F. dike and ditch.] (Fort.) A deep trench around the rampart of a castle or other fortified place, sometimes filled with water; a ditch.
Moat Moat, v. t. To surround with a moat. Dryden.

moate.c: Moate Moate (?), v. i. [See Mute to molt.] To void the excrement, as a bird; to mute. [Obs.]

mob.c: Mob Mob (?), n. [See Mobcap.] A mobcap. Goldsmith.
Mob Mob, v. t. To wrap up in, or cover with, a cowl. [R.]
Mob Mob, n. [L. mobile vulgus, the movable common people. See Mobile, n.] 1. The lower classes of a community; the populace, or the lowest part of it.
Mob Mob, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Mobbed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Mobbing.] To crowd about, as a mob, and attack or annoy; as, to mob a house or a person.

mobbish.c: Mobbish Mob"bish (?), a. Like a mob; tumultuous; lawless; as, a mobbish act. Bp. Kent.

mobcap.c: Mobcap Mob"cap` (?), n. [D. mop-muts; OD. mop a woman's coif + D. muts cap.] A plain cap or headdress for women or girls; especially, one tying under the chin by a very broad band, generally of the same material as the cap itself. Thackeray.

mobile.c: Mobile Mo"bile (?), a. [L. mobilis, for movibilis, fr. movere to move: cf. F. mobile. See Move.] 1. Capable of being moved; not fixed in place or condition; movable. “Fixed or else mobile.” Skelton.
Mobile Mo"bile (mō"bĭl; L. mŏb"ĭ*lē), n. [L. mobile vulgus. See Mobile, a., and cf. 3d Mob.] The mob; the populace. [Obs.] “The unthinking mobile.” South.

Mobile Mo"bile (mō"bēl`), n. a form of sculpture having several sheets or rods of a stiff material attached to each other by thin wire or twine in a balanced and artfully arranged tree configuration, with the topmost member suspended in air from a support so that the parts may move independently when set in motion by a current of air.

mobility.c: Mobility Mo*bil"i*ty (mo*bĭl"ĭ*ty̆), n. [L. mobilitas: cf. F. mobilité.] 1. The quality or state of being mobile; as, the mobility of a liquid, of an army, of the populace, of features, of a muscle. Sir T. Browne.

mobilization.c: Mobilization Mob`i*li*za"tion (?), n. [F. mobilization.] The act of mobilizing.

moble.c: Moble Mo"ble (?), v. t. [From Mob to wrap up.] To wrap the head of in a hood. [Obs.] Shak.

mobocracy.c: Mobocracy Mob*oc"ra*cy (?), n. [Mob rabble + -cracy, as in democracy.] A condition in which the lower classes of a nation control public affairs without respect to law, precedents, or vested rights.

mobocrat.c: Mobocrat Mob"o*crat (?), n. One who favors a form of government in which the unintelligent populace rules without restraint. Bayne.

mobocratic.c: Mobocratic Mob`o*crat"ic (?), a. Of, or relating to, a mobocracy.

moccasin.c: moccasin moc"ca*sin (?), n. [An Indian word. Algonquin makisin.] [Sometimes written moccason.] 1. A shoe made of deerskin, or other soft leather, the sole and upper part being one piece. It is the customary shoe worn by the American Indians.

moccasined.c: Moccasined Moc"ca*sined (?), a. Covered with, or wearing, a moccasin or moccasins. “Moccasined feet.” Harper's Mag.

mocha.c: Mocha Mo"cha (?), n. 1. A seaport town of Yemen, on the Red Sea, also spelled Mukha.

moche.c: Moche ‖Moche (?), n. [F.] A bale of raw silk.

mochila.c: Mochila ‖Mo*chi"la (?), n. [Sp.] A large leather flap which covers the saddletree. [Western U.S.]

mock.c: Mock Mock (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Mocked (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Mocking.] [F. moquer, of uncertain origin; cf. OD. mocken to mumble, G. mucken, OSw. mucka.] 1. To imitate; to mimic; esp., to mimic in sport, contempt, or derision; to deride by mimicry.
Mock Mock, v. i. To make sport in contempt or in jest; to speak in a scornful or jeering manner.
Mock Mock, n. 1. An act of ridicule or derision; a scornful or contemptuous act or speech; a sneer; a jibe; a jeer.
Mock Mock, a. Imitating reality, but not real; false; counterfeit; assumed; sham.

mockable.c: Mockable Mock"a*ble (?), a. Such as can be mocked. Shak.

mockado.c: Mockado Mock"a*do (?), n. A stuff made in imitation of velvet; -- probably the same as mock velvet. [Obs.]

mockbird.c: Mockbird Mock"bird` (?), n. (Zool.) The European sedge warbler (Acrocephalus phragmitis).

mocker.c: Mocker Mock"er (?), n. 1. One who, or that which, mocks; a scorner; a scoffer; a derider.

mocker nut mockernut mockernut, mocker nut n. 1. (Bot.), A smooth-barked North American hickory (Carya tomentosa) with 7 to 9 leaflets bearing a hard-shelled edible nut, which is far inferior to the true shagbark hickory nut.

mockery.c: Mockery Mock"er*y (?), n.; pl. Mockeries (#). [F. moquerie.] 1. The act of mocking, deriding, and exposing to contempt, by mimicry, by insincere imitation, or by a false show of earnestness; a counterfeit appearance.

mocking.c: Mocking Mock"ing, a. Imitating, esp. in derision, or so as to cause derision; mimicking; derisive.

mockingly.c: Mockingly Mock"ing*ly, adv. By way of derision; in a contemptuous or mocking manner.

mockingstock.c: Mockingstock Mock"ing*stock` (?), n. A butt of sport; an object of derision. [R.]

moco.c: Moco Mo"co (?), n. (Zool.) A South American rodent (Cavia rupestris), allied to the Guinea pig, but larger; -- called also rock cavy.

modal.c: Modal Mo"dal (?), a. [Cf. F. modal. See Mode.] 1. Of or pertaining to a mode or mood; consisting in mode or form only; relating to form; having the form without the essence or reality. Glanvill.

modalist.c: Modalist Mo"dal*ist, n. (Theol.) One who regards Father, Son, and Spirit as modes of being, and not as persons, thus denying personal distinction in the Trinity. Eadie.

modality.c: Modality Mo*dal"i*ty (?), n. [Cf. F. modalité.] 1. The quality or state of being modal.

modally.c: Modally Mo"dal*ly (?), adv. In a modal manner.

mode.c: Mode Mode (mōd), n. [L. modus a measure, due or proper measure, bound, manner, form; akin to E. mete: cf. F. mode. See Mete, and cf. Commodious, Mood in grammar, Modus.] 1. Manner of doing or being; method; form; fashion; custom; way; style; as, the mode of speaking; the mode of dressing.

model.c: Model Mod"el (?), n. [F. modèle, It. modello, fr. (assumed) L. modellus, fr. modulus a small measure, dim. of modus. See Mode, and cf. Module.] 1. A miniature representation of a thing, with the several parts in due proportion; sometimes, a facsimile of the same size; as, a 1/100 scale model of the B-52 bomber.
Model Mod"el (?), a. Suitable to be taken as a model or pattern; as, a model house; a model husband.

Model Mod"el, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Modeled (?) or Modelled; p. pr. & vb. n. Modeling or Modelling.] [Cf. F. modeler, It. modellare.] To plan or form after a pattern; to form in model; to form a model or pattern for; to shape; to mold; to fashion; as, to model a house or a government; to model an edifice according to the plan delineated.
Model Mod"el, v. i. (Fine Arts) To make a copy or a pattern; to design or imitate forms; as, to model in wax.

modeler.c: Modeler Mod"el*er (?), n. One who models; hence, a worker in plastic art. [Written also modeller.]

modeling.c: Modeling Mod"el*ing, n. (Fine Arts) The act or art of making a model from which a work of art is to be executed; the formation of a work of art from some plastic material. Also, in painting, drawing, etc., the expression or indication of solid form. [Written also modelling.]

modelize.c: Modelize Mod"el*ize (?), v. t. To model. [Obs.] B. Jonson.

modena.c: Modena ‖Mod"e*na (?), n. [From Modena, in Italy.] A certain crimsonlike color. Good.

modenese.c: Modenese Mod`e*nese" (?), a. Of or pertaining to Modena or its inhabitants. -- n. sing. & pl. A native or inhabitant of Modena; the people of Modena.

moder.c: Moder Mo"der (?), n. [OE. See Mother female parent.] 1. A mother. [Obs.] Chaucer.

moderate.c: Moderate Mod"er*ate (?), a. [L. moderatus, p. p. of moderate, moderati, to moderate, regulate, control, fr. modus measure. See Mode.] Kept within due bounds; observing reasonable limits; not excessive, extreme, violent, or rigorous; limited; restrained; as: (a) Limited in quantity; sparing; temperate; frugal; as, moderate in eating or drinking; a moderate table. (b) Limited in degree of activity, energy, or excitement; reasonable; calm; slow; as, moderate language; moderate endeavors. (c) Not extreme in opinion, in partisanship, and the like; as, a moderate Calvinist; a moderate Republican.

Moderate Mod"er*ate, n. (Eccl. Hist.) One of a party in the Church of Scotland in the 18th century, and part of the 19th, professing moderation in matters of church government, in discipline, and in doctrine.

Moderate Mod"er*ate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Moderated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Moderating.] 1. To restrain from excess of any kind; to reduce from a state of violence, intensity, or excess; to keep within bounds; to make temperate; to lessen; to allay; to repress; to temper; to qualify; as, to moderate rage, action, desires, etc.; to moderate heat or wind.
Moderate Mod"er*ate, v. i. 1. To become less violent, severe, rigorous, or intense; as, the wind has moderated.

moderately.c: Moderately Mod"er*ate*ly (?), adv. In a moderate manner or degree; to a moderate extent.

moderateness.c: Moderateness Mod"er*ate*ness, n. The quality or state of being moderate; temperateness; moderation.

moderation.c: Moderation Mod`er*a"tion (?), n. [L. moderatio: cf. F. modération.] 1. The act of moderating, or of imposing due restraint.

moderatism.c: Moderatism Mod"er*a*tism (mŏd"ẽr*a*tĭz'm), n. Moderation in doctrines or opinion, especially in politics or religion.

moderato.c: Moderato ‖Mod`e*ra"to (?), a. & adv. [It. See Moderate.] (Mus.) With a moderate degree of quickness; moderately.

moderator.c: Moderator Mod"er*a`tor (?), n. [L.: cf. F. modérateur.] 1. One who, or that which, moderates, restrains, or pacifies. Sir W. Raleigh.

moderatorship.c: Moderatorship Mod"er*a`tor*ship, n. The office of a moderator.

moderatress.c: Moderatress Mod"er*a`tress (?), n. A female moderator. Fuller.

modern.c: Modern Mod"ern (?), a. [F. moderne, L. modernus; akin to modo just now, orig. abl. of modus measure; hence, by measure, just now. See Mode.] 1. Of or pertaining to the present time, or time not long past; late; not ancient or remote in past time; of recent period; as, modern days, ages, or time; modern authors; modern fashions; modern taste; modern practice. Bacon.
Modern Mod"ern, n. A person of modern times; -- opposed to ancient. Pope.

modernism.c: Modernism Mod"ern*ism (?), n. 1. Modern practice; a thing of recent date; esp., a modern usage or mode of expression.

modernist.c: Modernist Mod"ern*ist, n. [Cf. F. moderniste.] 1. One who admires the moderns, or their ways and fashions.

modernity.c: Modernity Mo*der"ni*ty (?), n. Modernness; something modern. Walpole.

modernization.c: Modernization Mod`ern*i*za"tion (?), n. The act of rendering modern in style; the act or process of causing to conform to modern of thinking or acting.

modernize.c: Modernize Mod"ern*ize (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Modernized (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Modernizing (?).] [Cf. F. moderniser.] To render modern; to adapt to modern person or things; to cause to conform to recent or present usage or taste. Percy.

modernly.c: Modernly Mod"ern*ly, adv. In modern times. Milton.

modernness.c: Modernness Mod"ern*ness, n. The quality or state of being modern; recentness; novelty. M. Arnold.

modest.c: Modest Mod"est (?), a. [F. modeste, L. modestus, fr. modus measure. See Mode.] 1. Restraining within due limits of propriety; not forward, bold, boastful, or presumptious; rather retiring than pushing one's self forward; not obstructive; as, a modest youth; a modest man.

modestly.c: Modestly Mod"est*ly, adv. In a modest manner.

modesty.c: Modesty Mod"es*ty (?), n. [L. modestia: cf. F. modestie. See Modest.] 1. The quality or state of being modest; that lowly temper which accompanies a moderate estimate of one's own worth and importance; absence of self-assertion, arrogance, and presumption; humility respecting one's own merit.

modicity.c: Modicity Mo*dic"i*ty (?), n. [LL. modicitas; cf. F. modicité.] Moderateness; smallness; meanness. [Obs.]

modicum.c: Modicum Mod"i*cum (?), n. [L., fr. modicus moderate, fr. modus. See Mode.] A little; a small quantity; a measured supply. “Modicums of wit.” Shak.

modifiability.c: Modifiability Mod`i*fi`a*bil"i*ty (?), n. Capability of being modified; state or quality of being modifiable.

modifiable.c: Modifiable Mod"i*fi`a*ble (?), a. [From Modify.] Capable of being modified; liable to modification.

modificate.c: Modificate Mod"i*fi*cate (?), v. t. [See Modify.] To qualify. [Obs.] Bp. Pearson.

modification.c: Modification Mod`i*fi*ca"tion (?), n. [L. modificatio a measuring: cf. F. modification. See Modify.] 1. The act of modifying, or the state of being modified; a change; as, the modification of an opinion, or of a machine. Bentley.

modificative.c: Modificative Mod"i*fi*ca*tive (?), n. That which modifies or qualifies, as a word or clause.

modificatory.c: Modificatory Mod"i*fi*ca`to*ry (?), a. Tending or serving to modify; modifying. Max Müller.

modifier.c: Modifier Mod"i*fi`er (?), n. 1. One who, or that which, modifies. Hume.

modify.c: Modify Mod"i*fy (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Modified (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Modifying (?).] [F. modifier, L. modificare, modificari; modus limit + -ficare (in comp.) to make. See Mode, and -fy.] 1. To change somewhat the form or qualities of; to change a part of something while leaving most parts unchanged; to alter somewhat; as, to modify a contrivance adapted to some mechanical purpose; to modify the terms of a contract.

modillion.c: Modillion Mo*dil"lion (?), n. [F. modillon, It. modiglione. Cf. Module, n.] (Arch.) The enriched block or horizontal bracket generally found under the cornice of the Corinthian and Composite entablature, and sometimes, less ornamented, in the Ionic and other orders; -- so called because of its arrangement at regulated distances.

modiolar.c: Modiolar Mo*di"o*lar (?), a. [L. modiolus, dim. of modius the Roman corn measure.] Shaped like a bushel measure.

modiolus.c: Modiolus ‖Mo*di"o*lus (?), n.; pl. Modioli (#). [L., a small measure.] (Anat.) The central column in the osseous cochlea of the ear.

modish.c: Modish Mod"ish (?), a. According to the mode, or customary manner; conformed to the fashion; fashionable; hence, conventional; as, a modish dress; a modish feast. Dryden. “Modish forms of address.” Barrow.

modist.c: Modist Mod"ist (?), n. One who follows the fashion.

modiste.c: Modiste ‖Mo`diste" (?), n. [F. See Mode; cf. Modist.] One, esp. a woman, who makes, or deals in, articles of fashion, esp. of the fashionable dress of ladies; a dress-maker or milliner.

modius.c: Modius ‖Mo"di*us (?), n.; pl. Modii (#). [L.] (Rom. Antiq.) A dry measure, containing about a peck.

modocs.c: Modocs Mo"docs (?), n. pl.; sing. Modoc (?). (Ethnol.) A tribe of warlike Indians formerly inhabiting Northern California. They are nearly extinct.

modular.c: Modular Mod"u*lar (?), a. Of or pertaining to mode, modulation, module, or modius; as, modular arrangement; modular accent; modular measure.

modulate.c: Modulate Mod"u*late (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Modulated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Modulating (?).] [L. modulatus, p. p. of modulari to measure, to modulate, fr. modulus a small measure, meter, melody, dim. of modus. See Mode.] 1. To form, as sound, to a certain key, or to a certain portion.
Modulate Mod"u*late, v. i. (Mus.) To pass from one key into another.

modulation.c: Modulation Mod`u*la"tion (?), n. [L. modulatio: cf. F. modulation.] 1. The act of modulating, or the state of being modulated; as, the modulation of the voice.

modulator.c: Modulator Mod"u*la`tor (?), n. [L.] One who, or that which, modulates. Denham.

module.c: Module Mod"ule (?), n. [F., fr. L. modulus a small measure, dim. of modus. See Mode, and cf. Model, Modulus, Mold a matrix.] 1. A model or measure.
Module Mod"ule, v. t. [See module, n., Modulate.] To model; also, to modulate. [Obs.] Sandys. Drayton.

modulus.c: Modulus ‖Mod"u*lus (?), n.; pl. Moduli (#). [L., a small measure. See Module, n.] (Math., Mech., & Physics) A quantity or coefficient, or constant, which expresses the measure of some specified force, property, or quality, as of elasticity, strength, efficiency, etc.; a parameter.

modus.c: Modus ‖Mo"dus (?), n.; pl. Modi (#). [L. See Mode.] (Old Law) 1. The arrangement of, or mode of expressing, the terms of a contract or conveyance.
Modus operandi ‖Mo"dus op`er*an"di (?) [L.], manner of operating. Often abbreviated to MO
Modus vivendi ‖Mo"dus vi*ven"di (?). [L.] Mode, or manner, of living; hence, a temporary arrangement of affairs until disputed matters can be settled.

moe.c: Moe Moe (?), n. A wry face or mouth; a mow. [Obs.]
Moe Moe, v. i. To make faces; to mow. [Obs.]
Moe Moe, a., adv., & n. [AS. mā See More.] More. See Mo. [Obs.] “Sing no more ditties, sing no moe.” Shak.

moebles.c: Moebles Moe"bles (?), n. pl. [OE., fr. OF. moeble, mueble, movable, from L. mobilis.] Movables; furniture; -- also used in the singular (moeble). [Obs.] Chaucer.

moelline.c: Moelline Mo"el*line (?), n. [F. moelle, fr. L. medulla marrow.] An unguent for the hair.

moesogothic.c: Moesogothic Moe`so*goth"ic (?), a. Belonging to the Moesogoths, a branch of the Goths who settled in Moesia.
Moesogothic Moe`so*goth"ic, n. The language of the Moesogoths; -- also called Gothic.

moeve.c: Moeve Moeve (?), v. t. & i. To move. [Obs.] Chaucer.

moff.c: Moff Moff (?), n. A thin silk stuff made in Caucasia.

mog.c: Mog Mog (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Mogged (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Mogging.] [Etym. unknown.] To move away; to go off. [Prov. Eng. or Local, U. S.]

moggan.c: Moggan Mog"gan (?), n. A closely fitting knit sleeve; also, a legging of knitted material. [Scot.]

mogul.c: Mogul Mo*gul" (?), n. [From the Mongolian.] 1. A person of the Mongolian race.

moha.c: Moha Mo"ha (?), n. (Bot.) A kind of millet (Setaria Italica); German millet.

mohair.c: Mohair Mo"hair` (?), n. [F. moire, perh. from Ar. mukhayyar a kind of coarse camelot or haircloth; but prob. fr. L. marmoreus of marble, resembling marble. Cf. Moire, Marble.] The long silky hair or wool of the Angora goat of Asia Minor; also, a fabric made from this material, or an imitation of such fabric.

mohammedan.c: Mohammedan Mo*ham"med*an (?), a. [From Mohammed, fr. Ar. muhámmad praiseworthy, highly praised.] Of or pertaining to Mohammed, or to Islam, the religion and institutions founded by Mohammed; in the latter sense, synonymous with Islamic, the term preferred by Moslems. [Written also Mahometan, Mahomedan, Muhammadan, etc.]

Mohammedan Mo*ham"med*an, n. A follower of Mohammed, the founder of Islam (also called Islamism or Mohammedanism); an adherent of Islam; one who professes Islam; a Muslim; a Moslem; a Musselman; -- this term is used mostly by non-Moslems, and some Moslems find it offensive. [Written also Muhammadan, Mahometan, Mahomedan, etc.]

Mohammedan calendar Mo*ham"med*an cal"en*dar. The Muslim calendar, a lunar calendar reckoning from the year of the hegira (hejira), 622 a. d. Thirty of its years constitute a cycle, of which the 2d, 5th, 7th, 10th, 13th, 16th, 18th, 21st, 24th, 26th, and 29th are leap years, having 355 days; the others are common, having 354 days.
Mohammedan Era Mohammedan Era prop. n. The era in use in Moslem countries. See Mohammedan year, below.

Mohammedan year Mohammedan year prop. n. The year used by Muslims, consisting of twelve lunar months without intercalation, so that they retrograde through all the seasons in about 32½ years. The Mohammedan era begins with the year 622 a. d., the first day of the Mohammedan year 1332 being Nov. 30, 1913, according to the Gregorian calendar.

mohammedism.c: Mohammedism Mohammedanism { Mo*ham"med*an*ism, Mo*ham"med*ism } (?), prop. n. The religion, or doctrines and precepts, of Mohammed, contained in the Koran; Islamism; Islam. The term Islam is preferred by most Moslems, and some find the term Mohammedanism to be offensive, as they worship Allah, not Mohammed.

mohammedize.c: Mohammedize Mohammedanize { Mo*ham"med*an*ize, Mo*ham"med*ize } (?), prop. v. t. To make conformable to the principles, or customs and rites, of Islam. [Written also Mahometanize.]

mohawk.c: Mohawk Mo"hawk (?), prop. n. 1. (Ethnol.) One of a tribe of Indians who formed part of the Five Nations. They formerly inhabited the valley of the Mohawk River.

mohicans.c: Mohicans Mo*hi"cans (?), prop. n. pl.; sing. Mohican (?). (Ethnol.) A tribe of Lenni-Lenape Indians who formerly inhabited Western Connecticut and Eastern New York. [Written also Mohegans.]

moho.c: Moho ‖Mo"ho (?), n. [Native name.] (Zool.) A gallinule (Notornis Mantelli) formerly inhabiting New Zealand, but now supposed to be extinct. It was incapable of flight. See Notornis.

mohr.c: Mohr Mohr (?), n. (Zool.) A West African gazelle (Gazella mohr), having horns on which are eleven or twelve very prominent rings. It is one of the species which produce bezoar. [Written also mhorr.]

mohur.c: Mohur Mo"hur (?), n. [Hind., fr. Per. muhur, muhr, a gold coin, a seal, seal ring.] A British Indian gold coin, of the value of fifteen silver rupees, or $7.21 (in 1913). Malcom.

muharram.c: Muharram Mohurrum { ‖Mo*hur"rum (?), ‖Mu*har"ram (?) }, n. [Ar. muharram, prop., sacred, forbidden, n., the first month of the Mohammedan lunar year.] 1. The first month of the Mohammedan year. Whitworth.

moider.c: Moider Moi"der (?), v. i. To toil. [Prov. Eng. & Scot.]

moidore.c: Moidore Moi"dore (?), n. [Pg. moeda d'ouro, lit., coin of gold. Cf. Money, and Aureate.] A gold coin of Portugal, valued at about 27s. sterling.

moiety.c: Moiety Moi"e*ty (moi"e*ty̆), n.; pl. Moieties (moi"e*tĭz). [F. moitié, L. medietas, fr. medius middle, half. See Mid, a., and cf. Mediate, Mediety.] 1. One of two equal parts; a half; as, a moiety of an estate, of goods, or of profits; the moiety of a jury, or of a nation. Shak.

moil.c: Moil Moil (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Moiled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Moiling.] [OE. moillen to wet, OF. moillier, muillier, F. mouller, fr. (assumed) LL. molliare, fr. L. mollis soft. See Mollify.] To daub; to make dirty; to soil; to defile.
Moil Moil, v. i. [From Moil to daub; prob. from the idea of struggling through the wet.] To soil one's self with severe labor; to work with painful effort; to labor; to toil; to drudge.
Moil Moil, n. A spot; a defilement.

moile.c: Moile Moile (?), n. [F. mule a slipper.] A kind of high shoe anciently worn. [Written also moyle.]

moineau.c: Moineau ‖Moi"neau (?), n. [F.] (Fort.) A small flat bastion, raised in the middle of an overlong curtain.

moira.c: Moira ‖Moi"ra (moi"rȧ), n. [NL., fr. Gr. Moi^ra.] (Greek Myth.) The deity who assigns to every man his lot.

moire.c: Moire ‖Moire (mwär), n. [F. Cf. Mohair.] 1. Originally, a fine textile fabric made of the hair of an Asiatic goat; afterwards, any textile fabric to which a watered appearance is given in the process of calendering.
Moire ‖Moi`ré" (mwä`rā"; mō"rā), n. 1. A watered, clouded, or frosted appearance on textile fabrics or metallic surfaces.
